fix: close domain validation gaps surfaced by internal security audit (#219)

Internal audit (May 2026) surfaced two classes of bug that share
the same root cause: domain validators were applied at READ
boundaries but skipped at WRITE boundaries on several routes.

### C3 — primary `domain` on the create path

`POST /api/certificates/create`, `POST /api/web/certificates/create`,
and `POST /api/web/certificates/batch` validated whitespace and
the `http://` URL prefix on the primary `domain` body field, but
NOT the full structural format. SAN entries already went through
`validate_domain()` at the core layer
(modules/core/certificates.py:690); the primary did not.

`{"domain": "../poisoned", ...}` flowed into
`cert_output_dir = cert_dir / domain` →
`mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` and certbot was invoked with
`--config-dir`/`--work-dir`/`--logs-dir` pointing into the
attacker-chosen directory above the cert root. Worse, the malicious
domain was then persisted into `settings.json` via
`settings_manager.update`, so background `check_renewals()` would
replay it on every tick.

Fix: run `validate_domain()` immediately after the existing
whitespace/URL checks, before any side effect (scope check, cert
manager call, settings persist).

### H6 — `<domain>` path param on renew + dns-alias-check

`POST /api/certificates/<domain>/renew` and
`GET /api/certificates/<domain>/dns-alias-check` did not call
`_validate_domain_path` (other `<domain>`-bearing resources do —
DownloadCertificate, DownloadCertificateFile, CertificateDetail,
etc.). Flask's URL routing today scrubs `/` from a `<string:domain>`
slot, so traversal cannot reach the handler via the URL, but the
only line of defence was the routing layer. Once a poisoned domain
landed in `settings.json` via the C3 gap above, `check_renewals`
would replay it through `renew_certificate(domain)` unchecked.

Fix: add `_validate_domain_path` at the top of both handlers,
mirroring the pattern used by every other `<domain>`-bearing
resource.

### Tests

`tests/test_audit_domain_validation_gaps.py` (new, 14 cases):
- Parametrised: 8 invalid domain shapes (`../poisoned`,
  `../../etc/passwd`, `..`, `foo/bar`, `foo\\bar`, `foo;bar`,
  space-bearing, NUL-bearing) → 400 + `create_certificate` never
  called.
- Valid apex + wildcard accepted (200/201) + `create_certificate`
  called exactly once.
- Renew rejects traversal path → `renew_certificate` never called.
- Renew accepts valid domain → called with `force=False`.
- DNS-alias-check rejects traversal → `get_certificate_info` never
  called.
- The critical chain pin: an invalid create payload must NOT
  reach `settings_manager.update` (otherwise the malicious domain
  survives into background renewals).

Full local unit suite: 800 passed, 2 skipped, 115 deselected
(e2e/slow markers).

feat(dns): issue nested-subdomain wildcards against the parent hosted zone (#217)

* feat(dns): issue nested-subdomain wildcards against the parent hosted zone

A wildcard cert request for a nested subdomain failed when the DNS
provider only hosted the parent zone. For example: Azure DNS hosts
example.com; the user asks CertMate for example2.example.com +
*.example2.example.com. CertMate computed zone_domain by stripping
the wildcard from the cert FQDN (example2.example.com), wrote that
into azure.ini as dns_azure_zone1, and certbot-dns-azure failed
because no such zone exists in Azure.

The ACME TXT challenge _acme-challenge.example2.example.com is a
record inside the example.com zone, so certbot-dns-azure can succeed
if CertMate passes the actual hosted zone instead of the cert FQDN.
Other certbot plugins (cloudflare, route53, google, ...) self-discover
the zone for an ACME challenge by walking parent labels; Azure is the
outlier that requires explicit dns_azure_zoneN mappings.

This change adds a per-provider zone-discovery hook:

* utils.find_covering_zone(fqdn, zones) — pure longest-match helper
  with a TLD guard (zones with fewer than 2 labels are skipped). Strips
  leading "*." so wildcard FQDNs match on the bare apex.
* dns_zone_discovery.ZoneDiscovery — protocol + AzureZoneDiscovery
  adapter that lists hosted zones in the account's resource group via
  azure.mgmt.dns.DnsManagementClient (already installed transitively
  through certbot-dns-azure; no new top-level dependency).
* dns_zone_discovery.resolve_zones_for_domains — orchestrator called
  once per cert request that maps every FQDN (primary + SANs) to its
  longest covering zone, with a per-call cache so a SAN cert with N
  entries hits Azure once. Unmatched FQDN -> ValueError with the
  configured zones in the message; no zones at all -> ValueError
  pointing the operator at SP permissions / Azure setup.
* Registry _ZONE_DISCOVERY: providers absent from the map keep the
  legacy _zone_domain path (apex-derived from the cert FQDN). Only
  azure is in the registry today; adding rfc2136 or edgedns later is
  one line.

Wired into CertificateManager._dns_config_for_strategy on both the
create and renew paths. AzureStrategy.create_config_file now reads
_zone_domains (list, the new shape) when present and falls back to
_zone_domain (str, the legacy shape) when not — every existing test
that fed a single string continues to pass without changes.

37 new unit tests:

* TestFindCoveringZone — longest-match, no-match, case-insensitive,
  trailing-dot normalisation, TLD guard, label-boundary anchoring.
* TestAzureZoneDiscovery — Azure SDK mocked at DnsManagementClient
  boundary: sorted/lowercased return shape, credential argument
  forwarding, missing-creds rejection, upstream error wrapping,
  nameless-zone defence.
* TestResolveZonesForDomains — single-fqdn match, SAN spanning two
  zones (longest-first dedup), subdomain-vs-parent priority,
  per-cert cache hits exactly once across repeated calls.
* TestAzureCredentialsFileMultiZone — pins the multi-zone azure.ini
  shape end-to-end through AzureStrategy.create_config_file.
* TestAzureDnsConfigForStrategy — pins the CertificateManager bridge:
  primary + SAN -> deduplicated _zone_domains, uncovered FQDN raises,
  non-Azure providers bypass discovery entirely.

Full suite: 905 passed, 10 skipped, 0 failed.

Code-review pass on PR #217 surfaced five items. All addressed here:

fix: harden unified backup (mask secrets by default + re-validate hooks on restore) (#220)

* fix: harden unified backup (mask secrets by default + re-validate hooks on restore)

Internal security audit (May 2026) — two related findings on the
unified backup subsystem.

### C1 (CRITICAL) — backup ZIP wrote plaintext credentials

`create_unified_backup` serialised `settings.json` verbatim into the
archive. The resulting ZIP therefore contained plaintext:

- DNS provider tokens (`dns_providers.*.api_token`,
  `dns_providers.route53.secret_access_key`, every provider variant)
- Storage backend credentials (`certificate_storage.azure_keyvault.client_secret`,
  `vault_token`, `secret_access_key`, `infisical.client_secret`, …)
- `api_bearer_token`, `smtp_password`, webhook URLs with auth tokens
- OIDC `client_secret`, user password hashes

Admin-gated download, but ANY backup-file leak (errant rsync of
`data/backups/unified/`, accidental Docker image bake, ops bastion
download, misconfigured S3 sync) became a full credential dump.

### G (MEDIUM) — restore bypassed the deploy-hook safety validator

`restore_unified_backup` wrote the restored `settings.json` directly
via `safe_file_write`, with no call to `DeployManager._validate_hook`.
A `settings.json` saved under an older, more permissive validator
(or a hand-tampered backup zip) could install a hook that today's
validator rejects, and the next renewal would execute it via
`sh -c <command>`.

### Changes

- `modules/core/file_operations.py`
  - New `_mask_settings_secrets(settings_dict)` reuses the
    `_is_secret_key` predicate from PR #215 (the same one the
    masked GET on `/api/web/settings` uses) — every secret-bearing
    field becomes `SECRET_MASK_SENTINEL` before serialisation.
  - `create_unified_backup(..., include_secrets=False)` — default
    masks secrets. `include_secrets=True` is the opt-in plaintext
    path for disaster-recovery restore; the API layer audit-logs
    the opt-in.
  - Backup ZIP is now `chmod 0600` so the default umask cannot
    leave it world-readable on POSIX hosts.
  - Backup metadata records `secrets_masked: true|false` so an
    inspector can tell the modes apart from the archive alone.
  - `_revalidate_restored_deploy_hooks(settings_data)` runs the
    current `DeployManager._validate_hook` over every
    `deploy_hooks.global_hooks` entry; restore refuses if any hook
    fails. `pre_restore_backup` (created by the caller) is the
    rollback target.
  - `restore_unified_backup` deep-merges masked backups against
    the existing on-disk settings using `_strip_masked_values` +
    `_deep_merge_dict` (PR #215 pipeline) so existing secrets
    survive a masked restore. On a fresh restore the sentinel
    stays as-is and a warning is logged.

- `modules/api/resources.py`
  - `BackupCreate.post` accepts `include_secrets: bool` (default
    False) and records the opt-in in the audit log.

- `modules/web/backup_cache_routes.py`
  - `create_backup_web` mirrors the same `include_secrets` shape
    and exposes `secrets_masked` in the response.

### Tests

`tests/test_audit_backup_hardening.py` (new, 10 cases):

- Default backup masks every credential field name pattern; the
  excluded non-secrets (`default_key_type`, `default_key_size`,
  `dns_provider`, `email`, storage backend NAME) survive intact.
- Metadata records the masked-mode flag.
- Backup file mode is exactly `0o600`.
- `include_secrets=True` produces a plaintext archive; metadata
  records the opt-in.
- Restore refuses an unsafe hook command (`echo hi; cat /etc/passwd`);
  on-disk `settings.json` is never written when the gate fails.
- Restore accepts a safe hook command and writes the settings.
- Restore from a MASKED backup deep-merges: existing on-disk
  `client_secret` survives, the mask sentinel does NOT overwrite it.
- Restore from a PLAINTEXT backup overwrites: the opt-in
  disaster-recovery snapshot replaces the on-disk credentials
  (pinned as the contrast to the masked path).

* fix: log backup mode name, not the include_secrets boolean (CodeQL false positive)

The previous log line read `include_secrets={include_secrets}`. The
value is a Python boolean (True/False), not secret material. CodeQL's
`py/clear-text-logging-sensitive-data` rule still flags it because the
expression name contains "secrets".

Rename via a local `backup_mode` (`'plaintext'` or `'masked'`) and
log that instead. Same operational signal for the operator log, no
false positive. The audit-log entry's `include_secrets` / `secrets_masked`
fields are unchanged — they live in the structured audit channel,
not in the application log.

fix: client-cert API role gating + private-key download stratification (#221)

Internal security audit (May 2026), finding H1: every Resource in
`modules/api/client_certificates.py` declared

    method_decorators = [auth_manager.require_auth]

`require_auth` (modules/core/auth.py:703-718) only authenticates the
caller — it does NOT check role. A `viewer`-role API key (the safest
tier the admin hands out) could mint CA-signed mTLS identities,
revoke any identity org-wide, renew identities, batch up to 100 in
a single call, and pull private-key files. The TLS cert path
already runs `require_role('operator')` for `CreateCertificate`,
`require_role('admin')` for `CertificateDelete`, and `operator+`
gating inside `DownloadCertificate` for private-key material.

This PR brings the client-cert namespace to the same stratification:

- viewer floor on:
  - `ClientCertificateList` (list)
  - `ClientCertificateDetail` (metadata)
  - `ClientCertificateStatistics` (stats)
  - `ClientCertificateDownload` (route-level; per-file gate inside)
- operator floor on:
  - `ClientCertificateCreate` (mint identity)
  - `ClientCertificateRenew` (re-mint identity)
  - `ClientCertificateBatch` (batch mint up to 100)
  - `ClientCertificateDownload` for `file_type == 'key'` (the private
    key), mirroring `_PRIVATE_KEY_FILES` on the TLS side
- admin floor on:
  - `ClientCertificateRevoke` (destructive, parallel to TLS cert
    delete)
- public, no decorator (intentional, RFC 6960 / RFC 5280):
  - `OCSPStatus` — any relying party can query
  - `CRLDistribution` — distribution points are designed to be
    retrievable by anyone

`OCSPStatus` and `CRLDistribution` source comments now state the
RFC reasoning explicitly so future audits land them as "info,
intentional" rather than "missing decorator".

### Side-fix: HTTPException leak through broad except in download

`ClientCertificateDownload.get` wrapped its body in `except Exception:
abort(500, ...)`. Werkzeug's `abort(...)` raises `HTTPException`,
which is a subclass of `Exception`, so any 400/403/404 inside the
try block was silently rewritten to 500. The fix re-raises
`HTTPException` explicitly before the broad except. Surfaced by the
new 403 test for the per-file private-key gate but the pre-existing
400 paths benefited too.

### Scope note (H2 — deferred)

The audit also flagged H2: client-cert identifiers are orthogonal to
`allowed_domains`, so a scoped key intended for "tenant A only" can
read every other tenant's mTLS identities once authentication
passes. Fixing H2 requires extending the scope concept (today a list
of domain patterns) to cover client-cert identifier prefixes, which
is a design decision separate from the role gate. Tracked as a
follow-up; this PR closes H1 cleanly.

### Tests

`tests/test_audit_client_cert_rbac.py` (new, 16 cases):

- Viewer parametrised across create / revoke / renew / batch → 403,
  manager never invoked.
- Viewer can list / detail / stats.
- Viewer can download `crt` and `csr` (public material).
- Viewer cannot download `key` (private key, 403).
- Operator can download `key` (200).
- Operator can create / renew / batch (201).
- Operator cannot revoke (403).
- Admin can revoke (200).

fix: sanitize certbot stderr before surfacing in API error responses (#222)

Internal security audit (May 2026), finding H3: when certbot fails at
credential-parsing time, the DNS plugin echoes the offending ``.ini``
line verbatim into ``stderr``. ``CertificateManager.create_certificate``
and ``CertificateManager.renew_certificate`` wrapped that ``stderr``
into ``RuntimeError(...)`` whose ``str(e)`` flowed straight back into
the API JSON response (``modules/web/cert_routes.py:145, 202`` —
``return jsonify({'error': str(e)}), 422``). Operators reproducing a
plugin config bug therefore saw their own credentials echoed in the
422 body — and any HTTP-traffic logger / SaaS error tracker between
them and the API captured the plaintext secret along the way.

### Fix

- New ``sanitize_certbot_stderr(stderr_text)`` in
  ``modules/core/utils.py``. Two passes:
  1. Regex strips credential-bearing ``<name> = <value>`` lines and
     replaces the value with ``[REDACTED]``. The name regex anchors
     on any of ``secret|token|password|key|credential|hmac|api_bearer``
     as a substring of the field name, with digit-tolerant
     surroundings (provider names like ``route53`` carry digits in
     the middle, so a digit-free character class would have skipped
     ``dns_route53_access_key_id`` entirely — pinned by a regression
     test).
  2. Credential-config file paths (``letsencrypt/config/*.ini``) are
     replaced with the generic ``<credential file>`` marker.
- Output is capped at 4 KB; longer stderr (verbose certbot mode) is
  truncated with a marker pointing operators to the application log
  for the full unredacted trace.
- ``CertificateManager.create_certificate`` and ``renew_certificate``
  now log the raw ``stderr`` at ``logger.error`` (operator-visible in
  application logs, where the surrounding rate-limit + audit context
  already gates who reads it) and raise ``RuntimeError`` with the
  sanitised copy. The two consumers are the two places where the
  audit traced the leak.

### Tests

``tests/test_audit_certbot_stderr_sanitizer.py`` (new, 9 cases):

- Azure SP ``client_secret`` line redacted, ACME help URL preserved.
- Route53 AWS access key + secret access key redacted, plugin error
  narration ("Error 403 from Route53") preserved.
- Cloudflare api_token redacted.
- Generic ``smtp_password``, ``vault_token``, ``api_bearer_token``,
  ``dns_powerdns_api_key`` all redacted.
- Credential ``.ini`` paths (relative and absolute) replaced with
  ``<credential file>``.
- Non-secret narration (rate limit, ACME help URL) survives unredacted.
- 10 KB input is capped at 4 KB + truncation marker.
- ``None`` / ``''`` inputs return ``''``.
- Substring ``secret`` in a non-credential context (e.g. a domain
  name ``mysecretrecipe.com``) is NOT corrupted — the regex requires
  the secret name to be at column 1 of a ``name = value`` line, not
  arbitrary substrings.

fix: mask acme-dns shared secret + notifications GET response (H5 + M2) (#223)

Internal security audit (May 2026) — two masking findings sharing
the same root cause: the masking surface had no single source of
truth, so different routes (settings GET, notifications GET, backup
ZIP) drifted apart on what was treated as a secret.

### H5 — `GET /api/notifications/config` returned plaintext SMTP password

`modules/web/misc_routes.py::api_notifications_config` returned
`notifier._get_config()` verbatim. An operator-token holder reading
the endpoint received the raw `notifications` subtree including
`smtp_password` and any webhook URL with embedded auth tokens.
This bypassed the masking applied to the same subtree by
`/api/web/settings`.

### M2 — `acme-dns.username` and `acme-dns.subdomain` not masked

The masking regex `(token|secret|password|key|credential)` does not
match the ACME-DNS shared-secret fields, and `MaskedString` in
`modules/api/models.py` was only applied to `password`. Together
`username` (UUID) + `subdomain` (delegation FQDN) authorise TXT
record updates on behalf of the user's domains — both must be
masked. A generic `username` field elsewhere (notably SMTP login,
which is an email address) must NOT be touched.

### Fix

- `modules/core/settings.py`:
  - New `_PROVIDER_SPECIFIC_SECRET_FIELDS` registry — parent-key →
    field-name set. Today: `acme-dns → {username, subdomain}`.
    Future providers with similarly named shared-secret fields
    extend the registry without touching the walker.
  - New `mask_secrets_in_settings(settings_dict)` central helper.
    Two rules co-walk: generic regex (`_is_secret_key`) AND the
    provider-specific extras when the immediate parent key matches.
    Returns a deep-copied + masked structure; caller's input is
    never mutated.
- `modules/web/settings_routes.py::api_settings_get` — drop the
  local `_mask_dict` and route through the central helper. Same
  semantics for every prior case, plus the new acme-dns coverage.
- `modules/web/misc_routes.py::api_notifications_config` (GET) —
  route the response through `mask_secrets_in_settings` so
  `smtp_password` and any tokenised webhook URL are returned as
  the sentinel, matching the settings GET contract.
- `modules/core/file_operations.py::_mask_settings_secrets` —
  delegate to the central helper. Kept as an instance method for
  backwards compatibility with any caller that may have
  monkey-patched it.

### Tests

`tests/test_audit_notifications_and_acmedns_masking.py` (new, 8 cases):

- acme-dns `username` + `subdomain` + `password` all masked;
  `api_url` survives.
- SMTP `username` (under `notifications.smtp`) NOT masked — the
  rule is provider-specific, not blanket-on-name.
- Generic DNS provider tokens (Cloudflare `api_token`, Route53
  `access_key_id` + `secret_access_key`) still masked (regression
  guard for the prior contract).
- `default_key_type` / `default_key_size` / `default_elliptic_curve`
  pass through (the documented non-secret allowlist).
- Empty-string values pass through (the empty-as-preserve semantic
  lives in `_strip_masked_values` on the POST path, not in the
  masker).
- Lists are walked, and items inherit the dict-level parent
  context (so a future `acme-dns.accounts[*]` shape would still
  get the per-item masking).
- Flask integration: `GET /api/notifications/config` returns
  `smtp_password == SECRET_MASK_SENTINEL`; the plaintext value
  does not appear anywhere in the response body.

fix: settings-mutating routes preserve masked secrets (C2 + H4 + M3) (#224)

Internal security audit (May 2026): three findings, one root cause.
PR #215 added `_strip_masked_values` + `_deep_merge_dict` on the
central `/api/web/settings` POST path so a round-trip POST of the
masked GET response did not overwrite the on-disk credential with
the literal sentinel. The audit then found two OTHER mutation routes
that bypassed that pipeline.

### C2 (CRITICAL) — POST /api/storage/config

`StorageBackendConfig.post` wholesale-set the per-backend dict:

    storage['azure_keyvault'] = data.get('azure_keyvault', {})

When the UI POSTed back the masked GET, the sentinel `'********'`
rode inside that dict and the deep-merge propagated it to the leaf
— overwriting the on-disk credential. Same shape for AWS / Vault /
Infisical.

Fix: call `_strip_masked_values` BEFORE `atomic_update`, same as
the settings POST path.

### H4 (HIGH) — POST /api/notifications/config

`s['notifications'] = data` wholesale-replaced the subtree. SMTP
`smtp_password` and webhook URLs with embedded auth tokens returned
masked on GET were destroyed on the round-trip POST. Toggling a
non-secret notifications field (e.g. `enabled`) silently wiped the
SMTP password.

Fix: strip masked values and deep-merge against the existing
on-disk subtree inside the `settings_manager.update` mutator.

### M3 (MEDIUM) — `notifications` missing from `_DEEP_MERGE_SETTINGS_KEYS`

Even a future caller using `atomic_update({'notifications': ...})`
would shallow-merge and wipe siblings. Adding `notifications` to
the deep-merge registry closes the gap for any caller.

### Changes

- `modules/core/settings.py` — `_DEEP_MERGE_SETTINGS_KEYS` now
  includes `notifications`. Comment expanded to point at the audit
  reasoning.
- `modules/api/resources.py::StorageBackendConfig.post` — strip
  masked values via `_strip_masked_values` before `atomic_update`.
- `modules/web/misc_routes.py::api_notifications_config` (POST) —
  strip masked values, deep-merge against the existing on-disk
  notifications subtree inside the mutator.

### Tests

`tests/test_audit_settings_mutating_routes.py` (new, 9 cases):

- Registry: `notifications` is in `_DEEP_MERGE_SETTINGS_KEYS`;
  `certificate_storage` + `ca_providers` still present (defensive
  pin so a future refactor cannot silently drop them).
- StorageBackendConfig (HTTP integration test):
  - Round-trip with masked `client_secret` preserves on-disk value.
  - Genuine rotation (real new value) overwrites.
  - Sibling backend's secret survives a single-backend update.
- Notifications POST (handler-logic level — avoids the state
  pollution that registering the full misc_routes blueprint
  causes when paired with the CertificateManager lock tests):
  - Round-trip with masked `smtp_password` preserves on-disk.
  - Genuine rotation overwrites.
  - Empty-string secret preserves (same #215 semantic).
  - Webhook URL list-merge contract pinned (list overlay
    replaces wholesale — current behaviour; documented for any
    future list-merge improvement).

fix: scope-filter settings GET domains + check_dns_alias body scope (M4+M5) (#225)

Internal security audit (May 2026): two cross-tenant scope-bypass
findings on endpoints that already had role gating but missed the
scope check.

### M4 — `GET /api/settings` leaked the full `domains[]`

Both `modules/api/resources.py::Settings.get` (Flask-RESTX) and
`modules/web/settings_routes.py::api_settings_get` (web blueprint)
returned `settings['domains']` to any viewer-role caller. A scoped
API key (`allowed_domains` set to e.g. `['*.tenant-a.example']`)
could therefore enumerate every domain the org had ever issued a
cert for, regardless of scope. Other endpoints already filtered
correctly — `CertificateList.get` uses
`auth_manager.domain_matches_scope` per row — settings was the
outlier.

Fix: apply the same per-row filter to `settings['domains']`. The
filter is conditional on the caller having a non-None scope, so
unrestricted callers (legacy bearer tokens, local users) keep their
prior view — `domain_matches_scope(_, None)` is True by design.

### M5 — `POST /api/certificates/check-dns-alias` had no scope check

The path-style variant `CertificateDNSAliasCheck.get(domain)`
already runs `_check_domain_scope`. The body-style variant
`CheckDNSAlias.post` (operates on the JSON body) skipped the gate,
so a scoped viewer could probe `_acme-challenge` CNAME topology for
any out-of-scope domain — information disclosure: confirms which
alias targets exist, breaks the per-tenant mental model that a
scoped key is supposed to provide.

Fix: run `_check_domain_scope` on the primary `domain` AND every
SAN — if even one SAN is out of scope the whole request is
rejected, otherwise a caller could smuggle out-of-scope probes via
SAN entries on an in-scope primary.

### Changes

- `modules/api/resources.py::Settings.get` — scope-filter
  `domains` in place before the marshalled response.
- `modules/api/resources.py::CheckDNSAlias.post` —
  `_check_domain_scope` on `domain` and each entry in
  `san_domains` before invoking the manager.
- `modules/web/settings_routes.py::api_settings_get` — same
  scope-filter as the RESTX side, applied to the masked dict
  after `mask_secrets_in_settings` returns.

### Tests

`tests/test_audit_scope_filters.py` (new, 8 cases):

- Settings.get unrestricted caller sees every domain (legacy
  bearer / local user path).
- Settings.get with scope `*.tenant-a.example` sees only
  tenant-a domains.
- Defensive: the response body NEVER carries other tenants'
  domain names (no part of the JSON leaks them).
- Settings.get legacy string-form domain entries are also
  filtered correctly.
- CheckDNSAlias.post denies out-of-scope domain (403, manager
  never called).
- CheckDNSAlias.post allows in-scope domain.
- CheckDNSAlias.post denies if even ONE SAN is out of scope
  (smuggling guard).
- CheckDNSAlias.post unrestricted caller behaviour unchanged.

* fix(oidc): close email_verified gap + JIT race + audit false-positive

Independent second-pass review of PR #206 surfaced one critical
account-takeover vector and three smaller items. All addressed here.

1. Critical: account takeover via link_by_email without email_verified
   ----------------------------------------------------------------

   resolve_or_provision_user step 2 wrote oidc_subject onto an
   existing local user as soon as the IdP returned a matching email
   claim — with no check on email_verified. An attacker with a
   self-service-signup IdP could register admin@target.com, log into
   CertMate via SSO, and the link path would assign the attacker's
   oidc_subject to the local admin row. Next login: attacker is admin,
   role preserved.

   Gate: the email-match seam now requires claims['email_verified']
   to be True (or the string "true" — some IdPs serialise it that
   way per OIDC Core §5.1). Missing claim is treated as not-verified.
   New config field `require_verified_email` defaults to True; an
   operator who trusts their IdP to enforce email-ownership server-
   side can flip it off.

   Scope: the gate applies ONLY when an existing local user has a
   matching email. With no match the path falls through to JIT, where
   there is no row to take over and the verification status is
   irrelevant for safety. The subject-match seam is never gated (the
   IdP's own sub is the attestation).

   Refused links emit an `oidc_user_link_refused` audit entry naming
   the issuer + email so an operator can spot abuse attempts.

2. JIT race in resolve_or_provision_user
   ----------------------------------------------------------------

   The read-modify-write sequence (`_get_users` → mutate → `_save_users`)
   ran outside any lock. Two concurrent first-time callbacks for
   distinct subjects whose `_unique_username` candidates collided
   would both pick the same suffix and the second `_save_users` would
   overwrite the first. Silent data loss under multi-process gunicorn.

   Routed the whole sequence through `settings_manager.update(mutator)`
   which already serialises every read-mutate-write under the settings
   RLock. The mutator captures its outcome in a closure-bound dict;
   audit logging fires after update() returns so audit I/O does not
   hold the lock.

   New regression test test_oidc_jit_race_under_concurrent_callbacks
   spawns 8 threads with the same `preferred_username` and 8 distinct
   subjects; asserts every thread succeeds AND every row lands on
   disk (i.e. no silent overwrites).

3. False positive in client_secret rotation audit
   ----------------------------------------------------------------

   The detection in oidc_routes.api_oidc_settings_post fired the
   `sensitive_changed` audit on ANY non-sentinel client_secret in
   the payload — even when the admin resubmitted the same value
   already on disk. Pure SIEM noise.

   Now reads the unmasked on-disk value before update_config runs
   and only flags a rotation when raw_payload != prior_plaintext
   (in addition to the existing != SECRET_MASK_SENTINEL check).

   Test test_settings_post_resubmitting_same_plaintext_does_not_audit_rotation
   locks the no-noise behaviour.

4. Authlib pin relaxed
   ----------------------------------------------------------------

   `Authlib==1.3.2` → `Authlib>=1.3.2,<2.0.0`. Floor stays at 1.3.2
   (the version where GHSA-9c64-2c4r-vf2g was patched); ceiling at
   2.0.0 because any major bump warrants an explicit compatibility
   check. Operators can pick up future patches and minors without
   a CertMate bump.

fix(dns-alias): resolve Azure sub-delegated zones via dnspython (#243) (#250)

Azure DNS-01 alias mode against a sub-delegated validation zone (e.g.
acme-validation.example.com delegated under example.com) failed with
"Resource group … does not contain the DNS zone example.com".

Root cause: Lexicon resolves the hosted zone with tldextract by default,
which always collapses to the registered domain (example.com) — the
delegated zone (acme-validation.example.com) is never matched. The prior
fix (#246: pre-resolving / guessing the zone and passing it to Lexicon)
could not work, because Lexicon's tldextract collapses whatever domain it
receives unless resolve_zone_name is set.

Fix: set Lexicon's resolve_zone_name for Azure so it resolves the real
zone via a dnspython SOA lookup from the full alias FQDN. Removes the
ineffective _find_azure_zone fallback and the redundant pre-resolution in
_create_dns_alias_hook_config.

fix(dns-alias): v2.8.4 — resolve_zone_name via ConfigResolver for Azure sub-delegated zones (#243) (#252)

* fix(dns-alias): pass resolve_zone_name via ConfigResolver, not flat dict (#243)

The v2.8.3 hotfix set Lexicon's resolve_zone_name in the flat dict handed to
Client(), but Lexicon's LegacyDictConfigSource routes any key outside its
fixed generic-parameter list into the provider namespace. resolve_zone_name
landed at lexicon:azure:resolve_zone_name, while Client reads it at
lexicon:resolve_zone_name — so it resolved to None, the dnspython SOA lookup
never ran, and Azure sub-delegated validation zones still fell back to
tldextract. Issuance kept failing with "does not contain the DNS zone".

Build a ConfigResolver explicitly: lexicon-level keys (provider_name, domain,
resolve_zone_name) at the top level, provider credentials nested under the
provider name. This is the same namespacing LegacyDictConfigSource applies to
credentials, so it is behaviour-preserving for every provider while finally
delivering resolve_zone_name where Lexicon reads it.

The two FakeClient tests asserted against a flat dict, which is exactly why
the broken behaviour shipped twice — they now resolve through the real
ConfigResolver against lexicon:resolve_zone_name and the nested credential
keys, so a regression to the flat-dict path fails the suite.

Thanks to @jensaops for the diagnosis and proof-of-concept.

perf(certs): load settings once and single-read cert copy in create_certificate (#272)

create_certificate previously called settings_manager.load_settings() in up
to five separate conditional branches (CA default, challenge type, DNS
provider, key shape, propagation time), each re-reading settings (a flask.g
deepcopy in-request, or a real disk read for background/script callers). A
lazy-once `settings = None` initializer plus `if settings is None:` guards at
each site loads at most once and reuses the result, preserving the existing
laziness so a fully-specified HTTP-01 caller still never loads settings.

The cert copy block also read each live/ file twice (shutil.copy reads src +
writes dst, then re-opened dst to read it back into cert_files). It now reads
the source once and reuses the bytes. shutil.copy carried the source mode
across implicitly, so the rewrite calls shutil.copymode explicitly after
write_bytes -- intentional, to preserve privkey.pem's 0600 perms; a naive
write_bytes would create it world-readable (0644) under the umask, a security
regression.

Also documents why the existing-cert check must run under the per-domain lock.

fix(certs): wait briefly for the per-domain lock and return 409 when busy (#274)

create_certificate and renew_certificate acquired the per-domain lock with
acquire(blocking=False), failing instantly with a generic RuntimeError when
another operation for the same domain was in progress. That gave legitimate
CLI/automation retries no grace period, and the generic RuntimeError mapped
inconsistently (HTTP 422 on create, generic 500 on the API renew route).

Acquire with a bounded timeout instead (CERTMATE_DOMAIN_LOCK_TIMEOUT, default
5s, clamped 0-60). On timeout, raise a new DomainOperationInProgress exception.
It subclasses RuntimeError so any route still catching only RuntimeError keeps
working (degrades to its old status) rather than 500-crashing.

The four create/renew routes (web + API) now map the busy condition to HTTP
409 with machine code DOMAIN_OPERATION_IN_PROGRESS — a distinct bucket from the
422 certbot-error path and the generic 500. The API renew route does not
publish a certificate_failed event for a busy domain (busy is not a failure).

Behavior change: a "domain busy" condition previously surfaced as 422 (create)
or 500 (API renew); it is now 409.

Tests: manager-level raise + the four route 409 mappings + the timeout helper
(default/override/clamp/garbage); the lock-barrier invariant under timeout=0;
and the grace period itself with timeout > 0 (create waits for a release then
proceeds past the barrier; create blocks ~the timeout then raises; renew waits
then proceeds).

v2.11.0: certificate service layer + opt-in async issuance (#280)

* feat(certs): add CertificateService for shared create/renew orchestration

The create and renew request handling — primary-domain validation, API-key
scope enforcement, settings-driven defaults, the certbot call and the
settings.json write-back — was copied into both the flask-restx resources
(modules/api/resources.py) and the web blueprint (modules/web/cert_routes.py).
The two copies drifted, and security fixes such as the validate_domain
write-boundary gate had to be applied by hand in both places (the
create_certificate_web comment literally read "Same fix shape applied to the
API variant").

CertificateService is the single owner of that orchestration. It is
framework-agnostic (never touches flask.request): callers pass the resolved
auth context (user dict + ip_address) so a scope denial is audited here and
raised as DomainOutOfScope. Scope enforcement now raises instead of returning
an HTTP tuple, so the logic is unit-testable without a request context.

The factory wires a single instance into the manager set (cert_service). This
commit only adds the service; no adapter is migrated yet, so behavior is
unchanged.

* refactor(api): route CreateCertificate/RenewCertificate through CertificateService

CreateCertificate.post and RenewCertificate.post now parse the request, call
the shared CertificateService, and format the response — the validation,
scope, defaulting, issuance and persistence logic moves into the service. Each
resource keeps its rich error->status mapping (ValueError 400,
DomainOperationInProgress 409, RuntimeError 422, generic 500) and adds
DomainOutOfScope -> 403, replacing the inline _check_domain_scope helper that
returned the HTTP tuple. RenewCertificate keeps _validate_domain_path in the
adapter (it owns cert_dir resolution) and its 409-without-failure-event
contract.

The service is read from the manager set, with a fallback that builds one from
the managers passed in, so tests that construct the resources with a minimal
managers dict (no cert_service/events) keep working.

No external behavior change: response shapes, status codes and the
certificate_created / certificate_renewed events are preserved.

* refactor(web): route create/renew through CertificateService; drop dead shadow route

create_certificate_web and renew_certificate_web now delegate to the shared
CertificateService, matching the API layer. Two pieces of dead code go with
the migration:

- The @app.route('/api/certificates/create') binding. That exact path is owned
  by the flask-restx CreateCertificate resource, registered first in setup_api,
  so the duplicate web rule never matched. Only the /api/web/certificates/create
  alias is kept.
- The _scope_denied helper, now unused since the service enforces scope.

Behavior notes: the web create path now applies the same validation as the API
path (a strengthening — it previously validated only the primary domain), and
the settings.update audit reason is unified from "certificate_created_web" to
"certificate_created". The frontend is unaffected: it already calls the RESTX
/api/certificates/create and /api/certificates/<domain>/renew paths, which are
unchanged.

* test(certs): cover CertificateService and pin /api/certificates/create to RESTX

Unit tests for CertificateService.create/renew: happy path, invalid
domain/alias, non-list SAN, out-of-scope primary and SAN (DomainOutOfScope +
audit), missing email, missing DNS provider, HTTP-01 skipping the
DNS-provider requirement, DomainOperationInProgress passthrough, and the
idempotent add-domain mutator.

Adds a route-dedup assertion that POST /api/certificates/create resolves to the
RESTX resource (certificates_create_certificate) now that the shadowed web
binding is gone.

* feat(certs): split CertificateService into prepare/issue phases

create() and renew() are now thin compositions of a synchronous prepare_*
(validate + authorize + resolve defaults; no side effects; raises ValueError /
DomainOutOfScope) and a blocking issue_* (the certbot call + settings
persistence). The synchronous path is unchanged — create() is
issue_create(prepare_create(...)) — but the split lets async callers run the
cheap prepare_* inline (for an immediate 4xx on bad input) and defer the
expensive issue_* to a background job. No behaviour change; existing service
tests pass unmodified.

* feat(certs): add in-process IssuanceExecutor for async issuance

A bounded ThreadPoolExecutor (CERTMATE_ISSUANCE_WORKERS, default 2) plus an
in-memory, bounded job registry. submit(kind, domain, fn) runs the blocking
issuance on a pool thread — separate from the gunicorn request threads — and
tracks the job through queued -> running -> succeeded/failed, publishing the
completion event BEFORE marking the job terminal (so a poller that observes
'succeeded' is guaranteed the event has fired). Event semantics mirror the
synchronous routes: create/renew success emit certificate_created/renewed; a
real renew failure emits certificate_failed, but "domain busy"
(DomainOperationInProgress) does not.

In-memory state is acceptable because the MIT build is single-instance; a job
lost at restart is safe to re-submit thanks to the per-domain lock and
create/renew idempotency. The job wrapper pushes a Flask app context like the
scheduler's _run_manager_job.

* feat(api): opt-in async create/renew with 202 + job-poll endpoint

POST /api/certificates/create and /<domain>/renew accept an "async" flag (body
or ?async=); when set, the resource runs cert_service.prepare_* inline
(immediate 400/403/422 on bad input, scope or config) and submits the blocking
issue_* to the IssuanceExecutor, returning 202 + {job_id, status, status_url}.
A new GET /api/certificates/jobs/<job_id> (operator role + domain scope) polls
the job. Without the flag the path is unchanged (201/200 + result), so existing
clients and the E2E lifecycle keep working.

This moves the up-to-30-minute certbot call off the gunicorn request threads so
a burst of concurrent create/renew requests can no longer starve SSE, the
dashboard or /health on the single-instance deployment.

factory wires a single IssuanceExecutor into the manager set and registers the
jobs route.

* test(certs): cover async issuance executor, adapters, and E2E

Unit: IssuanceExecutor lifecycle (success/failure, result sanitisation,
completion-event mapping including renew-busy emitting no failure event),
parallel distinct-domain execution, and bounded-registry eviction; the RESTX
async branch (202 + job id, certbot not run on the request thread, bad
input/scope rejected synchronously before enqueue) and the jobs endpoint
(200/404/403).

E2E (real Cloudflare/LE, random subdomains, opt-in): async create polls to
succeeded and the cert exists; plus the non-starvation proof — while several
issuances run on the executor, /health stays responsive (< 2s), confirming
certbot is off the request threads.

* test(e2e): make the HTTP client resilient to gunicorn keep-alive drops

The async-issuance E2E polls the job endpoint every ~2s on a persistent
requests.Session. gunicorn closes idle keep-alive connections after ~2s, so the
next poll reused a just-closed socket and raised RemoteDisconnected — a
client-side race, not a server fault. A real-Cloudflare repro issued a cert and
polled it to success in 72.83s with the worker alive throughout, confirming the
async path itself is correct.

Mount a urllib3 Retry adapter on the shared api session so idempotent requests
transparently reconnect, with a ConnectionError backstop in the poll loop. No
product code changes.

test env) and assert real store->retrieve->list->delete round-trips plus the

* test(client-certs): cover the issue/list/revoke/renew/stats lifecycle

ClientCertificateManager was ~15% covered (RBAC only). Drive the real manager
against a real self-signed CA (cryptography signing, no network) through

A certificate with exactly renewal_threshold_days remaining evaluated
days_left < renewal_threshold_days as False, so it skipped renewal until
it dropped to threshold-1 — a silent one-day delay on every cert that
landed on the boundary. digest.py and metrics.py already use <=; align

* fix(certs): validate and clamp renewal_threshold_days

A 0, negative, or non-numeric renewal_threshold_days made the renewal
decision `days_left <= threshold` permanently False (no certificate ever
renews) or raised TypeError in the renewal worker — the worst failure
mode for a cert manager, and entirely silent. Nothing validated the
field on the way in.

- write path: validate_settings_post() rejects an out-of-range

  needs_renewal evaluation and the cert-info cache key so they agree.

* feat(audit): attribute cert-lifecycle actions (actor + trigger) and emit on the silent paths

* feat(audit): tamper-evident SHA-256 hash chain + standalone verifier

The audit log was a plain append-only text file with no integrity: a single
line could be edited, deleted, or reordered and nothing would detect it (the
readers even skip malformed lines silently, so a deletion left no trace).

This adds a parallel, append-only certificate_audit.chain.jsonl that records
every audit entry inside a SHA-256 hash chain:

- each line is canonical JSON of {seq, entry, prev_hash, hash}, where hash
  commits to seq + entry + prev_hash, and prev_hash links to the previous
  line's hash. seq is a gap-free monotonic counter, so a missing seq proves a
  deletion. canon uses sorted keys / no whitespace / UTF-8 with non-ASCII
  preserved, so an IDN domain hashes identically on writer and verifier.
- the writer keeps single-writer next-seq/last-hash state under a lock (Flask
  request threads and the APScheduler renewal thread share one AuditLogger),
  fsyncs each line, and only advances state after a durable write — a chain
  failure never breaks audit logging or the audited operation, and never
  fabricates a phantom gap. State is recovered from the last complete line on
  restart; a truncated trailing line (interrupted write) is tolerated.
- the chain is written under the persistent data/ tree (data/audit), not the
  ephemeral logs/ tree, so it is the durable verifiable artifact. Disable with
  CERTMATE_AUDIT_CHAIN=0.

A standalone verifier (python -m modules.core.audit_verify [chain.jsonl],
stdlib only, no CertMate import needed) recomputes the chain and reports PASS
or the exact seq and reason of the first break (modification / deletion /
reorder / truncation). Exit 0 intact, 1 broken, 2 missing/IO.

Honest threat model, stated in the module: the chain detects tampering by
anyone WITHOUT the writer's running state, but does not bind the operator, who
holds the file and can recompute the whole chain. Constraining the operator
needs external anchoring of signed checkpoints (Phase 3), deliberately not
implemented here. No new dependencies (json + hashlib).

18 new tests: canon determinism incl. non-ASCII, write+verify, modify/delete/
reorder detection, restart recovery, truncated-tail tolerance, kill switch,
separate chain dir, and the CLI exit codes.

* fix(audit): hardening from adversarial review — corrupt-line safety, lock-on-verify, tail-truncation docs

An adversarial review of the branch found one blocker and two refinements:

- BLOCKER: verify_chain and _recover_chain_state assumed every parsed JSON
  line was an object. A valid-JSON-but-non-object line ([1,2,3], 42, null)

  racing an in-flight append cannot observe a half-written final line and
  report a spurious truncation (the standalone CLI verifier still runs lock-free
  by design).

  from the end) is not detected without an external head anchor (Phase 3), in
  api.md, compliance.md, and a pinning regression test.

* feat(audit): Phase 3 — Ed25519-signed checkpoints + verifiable export bundle

Make the audit trail verifiable by a third party off the box. The tamper-evident
hash chain (Phase 2) proved authenticity and ordering; this signs it and lets an
auditor verify which instance produced the record without running or trusting
CertMate.

- Ed25519 signing key (modules/core/audit_signing.py), persisted at
  data/.audit_signing_key like the Flask secret key (generate-on-first-run,
  0600, off-box via AUDIT_SIGNING_KEY_FILE). A corrupt key disables signing
  rather than regenerating, to avoid forking the instance identity. Public
  identity = the PEM key + a base64(sha256(raw pubkey))[:16] fingerprint.
- Signed checkpoints: every N entries (default 100) and on demand, the chain
  head is signed and appended to certificate_audit.checkpoints.jsonl.
- GET /api/audit/public-key (admin) exposes the signing identity; GET
  /api/audit/export (admin, ?from_seq/?to_seq) returns a signed, self-verifying
  bundle {manifest, entries, bundle_signature}. The manifest pins the
  fingerprint, public key, seq range and head_hash; the signature over the
  canonical manifest transitively commits to every entry via head_hash.
- The standalone verifier gains --bundle and --pubkey: it checks the chain
  structure, manifest consistency, the Ed25519 signature, the fingerprint, and
  optional out-of-band key pinning. audit_chain.verify_chain was refactored to
  share a verify_records() core with the bundle verifier (no behaviour change).
- docs/api.md + docs/compliance.md updated: the signed export exists now; the
  remaining operator-binding gap (external anchoring of checkpoints) is the only
  deferred, opt-in follow-up.

* fix(renewal): fire deploy hooks on scheduled auto-renewal (#329)

Scheduled renewals call CertificateManager.renew_certificate() directly,

renewals updated the cert on disk but never notified the deployer — the

* fix(renewal): detect no-op renewals by artifact change, not certbot output

certbot 2.x under --quiet routes its "not yet due for renewal" notification
to /dev/null, so a production no-op renew exits 0 with EMPTY output. The
v2.20.0 sentinel check never matched, the code fell through to the success
branch, stamped renewed_at daily, counted the no-op as renewed and fired
deploy hooks — false telemetry masking genuinely stuck renewals. The
regression test only passed because MockShellExecutor emits the sentinel.

- Drop --quiet from the renew command (output is captured, never emailed).
- Primary no-op detection is now the SHA256 fingerprint of the live cert
  before/after the certbot run: unchanged (or still absent) bytes = no-op;
  changed or newly-materialised bytes = renewed. The output sentinel stays
  as the fallback for non-artifact-producing executors
  (produces_artifacts=False) and as a cross-check.
- API renew response now carries 'renewed' (additive; defaults True for
  legacy result shapes) and an honest "not yet due" message on no-op; the
  web renew route gains the same 'renewed' field.
- A no-op renew no longer publishes certificate_renewed (sync route and
  IssuanceExecutor), so deploy hooks only fire when something was replaced.
- check_renewals keeps routing renewed=False to skipped_not_due (covered).

Updated test_per_cert_renewal storage tests to stage renewed files DURING
the mocked certbot run, as the real binary does, instead of before it.

* fix(audit): fail closed when the checkpoint file is unreadable

read_checkpoints swallowed every OSError as "no checkpoints", so a
chmod-000 checkpoint file combined with a deleted chain produced a clean
200 state='absent' from GET /api/audit/verify — a fail-open verdict on a
tampered box. The absent-vs-tampered decision also hinged on a brittle
reason-substring match ('does not exist').

  any other OSError raises the new CheckpointReadError. has_checkpoints
  deliberately propagates it.

  and flips the verify result to ok=False with checkpoint_unreadable=True

  chain with an unreadable anchor is 409, not a silent pass.

  endpoint gates absent-vs-tampered on that flag plus has_checkpoints()

- Endpoint: unreadable checkpoints on the missing-chain path return 409

ci: run the test and frontend-css jobs on GitHub-hosted runners (#389)

The e2e suite binds a fixed-name container + port, so on the shared
self-hosted host two test jobs from different refs clobbered each other,
which forced a host-global concurrency group serializing every test job one
at a time. That made the whole box a single point of failure and a queue: a
burst of PRs plus Dependabot builds waited 10-20 min behind it, and external
contributors could not get CI at all without the box being up.

ubuntu-latest gives each job its own ephemeral VM and localhost, so there is
no cross-ref container collision and no need to serialize. Docker is
preinstalled, so the container e2e tests still run. The multi-arch image
build stays on self-hosted for now (QEMU multi-arch is slow on GitHub-hosted).

release: v2.21.2 (client-cert lifecycle, private CA and CRL correctness) (#391)

* fix: stop client-cert renewal runaway and split renewal locks

FIX 1 (HIGH): scheduled client-cert renewal re-issued every superseded
or expired cert on every run. check_renewals() selected candidates via
list_client_certificates(revoked=False), which filters only on 'revoked'
-- never on superseded_by or expiry -- so after a renewal marked cert A
superseded_by=B (leaving A revoked=False, renewal_enabled=True,
expires_at unchanged), the next daily sweep re-renewed A -> C -> D
forever, one fresh CA-signed key+cert per run (disk fill). check_renewals
now skips any cert with a truthy superseded_by and any already-expired
cert; renew_certificate also disables renewal_enabled on the superseded
cert as a belt-and-braces guard. Normal within-threshold certs are
unaffected.

FIX 2 (medium): both scheduled renewal jobs shared one .renewal.lock, so
a long TLS-cert renewal run silently suppressed the client-cert renewal
(mTLS certs could expire unrenewed). _renewal_process_lock now takes a
lock_name (default '.renewal.lock' for back-compat); the TLS job keeps
'.renewal.lock' and the client-cert job uses '.client-renewal.lock', so
they never contend. Also hardened the fallback contract: a failure
opening the lock file now yields True (proceed) instead of raising, so
the single-process default is never blocked by the guard.

Tests: new tests/test_client_cert_renewal_runaway.py pins the two-run
count (exactly one cert issued across two sweeps), superseded-skip, and
expired-skip. test_renewal_process_lock.py updated for the distinct
locks (holding one job's lock no longer suppresses the other) and the
OSError-on-open fallback.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: private-CA / CRL correctness and hardening

Four defects in the internal CA + revocation path:

1. CA private key was written world-readable then chmod'd (a TOCTOU
   window exposing the root key) and non-atomically (a crash mid-write
   corrupted the CA). Write ca.key atomically at 0600 via a mkstemp
   temp sibling + fsync + os.replace; apply the same crash-safe write
   to ca.crt / metadata / crl.pem (public, 0644).

2. generate_crl stamped every RevokedCertificateBuilder with now() and
   dropped reasons, so regenerating after a new revocation rewrote all
   older entries' revocation_date. Thread each cert's persisted
   revoked_at + reason_revoked through generate_crl (records carry
   serial/revoked_at/reason; bare ints still supported) and emit a
   CRLReason extension. Wire the persisted records through
   CRLManager.update_crl and ClientCertificateManager.revoke_certificate.

3. get_crl_pem served an expired on-disk CRL forever (strict validators
   reject; soft-fail validators skip revocation and accept a revoked
   cert). Detect next_update in the past and regenerate lazily-on-read,
   falling back to the stale CRL only if regeneration fails.

4. sign_certificate_request copied ALL CSR extensions verbatim, so a
   CSR with BasicConstraints(ca=True)+KeyUsage(keyCertSign) could mint a
   CA-capable cert under CertMate's root. Pin a leaf profile instead:
   BasicConstraints(ca=False) critical + fixed leaf KeyUsage; only carry
   SubjectAlternativeName over from the CSR.

Adds 15 regression tests (key mode 0600 at rename time; CRL date/reason
preserved across regeneration; expired CRL regenerated on read; ca=True
CSR yields a leaf).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: invalidate deployment-status cache on cert (re)issue/renew

The deployment-status cache was never invalidated when a certificate was
renewed or reissued, so the dashboard kept serving a stale "deployed &
matching" verdict for up to cache_ttl after a renewal even though the
load balancer might still be serving the OLD cert (the deploy hook may
not have run yet).

CacheManager now subscribes to certificate_created / certificate_renewed
on the EventBus (new on_certificate_event listener, wired in factory.py
alongside deploy_manager.on_certificate_event) and evicts the affected
domain, so the next dashboard read re-probes. One subscription covers
every publisher: the API sync route, the async IssuanceExecutor, the web
path, and the scheduled renewal all publish these events on the same bus
(create/reissue map onto them too).

release: v2.21.3 (wildcard deployment status + rootless podman) (#392)

* fix(deploy-probe): stop false "wrong cert" on wildcard certs + explain mismatches (#381/#207)

The deployment-status TLS probe stripped the leading label of a wildcard
domain and connected to the bare apex: `*.example.com` was probed at
`example.com:443`. A wildcard does NOT cover its own apex (RFC 6125), so the
apex commonly serves a different certificate and the fingerprint compare in
CertificateDeploymentStatus always failed -- a permanent, systematic false
"Wrong Cert" on every wildcard cert. The domain alias is unrelated: it only
affects DNS-01 validation, not where the cert is served (red herring).

Root cause: modules/api/resources.py _probe_tls_certificate host derivation
(`domain[2:] if domain.startswith('*.')`) feeding the certificate_match compare.

Fix (root-cause, additive, no removed keys -- REST contract is frozen):
- _probe_tls_certificate gains an explicit `probe_host` override for the TCP
  target + SNI, so a caller can point the probe at a real covered name.
- The endpoint no longer probes a wildcard apex. With no deployment_host it
  returns a distinct, non-alarming `probe_status='unverifiable'` (never a red
  mismatch) and a reason telling the operator to set a deployment_host.
- New optional per-cert `deployment_host` metadata (PATCH /api/certificates
  /<domain>) is the supported way to verify a wildcard: point it at a name the
  wildcard covers (e.g. www.example.com). Used for any cert.
- Every outcome now carries diagnostics the UI can show: probe_host,
  probe_status, mismatch_reason, and on a real mismatch served_subject /
  served_fingerprint / expected_fingerprint. The dashboard error icon tooltip
  now explains WHICH host was probed and WHAT it served vs expected, fixing the
  "unclear where that error is" complaint.

Model + dashboard.js updated (fields declared so marshal_with keeps them; a
neutral "Not Verifiable" chip for unverifiable; reason wired into the tooltip).

Regression tests: wildcard-without-host is not a hard mismatch and never probes
the apex; wildcard-with-host probes that host; real mismatch carries the
diagnostic reason; non-wildcard behaviour unchanged; deployment_host PATCH
set/validate/delete.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat: support rootless podman / arbitrary UID (OpenShift pattern) (#380)

The image ran as a fixed non-root UID 1000. Under rootless podman and
OpenShift the process is remapped to an arbitrary UID (not 1000, absent
from /etc/passwd) that belongs to group 0, so the bind-mounted volume
dirs — owned/permissioned for UID 1000 only (chmod 700) — were not
writable and CertMate failed with Permission denied on /app/data etc.

Apply the OpenShift arbitrary-UID pattern:

- Dockerfile: the runtime-writable trees (/app/data, /app/certificates,
  /app/logs, /app/backups) are now group 0, group-writable + setgid
  (mode 2770, no world access) instead of 700. Any UID in group 0 can
  write them; the default USER 1000 is unchanged. A named volume created
  from the image inherits these perms, so `--user <anyuid>:0` works with
  zero host prep.
- factory.setup_directories: dirs created at runtime get group rwx +
  setgid (in-container only) so subdirs created by the app / certbot stay
  group-0 writable; the not-writable startup error now explains the
  group-0 requirement and points at issue #380.
- docs/docker.md: new "Rootless podman / OpenShift (arbitrary UID)"
  section (named volume, bind mount with chgrp 0 / :U, compose, k8s
  fsGroup).

No passwd/nss shim was needed: CertMate, gunicorn, certbot and the
private-CA generation all start healthy as an unknown UID (whoami fails,
the app does not care). Security is unchanged — every secret (CA key,
audit-signing key, DNS creds, .secret_key) is still written 0600
owner-only; only the containing directories become group-writable.

Verified on a real Docker host by building the image and running it as
both `--user 1000:1000` (default, healthy) and `--user 4711:0` (arbitrary
UID, healthy, /health=200, CA generated, settings.json + ca.key written
0600) with fresh empty named volumes and group-0 bind mounts.

* fix: unblock first-run on bearer-only deployments without reopening the setup bypass (#397)

A Docker quick-start that sets API_BEARER_TOKEN (which the docs marked as
required) put the instance past is_setup_mode(), so the setup wizard never
ran, no admin could be created via the UI, and local auth stayed off —
locking the operator out with "Local auth disabled". The v2.21.1 world-open
hardening is correct; the documented onboarding path was simply incompatible
with it.

Security-first fix — the world-open gate is left byte-for-byte unchanged
(is_setup_mode() and _authenticate_request() untouched: +27/-0 in auth.py):

- add needs_credentialed_bootstrap() (auth.py), disjoint from is_setup_mode()
  and consumed only by two UI surfaces; guarded by _is_oidc_configured() so an
  OIDC+bearer box keeps routing to the SSO login page.
- ui_routes.index()/auth_routes.login_page() re-surface the create-admin form
  on a bearer-only box; the form authenticates both bootstrap POSTs with the
  operator's bearer token (proof-of-possession required), and both stay
  @require_role('admin') — an anonymous caller still 401s.
- setup.html: send Authorization on both POSTs, handle 401 (divergent stored
  token -> point at reset script), handle 409, check the config POST before
  redirect, add method="post" so a no-JS submit can't leak the token in the
  URL; remove the pre-existing bogus btoa() Authorization header.
- reset_admin_password.py: also set local_auth_enabled=True (closes the
  recovery lockout), and write atomically via temp + os.replace chmod'd 0600
  so the reset never widens settings.json permissions.
- docs: mark API_BEARER_TOKEN "recommended for network-exposed" instead of
  "required", and document the one-time first-run token paste (README,
  docs/docker.md + the it/de/fr/es copies).

Tests: needs_credentialed_bootstrap predicate matrix (bearer-only, provisioned,
fresh, OIDC-only, OIDC+bearer, token-file); request-layer proof the bearer-only
state is NOT world-open (rejects anonymous, accepts the operator token);
divergent-token fail-closed; reset enables local auth and keeps settings.json
at 0600.

Reviewed across two adversarial passes (world-open, functional, frontend,
tests+docs, then a delta review); all findings addressed. The full
env->stored token reconciliation for the divergent-token edge is tracked
separately as a follow-up.

fix: scrypt password fallback + close login next= open-redirect (code-scan triage) (#402)

* fix: scrypt password fallback + close login next= open-redirect (code-scan triage)

The two genuine issues surfaced by triaging the 375 open code-scanning alerts
(the rest were false positives or external container CVEs):

- auth.py: the password-hashing fallback used raw salted SHA-256 when bcrypt is
  unavailable — a fast, GPU/ASIC-crackable hash for low-entropy secrets. Replace
  it with hashlib.scrypt (a slow, memory-hard stdlib KDF). bcrypt stays the
  preferred path; verification stays backward-compatible with the legacy
  "sha256:salt:hash" / "salt:hash" formats so existing operators can still log
  in. (CodeQL py/weak-sensitive-data-hashing)

- login.html: safeNextUrl() rejected protocol-relative //host but not the
  backslash variant /\host, which browsers normalize to //host — an open
  redirect via ?next=/\evil.com. Reject any next whose second char is / or \.
  (CodeQL js/client-side-unvalidated-url-redirection)

Tests: scrypt fallback round-trip + not-raw-SHA-256 regression guard; legacy
sha256 verification still passes; safeNextUrl covers //, /\, \\ bypasses.

fix: close five P1 findings from the 360° audit (#433)

* fix: close five P1 findings from the 360° audit (#408 #409 #410 #411 #415)

#408 — OIDC login ignored the row's `enabled` flag, so disabling an SSO
user was a no-op: the IdP still authenticated them and CertMate minted a
fresh session with the old role. Both the subject-match and email-link
branches now refuse a disabled user, and the role is re-derived from the
current claims on every login (opt out with `sync_role_on_login: false`)
so an IdP demotion actually demotes.

#409 — The unified backup archived only certificates/ + settings.json,
silently omitting every PKI artefact under data/: the private CA signing
key, the client certificates it signed, the CRL and the audit chain. The
documented DR restore came back unable to issue, renew or revoke a single
client certificate. Both subtrees now travel under a `data/` prefix, and
the restore side is allowlisted to exactly those two — an arbitrary
`data/...` member would otherwise let a tampered archive write a
settings.json around the deploy-hook revalidation gate.

#410 — A ZIP cannot carry symlinks, so a restore flattened certbot's
live/<domain>/*.pem into regular files; certbot parsefails such a lineage
and skips it, so every scheduled renewal afterwards failed or reported
"renewed: False" forever, silently, until expiry. New
`repair_certbot_lineage_symlinks` rebuilds the links from the archive/
generation the backup did preserve, and runs both at restore time and at
the top of `renew_certificate` so instances restored by an older version
heal themselves.

#411 — certmate.service shipped `--workers 4` while sessions, session
revocation and the login rate limiter are per-process in-memory state
(the Dockerfile already used one worker). Revoking a compromised admin
only took effect on one worker in four. Aligned to `--workers 1
--threads 8`, docs included.

#415 — settings-notifications.js reported every save as a green success
because it read the JSON body without checking `r.ok`; the endpoint is
admin-only and answers JSON on 403 and 503. An operator could configure
SMTP, see "saved", and never receive an alert.

Adds 15 regression tests, including one that proves the ZIP flattening
happens and that the restore repairs it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* harden: validate the domain inside the lineage repair, tighten data/ perms

CodeQL flagged the new helper. Both are worth fixing properly rather than
triaging:

- repair_certbot_lineage_symlinks now validates `domain` with the project
  validator and confirms every path it touches resolves inside domain_dir.
  On the restore path `domain` is derived from ZIP entry names, so it is
  untrusted input; the ZIP-slip guard was the only thing standing between
  it and the filesystem. This makes the helper safe for any caller.
- Restored data/ files are 0600 for private material and 0640 for the
  rest, never world-readable. certificates/ stays 0644 because operators
  bind-mount and read it from other containers; nothing outside the app
  reads data/.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* harden: everything restored under data/ is 0600

CodeQL was right that 0640 is more than this needs. Nothing outside the
app process reads data/ — the CA cert and the CRL are public information,
but publishing them is the server's job (/api/crl/download), not the
filesystem's. certificates/ keeps 0644 because operators bind-mount it
and read it from other containers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: make the lineage repair all-or-nothing, and correct the OIDC docstring

Both from the review on #433.

The repair chose min(max(generation)) per member, so a lineage where
privkey exists only as gen 4 while cert runs 1..3 relinked three members
and left privkey a flat file — a half-repaired live/ that certbot handles
no better than the state we started in. It now links the newest
generation present for EVERY member (set intersection), verifies all four
targets exist before touching live/, and otherwise leaves the restored
flat PEMs alone.

The resolve_or_provision_user docstring still claimed a subject-match
login does not change the role, which stopped being true when
sync_role_on_login landed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: don't silently drop an oversized audit log on restore

Third finding from the review on #433. The data/ branch inherited the
10 MB per-entry cap that suits PEM files, but certificate_audit.log is
append-only and outgrows it on any long-lived instance. The entry was
skipped with a warning and the restore still returned True — leaving the
audit chain unverifiable on an instance that believed it was restored.

data/ entries now stream in 1 MB chunks under a 512 MB ceiling (a bound
on disk, not memory), an overflow is logged as an ERROR because the
result is an incomplete restore, and a failed extraction unlinks the
partial file: a truncated ca.key or audit chain is worse than an absent
one, because it looks restored.

fix: make four CI gates actually gate (#434)

* fix: make four CI gates actually gate (#412 #413 #414 #428)

Every item here reported success without checking anything.

#412 — The container CVE scan ran with no `exit-code` (so it could not
fail) against the floating `:latest` tag, which on a push to main is the
PREVIOUS release's image, and was skipped entirely on pull requests. A
CRITICAL introduced by a change was therefore never scanned by anyone.
The job now rebuilds the image under test from the same buildx cache and
loads it locally, runs on pull requests, and a second Trivy pass fails
the job on a CRITICAL **with a fix available**. The reporting pass stays
non-blocking on purpose: the image carries a long tail of unfixable
base-image findings (#403), and a gate that is always red is a gate
nobody reads. Also gives the build step the `id` that
`steps.build.outputs.digest` always referenced but never had, and drops
the checksum-less Trivy tarball install left over from the self-hosted
runner.

#413 — `release.sh publish` gated on version, tag, notes and emoji, but
never asked whether main builds: a Dependabot bump landing between
`prepare` and `publish` was enough to tag and push a broken tree, and the
tag push is what publishes `:latest`. It now reads the run status for the
exact commit being released and refuses unless the required workflows are
green. Cancelled counts as failed — that is precisely how a broken build
slipped through during v2.21.4. UI tests and E2E (staging) are reported
but never block, because they run on the self-hosted host and would hang
a release whenever that box is offline.

#414 — The Playwright suite could report green having executed zero
assertions: any Chromium launch failure became a skip, and CI installed
Chromium without `--with-deps`. Now: `--with-deps`, an explicit
launch-check step, `CERTMATE_UI_REQUIRE_BROWSER=1` which turns "no
browser" from a skip into a failure, and a final step that fails the job
if every collected UI test skipped.

#428 — flake8 ran with `--exit-zero` everywhere, so the `.flake8` config
added in v2.21.4 was advisory. The failing set now also carries the bug
classes that are already clean and must stay clean: F811, F632, E711,
E712, E713, E714 — which surfaced three real F811s (a shadowed
`tempfile`, two shadowed `re`), fixed here. Coverage gets a floor
(`--cov-fail-under=65`, below the current number) instead of nothing at
all, and pytest.ini's `source = .` is aligned to `modules/` so local and
CI numbers finally mean the same thing. `Lint (emoji)` also runs on push
now: PR-only meant a direct push could land emoji unchecked, and that the
check was absent from every commit on main.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: scope the Trivy gate to vulnerabilities, make --with-deps conditional

Both surfaced on this PR's own run — the new gates firing, but on the
wrong thing.

The CRITICAL that failed security-scan was a SECRET finding: Trivy reads
a .pyc inside the third-party certbot_dns_google package as a GCP service
account. A false positive there would have made the gate permanently red,
which is the failure mode this PR exists to remove. The gate is now
scanners: vuln; secret findings still reach the Security tab through the

playwright install --with-deps shells out to sudo, which the self-hosted
host does not grant passwordlessly, so the step died before any test ran.
It is now used only when passwordless sudo is available; the explicit
Chromium launch check is what decides either way, which is the part that
actually closes the skip-is-pass hole.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: make the release CI gate robust to paging and reruns

From the review on #434. `gh run list` defaults to 20 results, so reruns
plus the non-required workflows could push a required one off the first
page — reading as MISSING and blocking a good release. Now --limit 100.

Same class of false negative, caught while fixing it: a rerun creates a
