fix: seven backend correctness findings from the 360° audit (#435)

* fix: notify when an unattended renewal fails (#417)

The scheduler audited and logged a failed renewal but never published
certificate_failed — the event the notifier turns into an email or a
Slack message, and one the notifications UI lets you subscribe to. The
manual/API path and the async executor both published it; only the path
that runs at 02:00, the one nobody is watching, did not. A certificate
whose DNS credentials had been rotated could fail every night for a month
in silence.

Failures while *checking* a domain (unreadable metadata, a bad entry)
publish too — they are just as invisible. `domain` is now reset per
iteration so that branch cannot attribute a failure to the previous
certificate.

Follows _publish_renewed_event's contract exactly: no-op without an event
bus, and a raising notifier never turns into a renewal error.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: stop the log stream from pinning a worker thread at 100% CPU (#418)

`stream_logs` tailed the file with `while True: f.readline()` — no sleep,
no exit condition. At EOF readline() returns '' immediately, so the loop
never yielded and never blocked: the generator spun on the CPU forever,
and because nothing was ever written to the socket a client disconnect
was never detected. The Dockerfile runs one worker with 8 threads, so
opening the Logs page eight times wedged the container.

Now: sleep between empty reads, emit an SSE keepalive comment on each
idle poll (writing it is what makes a dead client raise and end the
generator, and it also stops proxies timing the stream out), and give up
after 30 idle minutes so an abandoned tab cannot hold a thread all day. A
backlog still drains at full speed — the sleep is only on the empty-read
path.

The tail moved to a module-level `_stream_log_file` so the pacing is
testable without a Flask app; the tests bound it by wall-clock, which is
what the old loop could never satisfy. Frames also stop carrying the
file's own newline, which was producing an extra empty SSE dispatch per
log line on the client.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: delete the certificate from the storage backend too (#419)

`CertificateDetail.delete` removed the local directory and the settings
entry but never called the storage backend's `delete_certificate` — which
was, consequently, dead code. With Vault / AWS Secrets Manager / Azure
Key Vault / Infisical configured as the certificate store, the API
returned 200 and the UI showed the certificate gone while the full PEM
bundle, private key included, stayed in the external secret store
indefinitely; a later storage migration or restore resurrected it.

The call lives in CertificateManager.delete_certificate rather than the
route, so every caller inherits it. Three deliberate details:

- The local_filesystem backend points at the directory the rmtree above
  already removed, so it is skipped instead of being asked twice.
- A certificate that exists only in the remote backend now deletes
  successfully. Reporting 404 there left the key both unreachable through
  the UI and undeletable through the API.
- A backend outage never fails the local deletion, but it logs at ERROR
  naming the domain and the backend: an operator who believes a key was
  destroyed and finds it in Vault six months later was misled by us.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: make the API rate limiter un-bypassable by varying the token (#420)

The bucket was sha256(<caller-supplied bearer token>), computed before the
token was validated, so every request carrying a different Authorization
header landed in a fresh bucket. A loop with a random token per request
was never limited — which also left the two deliberately unauthenticated
resources (OCSP status, CRL download) with no protection at all, and
flooded SimpleRateLimiter towards MAX_KEYS, whose eviction then discarded
legitimate per-IP buckets.

Rather than dropping the per-key bucket (it exists for a good reason:
many clients behind one NAT must not share one limit, and an abusive key
should be throttled independently of its source IP), every /api/ request
is now also checked against a coarse per-IP ceiling — 600/min by default,
far above the working limits, so it is a backstop and not the operating
limit. It is evaluated FIRST, so a token-varying caller is cut off before
a per-key bucket is ever allocated, which closes the MAX_KEYS flooding as
well as the bypass.

The existing wiring test asserted the bucket was always `key:`; updated to
assert the real contract — ip_ceiling first, working bucket second — plus
a test that a caller over the ceiling never reaches the key bucket at all.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: a reissue must not discard per-certificate configuration (#421)

create_certificate built `metadata` as a fresh dict and wrote
metadata.json wholesale, so replace=True (Edit & Reissue) silently
dropped every key the PATCH endpoint had stored there:
deployment_protocol / deployment_port / deployment_host — which
resources.py goes out of its way to preserve on a *partial* PATCH —
plus deployment_status and renewed_at.

An operator sets a mail server's probe to smtp-starttls:587, then adds a
SAN through Edit & Reissue: the probe reverts to https-tls:443 and the
dashboard reports the mail server as "not deployed".

The merge lives in _merge_reissue_metadata so it is testable without
certbot, and is driven by an explicit set of keys the reissue OWNS. That
set matters in both directions: everything outside it survives (including
keys a future version adds), and everything inside it is authoritative —
so a reissue that drops a domain alias actually clears it instead of
inheriting the old value from disk, which is the bug a naive merge would
have introduced. A test pins the owned set against the fields the
issuance path writes, so adding a new one without declaring it cannot
silently start preserving stale values.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: client-cert renewal keeps the validity and refuses CSR identities (#422)

renew_certificate called create_client_certificate without days_valid and
with generate_key=True unconditionally, which broke two different things.

A 730-day certificate came back as a 365-day one: the operator's chosen
validity silently halved on every renewal. days_valid is now persisted in
metadata and inherited; certificates issued before that field existed
derive it from created_at/expires_at, so they are not reset either.

Worse, a certificate issued from a client-supplied CSR was "renewed" into
a brand-new CertMate-generated keypair the client does not hold, while the
original was stamped superseded_by + renewal_enabled=False — so the
working mTLS identity expired with no further renewal and nothing usable
in its place. CertMate never had that private key and cannot renew such an
identity: renewal now refuses with an error that says what is actually
needed (a fresh CSR from the holder), and refuses BEFORE touching the
original, which stays in service.

The scheduled sweep skips those certificates rather than retrying nightly:
an identical audit failure every tick would drown the trail, and the
certificate remains visible as expiring in the UI. Guarded against
`days_valid: true` too — bool is an int subclass, and a one-day
certificate is a plausible way to lose an afternoon.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: set the external-copy warning on renewal, and clear it on recovery (#423)

A storage-backend failure during renewal was only logged, while the same
failure at creation set metadata['storage_warning'] — and nothing ever
cleared it. Two symmetric ways to mislead an operator:

A Vault token expires mid-life. Nightly renewals keep succeeding locally
while the DR copy silently stops updating, with nothing in the API or the
UI to show it; the stale external copy is discovered during a restore,
which is the worst possible moment.

And in the other direction, one failed store at creation left the warning
in metadata forever, so the dashboard kept warning long after the backend
recovered. An operator who learns to ignore a stale warning will ignore
the real one.

Create and renew now share _store_in_backend + _apply_storage_warning
instead of carrying two copies of the logic, which is precisely how they
drifted; a test asserts neither path calls store_certificate inline again.
The renew path persists the flag even when no metadata.json existed, since
that would otherwise be the one case where the signal is lost, and the
warning is surfaced on the renew result the way create already did.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: document the per-IP ceiling and the OIDC role-sync switch

Pre-PR pass: two places where the docs now contradicted the code.

docs/api.md described the rate-limit bucket as "per API key ... and per IP
for session/anonymous", which stopped being the whole truth with the
per-IP ceiling — and the ceiling shows up in the Settings rate-limit form
automatically, so an operator would have met an undocumented field.

README documented the OIDC settings block without sync_role_on_login, and
said nothing about a disabled user being refused at SSO login.

Also stamps renewed_at before pushing to the storage backend rather than
after, so the external copy carries the same timestamp as the local one —
the reordering in the previous commit had quietly dropped it from the
stored bundle.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: document the admin log-stream endpoint

Decided during the pre-PR review: keep /api/web/logs/stream rather than
remove it. It has no consumer in the UI — the only reference in the repo
besides the route itself is a line in RELEASE_NOTES about hardening it —
but it is admin-gated, genuinely useful with `curl -N` while watching an
issuance, and deleting it would silently break anyone scripting against
it.

The real defect was that it was invisible. An undocumented endpoint is how
code survives without ever being reviewed, which is exactly how it kept a
`while True` with no sleep in it for this long.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: don't upload the Trivy SARIF on pull requests

Fallout from #412, caught on this PR's own run. Now that the container
scan also runs on pull requests, the SARIF lands on the PR ref — so the
image's long tail of unfixable base-image CVEs (tracked in #403) appears
as new code-scanning alerts and blocks the merge. That is the
always-red-gate failure mode #412 existed to remove, reintroduced through
the reporting path instead of the gating one.

On a pull request the gate is the "Fail on a fixable CRITICAL" step, which
is actionable by definition. The Security-tab inventory is a property of
what is shipped, so it is uploaded from push and tag builds.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: four review findings — log redaction, stream encoding, bucket retention

From the review on #435; all four are real.

Backend exception text no longer reaches ERROR-level logs. Both
_store_in_backend and _delete_from_storage_backend log the exception class
and put the detail behind DEBUG: a storage-backend error can embed a token
or a signed URL, and application logs are readable by any admin — and, now
that it is documented, streamable over /api/web/logs/stream. The
warning message shown to the operator already carried no raw text; the log
line contradicted it.

The log stream opens with an explicit utf-8 + errors='replace', so a
single mangled byte from a subprocess cannot raise UnicodeDecodeError and
end an admin's session mid-watch, and it strips CRLF rather than LF alone,

then discards LIVE buckets. Retention is now tied to the window (2x), and
both are named constants instead of two magic numbers that disagreed.

feat: file logging, rotated by construction (#431, application-log half) (#438)

The audit reported "no log rotation anywhere". The situation turned out to
be one step stranger: configure_structured_logging accepted a `log_file`
and nothing ever passed one, so CertMate never wrote a log file at all.
`logs/certmate.log` — the path the web UI's log stream tails, and the file
the issue worried would grow without bound — was created by nothing.

So this is not "add rotation to the file handler". It is: make the file
handler exist, and make it impossible to have one without rotation.

  stdout is correct and stays the default — it is what `docker logs` and
  every shipper expect.

  5 backups, both tunable. There is no code path that produces an unbounded
  log file.
- An unwritable path warns and continues on console logging. A certificate
  manager that refuses to boot because it cannot write a *log* has failed at
  the wrong thing.

Documented in the README env table, and docs/api.md's log-stream section
now says the endpoint needs file logging on — it was describing a tail of a
file nothing wrote.

The audit chain is deliberately NOT touched: it is append-only and
tamper-evident, so rotating it needs its own design (checkpoint at the roll,
anchor the new file to the head hash, verification across files). That stays

fix(audit): make an incremental export slice actually self-verifying (#441) (#442)

* fix(audit): make an incremental export slice actually self-verifying (#441)

`GET /api/audit/export?from_seq=N` was documented as producing a
"self-verifying" slice and produced a bundle the shipped verifier rejected:
`verify_records` seeds `prev_hash` with the genesis and requires the first
record's `prev_hash` to be `""`, so every fragment failed on its first link —
and failed with the worst available wording, "broken link ... a deletion or
reorder", on a perfectly intact record.

The genesis requirement is not relaxed: it is precisely what makes head
truncation of a full chain detectable. Instead a fragment now declares, inside
the signed manifest, the predecessor hash it continues from:

- `verify_records(records, anchor_prev_hash=..., anchor_seq=...)` — the anchor
  is opt-in and never inferred from the records themselves.
- An anchored slice is `format_version: 2` and carries `anchor_prev_hash` /
  `anchor_seq`. Full exports stay byte-identical `format_version: 1`, so
  verifiers shipped before this change still accept them; meeting a v2 bundle
  they report "unsupported format" rather than a false "chain invalid".
- The anchor lives in the signed manifest, so the signature attests it, and it
  is checked against the entries rather than merely recorded.
- Neither the result dict nor the CLI may call a fragment "intact": both report
  it as a partial slice and name the anchor seq. It proves the entries from the
  anchor forward are authentic and ordered; it proves nothing about the prefix.

Found while analysing #437 — the same missing primitive (verify a fragment
against a declared, signed anchor) is what any segmentation or compaction
design needs at its seam.

`verify_chain()` did `f.read().splitlines()`, `load_records()` did the same,

feat(audit): prune an archived prefix of the chain, explicitly and on the record (#445) (#454)

* feat(audit): prune an archived prefix of the chain, explicitly and on the record (#445)

Retention on a tamper-evident record is a policy question, not a disk question.
You cannot make deletion impossible on a file the operator owns; what you can do
is make it non-deniable. So this is not a background handler that quietly rolls
files away — it is one command that refuses to delete anything it cannot see a
verified archive for, and that writes the deletion into the chain that continues.

`python -m modules.core.audit_prune --bundle <archive> --data-dir data/audit`
(dry run without `--yes`) requires that the archive bundle verifies, is signed
by this instance, starts exactly where the chain currently starts, and agrees
with the chain hash-for-hash at every seq it claims. It refuses to empty the
chain: a chain with no live records cannot be verified at all, only asserted.

Deliberately CLI-only, with no API endpoint. An authenticated request that
deletes audit history is precisely what someone who has just compromised an
administrator account wants, and an operator who can legitimately prune already
has shell access — they have to put the archive off the box anyway.

What it leaves behind:

- An `archive` entry in the chain, naming the seq range, count, head hash and
  the archive's SHA-256. The record of the deletion outlives what it deleted.
- `certificate_audit.anchor.json`, signed with the instance key, stating where
  the chain now starts and what it continues from — so a chain that was merely
  truncated cannot pass for a pruned one.
- Verification that never reports a bare "intact" again: both
  `/api/audit/verify` and the standalone verifier name the anchor seq, and the
  CLI says outright that entries before it live only in the archive.

Two failure modes this design exists to avoid, both tested:

- The anchor is written before the chain is replaced, so an interrupted prune
  loses nothing and reports "interrupted prune" rather than a broken chain.
- Checkpoints below the anchor attest entries that were archived; cross-checking
  against one would report routine maintenance as a truncation. Only checkpoints
  at or above the anchor are used, and a prune past all of them says so.

Fix race condition in tools/list response handling (#458)

The test sends the tools/list request unconditionally after a fixed 400ms delay, but the server may not have responded to the initialize request yet. detection was buying a weekly red X for coverage the release already guarantees.

fix: acme-dns issuance never worked — drive it with the native hook (#466) (#484)

* fix: acme-dns issuance never worked — drive it with the native hook (#466)

certbot rejected every acme-dns certificate request with

    certbot: error: unrecognized arguments: --acme-dns-credentials <file>

The pinned `certbot-acme-dns==0.3.1` plugin does register with certbot, but
it exposes only --acme-dns-server, --acme-dns-propagation-seconds and
--acme-dns-is-trusted. It implements no credentials-file option at all, so
the command line AcmeDNSStrategy built could never parse. Reproduced against
this repo's exact pins (certbot 2.10.0, cryptography 46.0.7, pyopenssl 26.0.0):
`certbot --help acme-dns` lists no --acme-dns-credentials.

That plugin is also the wrong shape for CertMate: it registers the acme-dns
account itself through interactive zope.component prompts, while CertMate
stores an already-registered account (api_url + username + password +
subdomain) in settings.

Publishing an acme-dns TXT record is a single authenticated POST, which
CertMate already performs in dns_alias_hook._acme_dns_change — but only when
the user explicitly asked for DNS-alias mode. Route every acme-dns issuance
and renewal through that hook instead. The alias target is inherently the
configured subdomain: acme-dns *is* CNAME delegation, so the user's CNAME
already points the challenge name there whether or not alias mode was
requested.

- certificates.py: add _acme_dns_native_alias() as the routing switch; use it
  on the create path, on renewal, and to skip the certbot-plugin preflight.
  Renewal routes on the provider rather than on metadata, so certificates
  issued before this fix renew without a metadata migration.
- dns_strategies.py: AcmeDNSStrategy.configure_certbot_arguments now raises
  instead of emitting the flags certbot rejects, so a future refactor cannot
  silently restore them.
- requirements.txt: drop certbot-acme-dns entirely. It never worked and it
  pulled zope.component/zope.interface into the image for nothing.
- docs: acme-dns needs no plugin, and list the required Subdomain field.

Reported-by: @mbw2001

* fix: report a missing acme-dns subdomain as a config error, scrub the log

Two review findings on this PR.

A blank/missing `subdomain` on the acme-dns account made
_acme_dns_native_alias return '', which silently dropped the request back
onto the plugin path — where AcmeDNSStrategy raises "this is a bug in the
caller". True of the code path, useless to someone who just left a settings
field empty. It now raises ValueError with the field to fill in, matching how
create_certificate reports every other validation problem, and it fails
before certbot is invoked.

The new renewal log line interpolated the domain straight from metadata
(CodeQL py/log-injection). Scrubbed CR/LF the same way modules/web/cert_routes.py
already does.

fix(docker): upgrade the runtime stage's bundled pip (#403) (#485)

* fix(docker): upgrade the runtime stage's bundled pip (#403)

Trivy keeps reporting pip 25.0.1 in the image (CVE-2026-8643,
CVE-2026-6357, CVE-2026-3219) even though the builder stage already runs
`pip install -U pip`. That upgrade applies to the BUILDER's interpreter
only; the runtime stage starts from the same base image with its own
bundled pip under /usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages, which nothing
ever touched.

Upgrade it in the runtime stage's existing apt layer, so no new layer is
added. The application runs from /opt/venv and does not use this pip, so
the change is invisible at runtime — it exists to stop shipping a
known-vulnerable copy to users who exec into the container.

This is the only Trivy finding in #403 that we can actually fix: the four
CRITICALs are perl-base with no fixed version published upstream.

fix: Google Cloud DNS-01 never worked — hand certbot the SA JSON (#385) (#493)

* fix: Google Cloud DNS-01 never worked — hand certbot the SA JSON (#385)

Every Google DNS-01 issuance failed. CertMate wrote an ini containing
`dns_google_project_id` / `dns_google_service_account_key` and passed that
ini as `--dns-google-credentials`, but certbot-dns-google calls
`google.auth.load_credentials_from_file` on whatever path it is given: the
credentials file must BE the service-account JSON. The ini is rejected with
"File ... is not a valid json file".

feat(cli): certmate cert download, so a host can pull what it deploys (#490) (#501)

* feat(cli): certmate cert download, so a host can pull what it deploys (#490)

Requested by @exterrestris, whose argument is the right one: pushing means
the certificate manager holds credentials for every target host, while
pulling means each host holds one credential for itself.

Every layer had this except the one you would use. The server exposes the
download endpoint in two shapes, and the SDK already implemented
json/pem/zip/pfx — but the CLI had no download command at all.

Per-file first, because that is what a deploy script wants:

    certmate cert download example.com --file fullchain -o /etc/ssl/certs/x.pem
    certmate cert download example.com --file privkey   -o /etc/ssl/private/x.key

with --bundle zip|json for the whole-certificate shapes and -o - for stdout.

Details that matter more than the command itself:

- Files are created 0600 via os.open with the mode, not chmod-ed after the
  write. Between an open() and a chmod() a private key is readable by anyone
  on the box.
- The success line reports the mode actually on disk. O_CREAT leaves an
  existing file's mode alone, so claiming 0600 unconditionally would
  sometimes be a lie.
- SDK.download_certificate_file sends ?file=<name>, not the path-style
  /download/<name> route: both exist server-side but only the query-string
  form accepts key_format, so the same call can serve the legacy PKCS#1 key
  (#398, #233).
- An unknown --file fails before any request is sent.

Clients bumped to 0.1.3, and the CLI's floor on certmate-sdk raised to
>=0.1.3 — installing the new CLI against SDK 0.1.2 would fail at runtime on
the missing method, which a >=0.1.2 floor would have allowed.

feat(k8s): Helm chart for running CertMate in a cluster (#504)

* feat(k8s): Helm chart for running CertMate in a cluster

CertMate ships a Kubernetes Secret deploy target and a guide for putting
certificates INTO a cluster, but no way to install CertMate itself there
beyond translating docker-compose by hand. Kubernetes users install with
helm; without a chart the project is not evaluated in the environment where
its closest comparison lives.

The chart encodes what CertMate actually is rather than emitting generic
boilerplate:

- ONE replica, hardcoded, with a template-time failure and an explanation if
  anyone sets replicaCount to anything else. APScheduler runs in the web
  process and gunicorn runs one worker; a second replica is a second
  scheduler renewing the same certificates against one RWO volume. That is
  not a scaled deployment, it is a duplicate-issuance incident that looks
  healthy in kubectl.
- Recreate, not RollingUpdate: the new pod cannot mount a ReadWriteOnce
  volume the old pod still holds, so a rolling update deadlocks.
- Refuses to render without persistence unless an existingClaim is given —
  certificates, the inventory and the audit chain are not pod-local state.
- The PVC carries helm.sh/resource-policy: keep, so `helm uninstall` does not
  take the certificates with it.
- One claim with subPaths rather than four RWO claims; there is nothing to
  share on a single-instance workload.
- existingSecret support, because values.yaml is not a secret store.

appVersion is wired into scripts/release.sh and pinned by
test_version_consistency, so it cannot become the next stale version string —
that lesson cost two hand-fixes for the docs pages and one for the lockfile
already.

Tests: the invariants are asserted statically (always run), plus render
assertions that exercise both guards and the existingClaim escape hatch when
helm is present, and skip honestly when it is not.

Two distribution gaps, both automated rather than left to memory.

## The chart is published

`helm install ./charts/certmate` only works from a checkout. Published as an
OCI artifact on every release, it becomes
`helm install oci://ghcr.io/fabriziosalmi/charts/certmate`.

GHCR rather than Docker Hub because nested repository paths exist there: the

`docker.io/fabriziosalmi/certmate`. Pushing both to one OCI repository would
put a chart and an image behind the same tag. GITHUB_TOKEN is also sufficient,
so this adds no secret.

The workflow gates the way publish-clients.yml does — an OCI push is
effectively write-once per tag, so it refuses to publish a chart whose version
disagrees with the release tag — and re-runs the two render guards, because
the pytest equivalents skip wherever helm is absent and CI is exactly where it
is absent.

Chart version and appVersion are both the CertMate version, bumped together by
release.sh and pinned by tests. A separate chart version is a second number to
bump, and every independent copy of a version in this repository has drifted
at least once: the docs landing pages twice, package-lock.json two releases
behind. `version` also has to move for a publish to be a new artifact rather
than a rejected duplicate.

## Releases are announced

1,240 stars, 7 watchers: shipping notifies almost nobody. A Discussion in
Announcements is the one surface people can subscribe to, and it appears on
the repository front page. Posted automatically when a release is published,
with the notes, the docker and helm upgrade commands, and a link back.

manual re-run announces the same thing, and it skips when a discussion with

fix: round-1 audit — a ReDoS, a shadowed dependency pin, and a documentation set that lied (#511)

A full pre-release sweep across the codebase, packaging, CI, the clients and the
documentation. No criticals, no secrets — but three real defects and a
documentation set that was actively misleading.

**A quadratic ReDoS on the path that redacts secrets from logs.** `PEM_RE`
restarted its `.*?` forward scan at every `-----BEGIN`, so input that opens
blocks it never closes cost O(anchors x length): 21.6 s on a 480 KB blob, burned
on one of the eight threads the process has, by a function that sanitises
unbounded deploy-hook output. Replaced with a linear scanner — 3.8 MB in 2.3 ms
— proven equivalent to the regex by differential fuzzing over 30,000 cases.

**`dns-lexicon==3.25.1` was not pinning anything.** `certbot-dns-hetzner==3.0.0`
depends on `dns-lexicon-coop`, a third-party fork shipping the same top-level
`lexicon/` package; pip installed both and let one overwrite the other. Held at
2.0.1, whose every .py file is byte-identical to 3.0.0 (sha256, both wheels) —
the releases differ only in that dependency line.

**Four EdgeDNS calls with no timeout**, inside the certbot auth hook on a
gunicorn worker thread. Fixed on the Session so the next call site cannot forget.

**The documentation.** 210 curl examples pointed at `localhost:5000` — Flask's
dev default, never CertMate's 8000. Nine pages promised a batch import of 30,000
against an API that 400s above 100. Eleven files documented a test command that
fails on a clean checkout. Thirteen relative links in the translations pointed
at nothing. CONTRIBUTING promised four tools that requirements-test.txt does not
contain. `docs/mcp.md` existed in five languages with nothing linking to it. And
`docs/index.md` was a feature launch write-up wearing the index's filename.

Every stale claim that had a gate shared one blind spot: the gate only checked
the English. The batch-limit test searched for "30,000" in two files that write
"30k", while the four that write "30.000" were not in its list at all — it could
not have failed for any page in any language.

Fourteen new gates, each verified to fail without its fix. Suite 2343 green.

fix: the minimal image never started, and nothing ever built it (#514) (#520)

* fix: the minimal image never started, and nothing ever built it (#514)

Reported by @mackboylens against 8a15f52, and reproduced exactly: an image
built with `--build-arg REQUIREMENTS_FILE=requirements-minimal.txt` dies during
gunicorn's worker import and restart-loops forever.

`requirements-minimal.txt` has no SQLAlchemy, and `modules/core/factory.py`
imports APScheduler's `SQLAlchemyJobStore` at module scope. So the import of
`app` cannot complete, and the container never serves anything. Verified in a
container that SQLAlchemy is the *only* missing distribution — bcrypt, Authlib
and prometheus_client are each wrapped in try/except with a working fallback,
which is why their absence is survivable and this one is not.

The Dockerfile advertises `REQUIREMENTS_FILE` as a supported build argument, so
this is a shipped surface, not an internal file. It had been broken for months
and it took a user building it to find out, because **nothing in the repository
ever built it** — no workflow, no test, no script referenced the file at all.

The deeper gap is that the CI step was `docker build -t certmate:test .` and
nothing more. A successful build proves the layers assemble; it says nothing
about whether the process starts. Replaced with a step that builds *and boots*
every advertised requirements set and requires each to answer /health, failing
fast (with logs) when a container is already dead rather than waiting out the
timeout on a corpse.

tests/test_requirements_sets.py covers the cheap half in milliseconds: a
boot-critical distribution going missing, minimal drifting out of subset with
the full set, a shared pin diverging between the two files, and ci.yml ceasing
to build an advertised variant or to check /health at all.

Verified end to end with Docker: both variants build, boot, and report
`{"status":"healthy", "scheduler":"running"}` — the scheduler being exactly
what SQLAlchemy makes possible. Both new gates checked to fail without their
fix. Suite 2356 green.

fix(release): the gate that demands a real certificate could not see the DNS code (#521)

* fix(release): the gate that demands a real certificate could not see the DNS code

`scripts/release.sh` runs an end-to-end issuance against Let's Encrypt staging
before a release, and `SENSITIVE_RE` decides whether that run is MANDATORY —
whether `--skip-real-cert` is refused. It had rotted:

    modules/(core/(certificate|client_cert|deployer|acme|storage)|dns|...)
                                                                 ^^^

`modules/dns` matches nothing. There is no such directory — the DNS code lives
at `modules/core/dns_*.py`. So a release changing only `dns_providers.py`,
`dns_strategies.py`, `dns_alias_hook.py` or `dns_zone_discovery.py` would have
accepted `--skip-real-cert`, in the gate that exists *because* two DNS providers
had each shipped in a state where they had never worked in any release.

Sixteen issuance-critical files were uncovered in total, including
`modules/core/shell.py` — the file that invokes certbot at all — plus
`cert_service.py`, `cert_jobs.py`, `private_ca.py`, `ca_manager.py`,
`csr_handler.py`, `ocsp_crl.py`, `deploy_targets.py`, `settings.py`, `utils.py`,
`api/models.py` and `web/cert_routes.py`.

Adding the missing prefixes would have been the wrong fix: the next rename
breaks it again, silently, and nobody reads a regex that long closely enough to
notice. So the rule is inverted to fail closed — everything under `modules/`,
plus what the image is built from, is sensitive; the escape hatch survives only
for changes that provably cannot reach a certificate (docs, CI, static assets,
the chart's siblings). The asymmetry justifies it: a false positive costs one
four-minute staging issuance, which is already the default; a false negative
ships a DNS provider that cannot issue.

tests/test_release_gate.py reads the live pattern out of the script rather than
duplicating it, and asserts three things: that every issuance-critical path is
covered, that docs-only paths still are not, and — the check that was missing —
that **every branch of the pattern matches a real file**. A dead branch now
fails the suite instead of quietly disarming the gate.

Verified both ways. Restoring the old pattern turns the DNS and shell.py cases
red; injecting a fresh dead branch turns the dead-branch test red. And the
release currently pending is correctly judged MANDATORY.

Suite 2394 green, flake8 gate 0, bandit medium+ 0.

chore(mcp): drop node-fetch rather than bump it (closes #348) (#523)

* chore(mcp): drop node-fetch rather than bump it (#348)

Dependabot proposed node-fetch 2.x -> 3.x. 3.x is ESM-only and mcp/index.js is
CommonJS, so `require("node-fetch")` would throw ERR_REQUIRE_ESM — but only on
Node 20.0 through 20.18. Node enabled `require(esm)` by default in 20.19.0
(2025-03-13), so on anything newer the bump loads fine.

That split is the actual hazard, and it is the same shape as the undici finding
on the website: `engines` admits `>=20.0.0` and CI pins `node-version: 20`,
which resolves to the newest 20.x. CI would have been green while an operator
on an older Node 20 got a server that will not start.

`fetch` has been global since Node 18 and this package already requires >= 20,
so the dependency was not needed at all. Removing it deletes the question
instead of answering it, and takes the last runtime dependency other than the
MCP SDK out of the tree.

Checked the two call sites first: they use only `.ok`, `.status`, `.json()` and
`.text()`, which behave identically under node-fetch 2 and the global
implementation. Nothing touches `.body` as a Node stream, `.buffer()`, or the
`timeout`/`agent` options, which is where the two actually differ.

Both MCP suites pass before and after — including test-tools.js, which drives
the fetch call sites (DELETE, POST reissue, and the raw-PEM download).

I first wrote that the bump "would not have worked at all" and then disproved it
on Node 26 while trying to demonstrate it. The comment in index.js records the
version boundary rather than the wrong version of the claim.

release(clients): 0.1.4, and a publish gate that checks what gets installed (#526)

* release(clients): 0.1.4, and a publish gate that checks what gets installed

certmate-sdk and certmate-cli 0.1.3 are on PyPI reporting `__version__ ==
"0.1.2"`. The fix for that, and the `--version` flag added alongside it, landed
in #511 after 0.1.3 had already been published — so the repository's 0.1.3 and
the index's 0.1.3 are different code under the same number. 0.1.4 is what makes
the published packages match what the tree says they are.

What ships: `--version`/`-V` on the CLI, and `__version__` finally telling the
truth in both packages.

**The publish gate could not have caught the original drift.** It compared the
tag against the two `pyproject.toml` versions and stopped there, while
`__version__` — the number an installed package actually reports, and the one
a user quotes in a bug report — went unchecked. `tests/test_version_consistency
.py` covers it, but that suite does not run in the publish workflow, and PyPI
uploads are write-once: a mismatch has to be caught before the upload, not

security: upgrade legacy password hashes on login instead of keeping them for ever (#527)

* security: upgrade legacy password hashes on login instead of keeping them for ever

`_verify_password` accepts the pre-bcrypt formats — "sha256:<salt>:<hex>" and
the bare "<salt>:<hex>" — so operators who installed before those were replaced
can still log in. Nothing ever rewrote them.

So an admin account created before that change kept a salted SHA-256 for ever,
however many times it signed in. SHA-256 is fast: a leaked settings.json is
brute-forceable at GPU speed, where bcrypt and scrypt are deliberately slow.
The only way out was changing the password by hand, and nothing told anyone to.
CodeQL has flagged it as py/weak-sensitive-data-hashing since 2026-05-17, and
the alert was right — the fix in #402 changed how new passwords are hashed, not
what was already stored.

A successful login is the one moment the plaintext is in hand, so it is the
only place this can be done without asking the operator for anything. The hash
is now re-derived with the current algorithm and persisted, transparently.

Two more defects fell out of writing it, both proven by tests that fail against
the old code:

- **A failed write denied a correct login.** `_save_users` raising OSError was
  caught by the outer handler and returned None, so a full disk turned a valid
  password into "login failed". Persisting when the login happened is not worth
  refusing entry over.
- **A login racing a user deletion resurrected the user.** `_save_users(users)`
  wrote back the whole users map as this request had read it, so the deleted
  account came back. The write is now a targeted mutation that re-reads the
  record under the settings lock; the delete wins, which is correct.

Eight tests. Four of them fail against the old code: both legacy formats, the
write-failure case and the deletion race. The other four are the ones that must
NOT change — a modern hash is left byte-identical, a failed login rewrites
nothing, a hashing error does not lock anyone out, and the upgraded hash still
accepts the same password and rejects the wrong one.

Suite 2404 green, flake8 gate 0, bandit medium+ 0.

security: the audit chain called a double write "a deletion", and could not stop one (#530)

* security: the audit chain called a double write "a deletion", and could not stop one

Found while verifying artefacts a review pass had left on a development
instance: the tamper-evident chain there fails verification at seq 45, and the
verifier said "a deletion or reorder" — the vocabulary of tampering, on the one
file whose entire purpose is to be trustworthy evidence.

Nothing had been deleted. Seq 44 and 45 were each written twice, with identical
timestamps, on 2026-06-25, by two `migrate` operations. Two processes had
started against the same data directory: each ran `_recover_chain_state()`,
each cached the same `_next_seq`, and each appended with it. The
`threading.Lock` guarding the append cannot see another process.

**The diagnosis was wrong, which is the part that matters.** A seq that goes
backwards proves the opposite of a deletion: nothing was removed, something was
written twice. An operator reading "a deletion or reorder" concludes their audit
log was tampered with, and acts accordingly. `verify_chain` now separates three
cases it used to collapse into one:

- seq repeated / backwards -> "duplicate or out-of-order seq (the same seq
  written more than once - typically two processes appending to one chain file,
  not tampering)"
- seq jumped forward -> "missing entries (N entries absent - a deletion or
  truncation)"
- the first record disagreeing with a caller-supplied anchor -> "anchor
  mismatch", which is neither.

That third case was not in the original fix. An existing test caught it:
`test_a_wrong_anchor_seq_is_caught` passes an anchor of 99 against a file
starting at 3, and my first version called that "written more than once", which
is false. The suite did its job on me.

`sequence break: ` is kept as the leading phrase on all three, because two tests
and any operator tooling grep for it. The message is more specific, not
differently shaped.

**And the fault is now prevented, not just described.** `_chain_append` takes an
advisory `flock` on the chain file and, under it, re-reads the head when the
file has grown since our last write — a stale cached `_next_seq` is exactly how
the duplicate is produced, and a lock alone would not fix that. Cost in the
normal case is one `stat`. `fcntl` is imported defensively so a platform without
it degrades to the previous behaviour rather than refusing to log.

CertMate is single-instance by design and the Helm chart refuses a second
replica, but "by design" is not an enforcement, and this instance proves it.

Five tests. Three fail against main, including one that spawns two real
processes and reproduces the incident exactly: without the fix the chain comes
back `[0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, ...]`. The other two are controls — an intact chain
still verifies, and a genuine gap is still called a deletion.

fix(mcp): the documented job-polling loop could not run (#531)

* fix(mcp): the documented job-polling loop could not run

docs/mcp.md tells an agent to create or renew a certificate and then poll
`certmate_get_job` until it reports done. That loop was impossible.

The server only takes the background-job branch when the caller opts in —
`_wants_async` (modules/api/resources.py) looks for an `async` flag in the body
or `?async=` in the query. The MCP server sent neither: create sent four fields
and no flag, renew sent no body at all, reissue sent only the SAN/alias changes.

So every one of them took the synchronous certbot path. The tool call blocked
for the whole ACME exchange — minutes on a slow DNS provider — and `fetch` is
called without a timeout, so the MCP client's own timeout aborted the call while
certbot kept working. No `job_id` was ever produced, leaving
`certmate_get_job` correct, wired to the right endpoint, and unreachable.

All three now request async issuance.

**The server's contract did not declare the flag either.** `create_cert_model`
has no `async` field, while `ReissueCertificate` has always had one — yet
certmate-sdk has sent `async: True` on every create since 0.1.x. It worked only
because flask-restx validation is off: the published Swagger described a request
the shipped client does not make, and would have rejected it the day validation
was turned on. Declared.

**docs/mcp.md documented 13 of the 16 tools.** The three missing were
`certmate_update_certificate`, `certmate_get_certificate_file`, and
`certmate_delete_certificate` — which removes certificate files from disk and is
not reversible. An operator reading the documented surface would not have known
an agent could do it.

**And the role guidance was wrong in a way that produces a 403.** The docs said
`operator` for renew/deploy and told the reader to have the agent call
`certmate_list_dns_accounts` to pick an account id. Both `CertificateRunDeploy`
and `DNSAccounts` are `require_role('admin')` on the server, as is certificate
deletion. There is now a role table, with the three surprises called out and the
reason: they read or act on stored credentials.

Node.js "v18 or higher" corrected to ">= 20", which is what
`mcp/package.json` has always declared.

**The mcp/ suites were run by nothing.** No workflow, no Makefile target, not
run-tests.sh, not release.sh — while Dependabot updates mcp/ dependencies, so
those bumps shipped with a suite that never executed. That is why this
regression sat undetected. ci.yml now has an `mcp` job that runs them.

Gates, each checked to fail without its fix: the MCP suite asserts create/renew/
update send the flag, and three Python tests cover the tool enumeration, the
async contract and the CI wiring. The async test anchors on each tool's `case`
handler — my first two attempts looked at a fixed window around the call and
were satisfied by a comment in one direction and missed reissue's body in the
other.

fix: DigiCert ACME pointed at a hostname that stopped existing in February (#538)

* fix: DigiCert ACME pointed at a hostname that stopped existing in February

`acme.digicert.com` does not resolve. NXDOMAIN from Cloudflare's resolver,
while `one.digicert.com`, `www.digicert.com` and `docs.digicert.com` all
answer — so the name is gone, not the network. It was CertCentral's legacy
ACME service, which DigiCert stopped supporting on **24 February 2026**.

CertMate went on naming it for the six months since, in four places at once:
the CA registry (`production_url` and an invented `/v2/DV/staging` path), the
settings UI's pre-filled default and its placeholder, the CA guide in five
languages, and a test that asserted the dead URL. Meanwhile the README
advertises DigiCert ACME with EAB as a supported CA. Anyone who tried it got a
DNS failure.

The replacement is the DigiCert ONE mPKI directory, which returns a real one —
`newAccount`, `newNonce`, `newOrder`, `renewalInfo` — and sets
`externalAccountRequired: true`, matching `requires_eab`. It is regional: an
account outside the default region has its own URL, shown in CertCentral, and
`acme_url` already overrides it per certificate.

**Google's staging endpoint was broken too, differently.**
`dv.acme-staging.api.pki.goog` serves a certificate issued for another name, so
the TLS handshake fails hostname verification and no ACME client will talk to
it. Google's staging directory is `dv.acme-v02.test-api.pki.goog`, which
answers correctly. Found by the new test, not by looking.

`tests/test_ca_endpoints_are_live.py` asks every CA in the registry whether its
directory still exists. Two halves:

- offline, runs everywhere: every URL is https, and no URL names a host in
  RETIRED_HOSTS — so `acme.digicert.com` cannot come back quietly;
- network-marked, weekly: fetch each directory and check it is one, and fail if
  a directory demands EAB the registry does not know about.

The network half is deliberately **not** a required check. It found two real
defects, but five external CAs as a merge gate means someone else's outage
blocks a pull request; a CA does not retire an endpoint between two PRs. It
runs Mondays at 06:00 UTC and on demand.

The EAB check is one-directional on purpose. Requiring symmetry failed on
SSL.com, whose directory reports `externalAccountRequired: false` while its
ACME credentials come from the customer portal — RFC 8555 does not oblige a CA
to advertise the field, and only the other direction breaks issuance.

The other four CAs — ZeroSSL, Google production, SSL.com, Actalis — were probed
at the same time and all answered correctly. Suite 2541 passed / 6 skipped;
every check negative-verified, including one mutation that silently failed to
apply and had to be redone before it proved anything.

* test: three Copilot findings on #538

**A module-level `unit` mark put the network tests in the offline suite.**
Marks are additive, so `make test-unit` collected all 44 tests here — fifteen
of which reach five external CAs. An offline suite that quietly goes to the
internet is worse than one that says it does. The mark is now on the offline
tests individually; `-m unit` collects 29, `-m network` the other 15.

**`response.read(4096)` could truncate a directory mid-object**, so a healthy
CA would have failed on a JSON error. Reads to EOF now, capped at 1 MiB — far
past any real directory, still bounded against a misbehaving server.

**A comment that said something nothing made true.** It claimed only the
ca-endpoints job runs on the schedule trigger; the workflow-level `on:
schedule` starts every job. Rather than soften the comment, the other three
jobs now opt out of that trigger — a weekly full run would bury a CA

The ignore list named `certbot`, `josepy` and `acme` — the three obvious ones —
and blocked `certbot-dns-*` at MAJOR only, reasoning that minor and patch fixes
are compatible. They are not, and the exception cost a release. Every plugin

Worse, the list left out the pins that actually hold the stack together, with
nothing stopping a bump to any of them:

package is ignored with no narrowing, and every ignore entry corresponds to a

frozen dependency nobody can justify is how a CVE goes unnoticed, so an

deps: bcrypt 5.0.0, with the long-password lockout it would otherwise cause (#542)

* deps: bcrypt 5.0.0, with the long-password lockout it would otherwise cause

Dependabot proposed the bare bump in #354. Taken as-is it would have locked out
every operator whose password is longer than 72 bytes — silently, permanently,
with nothing in the logs.

bcrypt has always ignored everything past the 72nd byte. Up to 4.x it truncated
and carried on; **5.0.0 raises `ValueError`**. The stored hash was derived from
the truncated form and is still perfectly valid — only the call to check it
fails. And `_verify_password` catches `ValueError` and returns `False`, so the
operator is told their password is wrong. Setting a long password was worse
still: `_hash_password` has no such catch, so it would have raised out of the
request.

Measured before taking the bump, not reasoned about:

    >>> h = bcrypt.hashpw(("a"*100).encode()[:72], bcrypt.gensalt())   # 4.x
    >>> bcrypt.checkpw(("a"*100).encode(), h)                          # 5.0.0
    ValueError: password cannot be longer than 72 bytes

The truncation is now explicit and applied on both sides, so behaviour is
identical to 4.x rather than changing during a dependency upgrade. Two
passwords sharing their first 72 bytes remain equivalent, as they always have
been under bcrypt — a property of the algorithm, not something introduced here,
and now written down where the next reader will find it.

`tests/test_bcrypt_long_password_compat.py` covers the round trip, the
upgrade case (a hash written by 4.x, checked by 5.x), and — reading the source
rather than the library — that neither side hands bcrypt an untruncated
password. That last one replaced a first attempt that asserted bcrypt *raises*,
which tested bcrypt instead of CertMate and failed under 4.x; the suite now
passes on both versions.

Suite 2593 passed / 6 skipped. Negative-verified by removing the truncation and
watching the upgrade case fail.

* test: read the call, not the line (Copilot review, #542)

The regression check searched auth.py line by line, so it missed the very
pattern it guards against the moment the call wrapped:

    return bcrypt.checkpw(
        password.encode(),
        stored_hash.encode())

which is what black produces as soon as the expression grows. Confirmed before
fixing: the per-line regex does not match that, the same regex over the whole
text does.

It parses the AST now and asks about the call rather than about how it is
typed, plus fails if no bcrypt call is found at all — a check that has lost its
subject passes whatever the file says. Negative-verified three ways: the
single-line form, the wrapped form, and the calls disappearing entirely.

* docs: the API reference mixed two path conventions, and the translations lost the one that made it work

`templates/help.html` got a route-map check yesterday, when `GET /{domain}/tls`
turned out to be a 404 advertised four times. The API reference — the document
people integrate against — did not, and it had drifted a different way.

`docs/api.md` declared `Base URL: http://localhost:8000/api`, then wrote
thirteen paths relative to that base (`POST /client-certs/create`) and eight
with the prefix already on them (`GET /api/settings/rate-limits`). Read against
its own stated base, the second set resolves to `/api/api/...`. Whichever
convention a reader picked, one set was wrong.

The four translations were worse: they had **lost the base-URL line entirely**
while keeping the thirteen relative paths, so those had nothing to resolve
against at all. Fourth time in this sweep that the English page carried the
piece that made it work and the translations did not.

base URL is the host alone, so the convention no longer depends on a line a
translation can drop.

exists, and whether it accepts the verb documented beside it. Its matcher
prefers literal segments over parameters the way a router does: without that,

* ci: check the wiki, which nothing has ever looked at

The wiki is a separate git repository, so no workflow has ever read it — and it
has drifted three times, each time the same way: it keeps a second copy of
something this repo has since corrected, and nobody notices until someone
reads it.

Swept today with the checks built over the last week. Four findings, every one
already fixed in `docs/` months or days earlier:

- **Python 3.9**, five times, including "Tests on Python 3.9, 3.11, 3.12" when
  the matrix has one entry — and 3.9 cannot install requirements.txt at all.

`scripts/check_wiki.py` reads the expected port, Python version and pins from

a checker with its own copy of the numbers is a third thing to keep in sync. It
aborts rather than reporting success when it cannot read those sources, when
the wiki clone is empty, or when fewer than twenty pins parse: verified, all
three exit non-zero.

wiki is not part of the merge decision and a clone failing must never block a
pull request; a finding is news.

* test: tie SECURITY.md's deploy-hook claim to the control that enforces it

The policy tells a researcher, in as many words, that a hook command

whether to report a vulnerability — and adding `privkey.pem` to it would have

document stays the source; a second copy is the thing that drifts. The

different rule and a change to one has no reason to touch the other.

nowhere, arriving as certbot's dependency — is exactly what the published

fix: the pip pin defended the copy nothing uses (#553)

* fix: the pip pin defended the copy nothing uses

The runtime stage pinned pip with a comment giving reproducibility as the
reason — "an unpinned `--upgrade pip` would make the runtime stage's contents
depend on whatever PyPI happens to serve at build time, so two builds of the
same commit could differ".

The reasoning was right and it applied to the other copy. The builder stage ran
a bare `pip install -U pip` into /opt/venv, and `ENV PATH` puts /opt/venv/bin
first — so the pinned pip was the one nothing uses, and the one on PATH
floated. Measured inside the published v2.25.4 image, not inferred:

    /usr/local/bin/pip   26.1.2      pinned
    /opt/venv/bin/pip    26.2.1      whatever PyPI served that day
    which pip         -> /opt/venv/bin/pip

Two builds of the same commit did differ, precisely where the comment said they
must not. Found while verifying the release image from the inside.

Both stages take the same `PIP_VERSION` now, so a `--build-arg` moves them
together. Verified by building: all three of `pip`, `/usr/local/bin/pip` and
`/opt/venv/bin/pip` report 26.1.2, with certbot still on 2.10.0 and the app at
2.25.4.

`tests/test_pip_is_pinned_where_it_is_used.py` fails if either install loses
its version or the two ARG defaults drift apart — Docker scopes ARG per stage,
so the number has to be written twice and can diverge silently. It skips
comment lines, because the comments quote the old unpinned form to explain why
it was wrong and the first version of the check failed on its own
documentation.

* test: three Copilot findings on #553

**The check accepted a hard-coded pin.** `pip==[0-9]` in the pattern would have
let one stage sit at `pip==26.1.2` while `ARG PIP_VERSION` moved on — pinned
and drifted, which is the state this file exists to prevent rather than a
milder version of it. It requires the shared ARG now.

**`_pip_installs()` ran twice at collection**, once for the values and once for
the ids. Third time this shape has come up here; parsed once into a constant.

**`-U` next to an exact pin was misleading.** Verified before dropping it that
an exact `==` specifier installs that version regardless of what is present,
including downgrading 26.2.1 to 26.1.2, so the flag added nothing. setuptools
and wheel keep theirs. Rebuilt: pip is 26.1.2 on both paths, certbot 2.10.0.

ci: ask the built image whether its providers can actually reach certbot (#558)

* ci: ask the built image whether its providers can actually reach certbot

The suite validates the issuance path against mocks. Nine test files stub
`check_certbot_plugin_installed` to return True, so the one guard between a
configured provider and certbot's "unrecognized arguments" is never exercised
against reality.

That is how Infomaniak shipped: a strategy, a credentials writer, a factory
entry, a README row, and no plugin in any image ever published. Nothing was
wrong with the code — the plugin simply was not there, and nothing looked.

`scripts/check_providers.py` looks, inside the artefact rather than in a
developer's virtualenv where the answer is whatever happens to be installed
locally. It needs no test dependencies (the image has no pytest) and no
hand-maintained table of names: the environment says which distribution
provides which certbot plugin, and the requirements file says what the build
was meant to carry. It catches two failure modes, both verified by mutating a
real image:

  infomaniak: certbot has no plugin 'dns-infomaniak', but
  certbot-dns-infomaniak is pinned in requirements.txt (requirements.txt:63) —
  this build was meant to carry it.

  infomaniak: certbot has no plugin 'dns-infomaniak', yet
  certbot-dns-infomaniak is installed — the entry point is named something
  else.

The second is the shape of #364, where porkbun's credential keys did not match
its entry point.

The requirements file is an explicit argument, not a guess: reading every
requirements*.txt made `he-ddns` — which lives in requirements-extended.txt —
look missing from an image that never claimed to carry it. Verified against
both published variants: the default image reports five providers it does not
carry and exits zero; the minimal image reports many more and also exits zero,
because neither was meant to carry them.

Two bugs of mine, found by running it rather than by reading it. It first
reported three problems, all false: I normalised distribution names PEP 503 on
the requirements side and not on the metadata side, so `certbot_dns_porkbun`
never matched `certbot-dns-porkbun` and two working plugins looked broken —
the same mistake the entry-point contract test made before it, which is why
normalisation is one function now, used on both sides.

And the first mutation test said the check did not catch Infomaniak. It did:
`pip uninstall` had failed with PermissionError because the container runs as a
non-root user, so the plugin was never removed and I read the result of a
mutation that never happened.

* fix: resolve the distribution before testing it, not the guess (Copilot, #558)

The misnamed-entry-point branch tested `candidate` — the naive
`"certbot-" + plugin` guess — against the installed set, while `owner` held
the distribution actually resolved from the pins. For any provider whose
package is not literally `certbot-<plugin>` that branch could never fire.

EdgeDNS is the case: plugin `edgedns`, distribution `certbot-plugin-edgedns`.
The guess `certbot-edgedns` matches nothing, so a renamed entry point there
would have been reported as an absent optional provider rather than as broken
packaging.

Now the installed and pinned sets are searched for a distribution matching the
provider key, and the guess is the last resort — normalised, or it could never
match either set anyway. Verified on a real image by renaming edgedns's entry
point: it fails, and names certbot-plugin-edgedns rather than a package that
does not exist.

test: exercise the storage backends against MinIO and Vault, not a fake of them (#559)

* test: exercise the storage backends against MinIO and Vault, not a fake of them

Second item of the validation plan. `tests/test_s3_compatible_backend.py` is a
good test — a faithful in-memory S3, a real round-trip, no mocks — and it
cannot disagree with me: a fake reproduces my understanding of the protocol,
including wherever that is wrong. Two of the five remote backends run for real
at no meaningful cost.

The first live run found two things the fake never asked about.

**Every remote backend silently mangled anything that is not UTF-8.** All five
decoded with `errors='replace'`. Measured against MinIO:

    in:  b"\x00\x01\xff\xfe"
    out: b"\x00\x01\xef\xbf\xbd\xef\xbf\xbd"

Nothing sends such content today: both places that assemble `cert_files`
iterate CERTIFICATE_FILES, four PEM files. But the signature says
`Dict[str, bytes]` and `cert.pfx` — PKCS#12, binary — already exists elsewhere
in the product. The day it joins that tuple, the local copy would be correct
and every remote copy quietly ruined, with a successful store reported. They
refuse now, which turns a corrupt disaster-recovery copy into a failed store
and a logged reason.

**S3 and Vault claimed to have deleted certificates that were never there.**
Both return success for a delete of an absent key — idempotent, and the local
filesystem backend returns False for the same situation. That difference
reaches the operator: CertificateManager logs "verify by hand that no private
key remains there" on a False and stays quiet on a True. So the same deletion
was reassuring on one backend and alarming on another, on the path that removes
private key material. All three now agree: removed is True, nothing to remove
is False.

The suite skips when its endpoints are unset — a laptop without containers is
not punished — and **fails** when one is set and the server does not answer.
CI always sets them, so a service that never started cannot pass as a green run
of zero tests; the job also asserts the test count, because "0 passed" is a
suspiciously agreeable result.

One thing to flag: I first wrote both service images with digests I had made
up. They looked exactly like digests. Replaced with the real ones and each
verified to resolve before committing.

Suite 2825 passed / 6 skipped offline; 10 passed live against MinIO and Vault.

* fix: six Copilot findings on #559, and the CI job that did not start

**The job never ran.** MinIO as a `services:` container failed to initialise:
a service container cannot be given a command, and MinIO's image does nothing
without `server /data`. Both containers start in a step now, with an explicit
readiness wait and their logs dumped on timeout — which is also what acme-dns
will need next, since it has the same constraint.

**The existence probe reported "nothing to delete" for questions it could not
answer.** `delete_certificate` used `certificate_exists()`, which returns False
on *any* exception — so a timeout, an expired Vault token or a 403 would have
been reported as an absent certificate. On the path whose caller warns "verify
by hand that no private key remains", that is the wrong direction to guess in.
Both backends now probe precisely: only a 404/NoSuchKey (S3) or InvalidPath
(Vault) means absent, and anything else propagates to the handler that logs a
real failure. Measured with deliberately wrong credentials: 403 and "failed to
authenticate" are now logged errors, not a quiet "there was nothing there".

**hvac was installed by name in CI**, making that job the one place its version
floats. It comes from requirements-vault-storage.txt now, the same constraint a
real Vault deployment gets.

Three smaller ones, all accurate: the module docstring claimed the live run
found one thing when the file pins two; `_as_text` listed Infisical under both
"JSON blob" and "one secret per file" (it is the latter); and the reachability
probe left an HTTPError unclosed, which is a file-like response holding a
socket.

Suite 2829 offline, 10 live against MinIO and Vault.

* fix: do not import an optional dependency in a path that must work without it

The Vault existence probe added `import hvac.exceptions` to catch InvalidPath
precisely. hvac is optional — it lives in requirements-vault-storage.txt, not
the core set — and the offline suite exercises this method with a fake client
in an environment where the real package is absent. Every fake-backed delete
turned into 'No module named hvac', which CI caught on
test_storage_backends_cloud_crud.py.

Matched by class name instead. Less elegant, and it keeps the method working
where it was built to work. Reproduced the CI environment by uninstalling hvac
locally before believing the fix: 29 passed on the fake-backed suite, 2829 on
the offline suite, 10 still passing live against a real Vault.

* chore: move the acme-dns live tests out of this PR

They arrived here by a `git add -A` after a branch switch — the same slip
twice before in this repo — and they do not belong: this PR is the storage
backends, and the acme-dns suite needs its own containers (acme-dns plus the

test: drive the acme-dns hook against a real acme-dns, and ask DNS (#560)

* test: drive the acme-dns hook against a real acme-dns, and ask DNS

Third item of the validation plan, and the path with the worst precedent in
this product. The certbot plugin CertMate used until v2.24.0 exposes no
credentials-file option at all, so certbot rejected the command line and every
acme-dns issuance failed — in every release that advertised the feature. The
replacement publishes the TXT record itself and was verified by hand once,
against acme-dns.io. Nothing has verified it since.

A mock cannot verify it. The failure was an API contract that looked right, so
the only test worth writing drives the real hook and then asks DNS whether the
record is there. That last step is the whole point: "the POST returned 200" is
what a fake would have told you, and is what the broken implementation
effectively said for releases.

Five tests: the record is served and matches, a second validation replaces the
first (a renewal against the same subdomain), wrong credentials are refused
rather than ignored, a mismatched alias is caught before the network, and
delete is a no-op — acme-dns has no delete, and a hook that raised there would
fail certbot's cleanup after a successful validation.

The suite skips when its endpoint is unset and **fails** when it is set and the
server is silent; the job asserts the test count too. Three things learned the
hard way while building it, all recorded in the workflow:

- acme-dns needs postgres. The official image is built without the sqlite
  driver and dies on the first API call with `sql: unknown driver "sqlite3"`.
- its `port` must be quoted in the config, or it refuses to start on
  "incompatible types: TOML value has type int64".
- acme-dns rejects a TXT that is not exactly 43 characters — the length of a
  base64url SHA-256 digest — so a test that sends a friendly string tests the
  error path by accident. The suite generates real validation values.

Both image digests were read from the registry and are not the invented ones I
nearly shipped in the storage PR.

by querying its DNS on port 18053.

* test: fail loudly if postgres never comes up; assert what acme-dns actually keeps

acme-dns serves the two most recent TXT values by design, so the second
validation joins the first rather than replacing it. The test now drives
three and checks both halves: the two newest are served, the oldest is
not. The pg_isready loop gets the post-loop check it was missing.

Both are Copilot findings on #560.

fix: follow the IdP end-session URL on logout, and build it after a restart (#573)

* fix: follow the IdP end-session URL on logout, and build it after a restart

The backend returned oidc_logout_url; doLogout() in base.html never read
the body and went to /login. So the IdP session survived every CertMate
logout and the next SSO login signed the user back in without a prompt
(#564). The button now follows an absolute http(s) URL when one comes
back, /login otherwise.

build_end_session_url() also fetches the discovery document when
Authlib's lazy metadata cache is empty — the case after a process
restart, which is exactly when a still-valid SSO session is most likely
to log out. The settings hint now says the post-logout URI has to be
registered at the IdP too.

Closes #564

fix: the four defects that survived the full-field audit (#581)

* fix: the settings lock protected a snapshot, not the file

`update()` and `atomic_update()` hold `self._lock` for the whole
read-modify-write, so two writes cannot interleave. But the "read" was
`load_settings()`, which inside a Flask request returns the dict cached on
`flask.g` when the request started — so the merge base was a snapshot, and
whichever request finished last silently reverted the other.

The window is not milliseconds. On the synchronous issuance path — the
default, since async is opt-in — cert_service.py loads settings at :183, runs
certbot, and writes at :242, all in the same request thread. For the whole
duration of an issuance every other write to settings.json was rolled back: a
user created, a domain registered, a DNS credential saved. A domain rolled out
of settings['domains'] is never visited by check_renewals again and its
certificate expires in silence.

The same snapshot defeated the protection it was supposed to feed:
`atomic_update`'s `protected_keys` restores `users` and `api_keys` from
`existing`, so a cached `existing` restored a deleted account — password hash
included — after delete_user had reported success.

load_settings grows `use_cache`, and the two write methods pass False. That is
the whole product: nothing outside settings.py calls save_settings, so every
write path funnels through these two methods. The read path is untouched —
`/api/certificates` still parses settings.json once per request, and all six
contracts in test_settings_request_scoped_cache.py still hold.

The tests are a real race: two threads, two real request contexts, no mocks,
the file on disk as the judge. Both fail on the code they describe.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: a backup that cannot restore is not a backup

Every automatic backup is masked. save_settings calls
create_unified_backup(settings, reason) and include_secrets defaults to False,
which writes the mask sentinel in place of every credential. That default is
right: a leaked backup must not also be a credential dump. What was wrong is
that every restore path treated those archives as authoritative.

The manifest has recorded `secrets_masked` since unified backups existed.
Nothing read it. So when settings.json could not be parsed, load_settings
installed the newest masked archive as live settings: every password hash,
bearer token, API key hash, OIDC client secret and DNS credential became the
literal sentinel. No login works, no token works, SSO is broken, every renewal
fails at the provider — and setup_completed is still True, so the wizard does
not reopen. The log said "Settings restored successfully from backup".

Four changes, one defect:

- The restore now skips archives that cannot restore and picks the newest one
  that can, saying loudly in the log what it found and how to make a usable
  backup.
- When nothing usable exists it refuses instead of recreating the file.
  safe_file_read returns the default for a JSON typo, a PermissionError and an
  empty read alike, and settings.json is written atomically (mkstemp + fsync +
  rename), so the app never produces this state itself: something outside it
  did, and overwriting destroys the operator's only copy of a file a text
  editor could have repaired. SettingsUnreadableError deliberately escapes the
  catch-all below it, because returning the defaults in-memory leaves
  setup_completed False — i.e. an instance that cannot read its own
  credentials would come up world-open. app.py exits 1 with one actionable
  line instead.
- The pre-restore rollback archive is written with include_secrets=True. It
  exists solely to undo the restore that follows it; masked, it was a safety
  net that could not catch anything. It never leaves the host, is chmod 0600,
  and the opt-in is audit-logged with the restore entry.
- A login no longer writes a backup. Recording last_login wrote a full ZIP of
  settings + certificates and then pruned to MAX_BACKUPS_PER_TYPE, so login
  traffic alone evicted every restore point an operator wanted. A password
  hash upgrade still writes one, because that is a real change.

test_disaster_recovery_round_trip.py is the test nobody had written: configure

tests for creating backups, listing them, masking them, and the restore

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: setup mode must be a door that only closes

is_setup_mode() is not a mild state. _authenticate_request returns
{'username': 'setup_user', 'role': 'admin'} for a caller with no credential at
all — enough to read /api/settings, mint API keys, create admin users and
download private keys, since resources.py gates the private-key download on
the operator role and setup_user is admin.

It exists so a fresh install can be bootstrapped, and it closes as soon as any
credential is configured. Nothing checked the way back.

v2.21.4 added the OIDC branch to is_setup_mode() to CLOSE a real hole: an
SSO-only box has no bearer token and never gets local_auth_enabled set,
because OIDC JIT provisioning does not flip it, so it sat world-open forever.
That fix was right. Its side effect was that closure now depends on a
checkbox — and unchecking "Enable OIDC/SSO" put the whole instance back into
anonymous-admin, with no guard on the route and no warning beside the toggle
(the "Authentication is disabled" banner lives on the Users tab).

is_setup_mode() is now expressed once, as setup_mode_for(settings), and the
new would_open_setup_mode(candidate) asks the same question about a change
that has not been written yet. One definition, two callers: a guard that
re-implements the predicate it defends drifts away from it, and the drift is
invisible until the day it matters. It returns False when the instance is
already in setup mode, so a fresh install stays configurable.

Two routes call it. POST /api/auth/config guarded only the ENABLE direction
("Create admin first"); disabling was unguarded. POST /api/auth/oidc/settings
had no guard at all — and there it fires only for the deliberate turn-off,
because a payload that clears issuer_url while enabled stays true is already
rejected by _validate_config with a 400 and never written: "client_id is
required" tells the admin what they got wrong, and a security refusal does
not. delete_user already refuses to remove the last admin, so the third way in
was closed.

The toggle also carries a line saying what turning it off means, which is
where an operator would actually read it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: publish the four PEMs as one unit, and repair a copy that disagrees

The renewal path copied certbot's four files from live/<domain>/ to the flat
directory one at a time. _atomic_binary_copy is atomic per file; there was no
atomicity across the four, the exception handlers unlink credential files and
release the domain lock but roll nothing back, and privkey.pem is LAST in
CERTIFICATE_FILES.

A failure on the fourth file therefore left a new cert.pem, chain.pem and
fullchain.pem beside the PREVIOUS privkey.pem. Those flat files are what
/api/certificates/<domain>/download serves off local disk, what deploy hooks
ship and what the storage backends push. The pair cannot complete a handshake.

The permanence is what made it dangerous rather than merely unlucky: the next
scheduled renewal fingerprints live/, finds it already fresh, concludes
renewed=False and returns BEFORE the copy loop, so nothing ever retried it.
check_renewals booked the domain as skipped_not_due — no failure, no
certificate_failed event, no email. Only force=true broke out, and an operator
has no reason to force a certificate the dashboard says is fine.

_publish_flat_files stages all four and only then promotes them, so a failure
mid-way leaves the previous generation intact and internally consistent —
still the old certificate, still serving. The promote loop is four renames
within one directory, which is as close to atomic as a multi-file publish gets
on POSIX.

And the no-op branch now reconciles instead of returning blind:
_stale_flat_files compares the served copy against live/ (the only ground
truth; an absent live/ means an imported cert with nothing to reconcile) and
republishes when they disagree, reporting what it repaired rather than doing
it silently. That is what heals an instance already in this state — the staged
publish alone would only stop it happening again.

Reproduced the pre-fix outcome directly: the old per-file loop failing on the
fourth file leaves cert.pem NEW and privkey.pem OLD. Both halves of the fix
have a test that fails without them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: a share-safe backup now carries no private key, and says so

include_secrets=False masked the settings tree and called the archive
share-safe — in the manifest (secrets_masked), in its own docstring and
in the web route's. The zip walk never looked at what it was adding:
every ACME privkey.pem (flat, live/, archive/), the ACME account
private_key.json, data/certs/ca/ca.key and any .pfx went into every
automatic backup, 0600 and unencrypted unless a passphrase was set.

Share-safe now means it: no privkey*.pem, private_key.json, .key, .pfx
or .p12 from either tree; key_material_excluded + key_files_excluded in
both copies of the manifest; the log line says keys=excluded (N files).
include_secrets=True is unchanged — the disaster-recovery archive with
plaintext settings and every key, encrypted at rest with
CERTMATE_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE.

Also: backup_reason lands in the archive file name and was concatenated
raw; it is now a short [A-Za-z0-9_.-] token, so '../../x' cannot steer
the write outside backups/unified/ (audit, file_operations.py:292).

Stacked on #581, which makes the restore path honest about what a
masked archive can do.

* review: exclude certbot's keys/ too, and let the restore read the flag it writes

keys/NNNN_key-certbot.pem — certbot's copy of every key it generated,
