Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: a backup that cannot restore is not a backup

Every automatic backup is masked. save_settings calls
create_unified_backup(settings, reason) and include_secrets defaults to False,
which writes the mask sentinel in place of every credential. That default is
right: a leaked backup must not also be a credential dump. What was wrong is
that every restore path treated those archives as authoritative.

The manifest has recorded `secrets_masked` since unified backups existed.
Nothing read it. So when settings.json could not be parsed, load_settings
installed the newest masked archive as live settings: every password hash,
bearer token, API key hash, OIDC client secret and DNS credential became the
literal sentinel. No login works, no token works, SSO is broken, every renewal
fails at the provider — and setup_completed is still True, so the wizard does
not reopen. The log said "Settings restored successfully from backup".

Four changes, one defect:

- The restore now skips archives that cannot restore and picks the newest one
  that can, saying loudly in the log what it found and how to make a usable
  backup.
- When nothing usable exists it refuses instead of recreating the file.
  safe_file_read returns the default for a JSON typo, a PermissionError and an
  empty read alike, and settings.json is written atomically (mkstemp + fsync +
  rename), so the app never produces this state itself: something outside it
  did, and overwriting destroys the operator's only copy of a file a text
  editor could have repaired. SettingsUnreadableError deliberately escapes the
  catch-all below it, because returning the defaults in-memory leaves
  setup_completed False — i.e. an instance that cannot read its own
  credentials would come up world-open. app.py exits 1 with one actionable
  line instead.
- The pre-restore rollback archive is written with include_secrets=True. It
  exists solely to undo the restore that follows it; masked, it was a safety
  net that could not catch anything. It never leaves the host, is chmod 0600,
  and the opt-in is audit-logged with the restore entry.
- A login no longer writes a backup. Recording last_login wrote a full ZIP of
  settings + certificates and then pruned to MAX_BACKUPS_PER_TYPE, so login
  traffic alone evicted every restore point an operator wanted. A password
  hash upgrade still writes one, because that is a real change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: publish the four PEMs as one unit, and repair a copy that disagrees

The renewal path copied certbot's four files from live/<domain>/ to the flat
directory one at a time. _atomic_binary_copy is atomic per file; there was no
atomicity across the four, the exception handlers unlink credential files and
release the domain lock but roll nothing back, and privkey.pem is LAST in
CERTIFICATE_FILES.

A failure on the fourth file therefore left a new cert.pem, chain.pem and
fullchain.pem beside the PREVIOUS privkey.pem. Those flat files are what
/api/certificates/<domain>/download serves off local disk, what deploy hooks
ship and what the storage backends push. The pair cannot complete a handshake.

The permanence is what made it dangerous rather than merely unlucky: the next
scheduled renewal fingerprints live/, finds it already fresh, concludes
renewed=False and returns BEFORE the copy loop, so nothing ever retried it.
check_renewals booked the domain as skipped_not_due — no failure, no
certificate_failed event, no email. Only force=true broke out, and an operator
has no reason to force a certificate the dashboard says is fine.

_publish_flat_files stages all four and only then promotes them, so a failure
mid-way leaves the previous generation intact and internally consistent —
still the old certificate, still serving. The promote loop is four renames
within one directory, which is as close to atomic as a multi-file publish gets
on POSIX.

And the no-op branch now reconciles instead of returning blind:
_stale_flat_files compares the served copy against live/ (the only ground
truth; an absent live/ means an imported cert with nothing to reconcile) and
republishes when they disagree, reporting what it repaired rather than doing
it silently. That is what heals an instance already in this state — the staged
publish alone would only stop it happening again.

Reproduced the pre-fix outcome directly: the old per-file loop failing on the
fourth file leaves cert.pem NEW and privkey.pem OLD. Both halves of the fix
have a test that fails without them.

* fix: renewal hands certbot the private CA's trust bundle, and quarantines corrupt metadata

Two properties issuance had and renewal did not.

REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE: build_certbot_command writes the private CA's
ca_cert to a temp file and passes it at issuance; renew_certificate built
its own environment and never read metadata['ca_provider'], so every
renewal against a private ACME CA whose endpoint presents a certificate
from its own root failed TLS verification — silently, until expiry.

deployment_* key gone, no .corrupt-* copy, success reported. The path
now uses _load_metadata(), which quarantines.

literal sentinel. No login works, no token works, SSO is broken, every renewal
fails at the provider — and setup_completed is still True, so the wizard does
not reopen. The log said "Settings restored successfully from backup".

Four changes, one defect:

- The restore now skips archives that cannot restore and picks the newest one
  that can, saying loudly in the log what it found and how to make a usable
  backup.
- When nothing usable exists it refuses instead of recreating the file.
  safe_file_read returns the default for a JSON typo, a PermissionError and an
  empty read alike, and settings.json is written atomically (mkstemp + fsync +
  rename), so the app never produces this state itself: something outside it
  did, and overwriting destroys the operator's only copy of a file a text
  editor could have repaired. SettingsUnreadableError deliberately escapes the
  catch-all below it, because returning the defaults in-memory leaves
  setup_completed False — i.e. an instance that cannot read its own
  credentials would come up world-open. app.py exits 1 with one actionable
  line instead.
- The pre-restore rollback archive is written with include_secrets=True. It
  exists solely to undo the restore that follows it; masked, it was a safety
  net that could not catch anything. It never leaves the host, is chmod 0600,
  and the opt-in is audit-logged with the restore entry.
- A login no longer writes a backup. Recording last_login wrote a full ZIP of
  settings + certificates and then pruned to MAX_BACKUPS_PER_TYPE, so login
  traffic alone evicted every restore point an operator wanted. A password
  hash upgrade still writes one, because that is a real change.

test_disaster_recovery_round_trip.py is the test nobody had written: configure
an instance, back it up, destroy it, restore it, and try to log in. There were
tests for creating backups, listing them, masking them, and the restore
endpoint's authorization and zip-bomb limits — none that asked whether a
backup can bring the instance back. It could not.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: publish the four PEMs as one unit, and repair a copy that disagrees

The renewal path copied certbot's four files from live/<domain>/ to the flat
directory one at a time. _atomic_binary_copy is atomic per file; there was no
atomicity across the four, the exception handlers unlink credential files and
release the domain lock but roll nothing back, and privkey.pem is LAST in
CERTIFICATE_FILES.

A failure on the fourth file therefore left a new cert.pem, chain.pem and
fullchain.pem beside the PREVIOUS privkey.pem. Those flat files are what
/api/certificates/<domain>/download serves off local disk, what deploy hooks
ship and what the storage backends push. The pair cannot complete a handshake.

The permanence is what made it dangerous rather than merely unlucky: the next
scheduled renewal fingerprints live/, finds it already fresh, concludes
renewed=False and returns BEFORE the copy loop, so nothing ever retried it.
check_renewals booked the domain as skipped_not_due — no failure, no
certificate_failed event, no email. Only force=true broke out, and an operator
has no reason to force a certificate the dashboard says is fine.

_publish_flat_files stages all four and only then promotes them, so a failure
mid-way leaves the previous generation intact and internally consistent —
still the old certificate, still serving. The promote loop is four renames
within one directory, which is as close to atomic as a multi-file publish gets
on POSIX.

And the no-op branch now reconciles instead of returning blind:
_stale_flat_files compares the served copy against live/ (the only ground
truth; an absent live/ means an imported cert with nothing to reconcile) and
republishes when they disagree, reporting what it repaired rather than doing
it silently. That is what heals an instance already in this state — the staged
publish alone would only stop it happening again.

Reproduced the pre-fix outcome directly: the old per-file loop failing on the
fourth file leaves cert.pem NEW and privkey.pem OLD. Both halves of the fix
have a test that fails without them.

fix: the list of advisories we are living with had stopped being the list (#601)

CertMate holds cryptography and pyopenssl behind their fixed versions on
purpose: every release that clears the advisories needs a pyOpenSSL that
breaks the pinned ACME stack, and cryptography==50.0.0 installs cleanly and
then kills `certbot --version`. That decision is recorded in SECURITY.md and
the Dependabot alert is dismissed as tolerable_risk pointing at it. Two steps,
and the pair is the whole record.

The record had drifted. SECURITY.md documented GHSA-537c-gmf6-5ccf, dismissed
months ago. Three more advisories against the same pin were published on
2026-08-03 and were open, unassessed and unmentioned — GHSA-g6cj-pr64-35w5
(HIGH), GHSA-jwv3-5hgf-82ww (HIGH) and GHSA-m2h6-j472-rp4c (MEDIUM). The
comment beside the pin named the dismissed one too. Nothing in the reasoning
was wrong; it had simply stopped being the complete list, and nothing looked.
v2.26.0 shipped past it.

Assessed: none of the three is reachable. Two need the X.509 verifier
(PolicyBuilder / ClientVerifier / ServerVerifier), one needs PKCS#7
EnvelopedData decryption. Neither API is called anywhere in the shipped stack
— checked across modules/, app.py and the pinned certbot==2.10.0 /
acme==3.3.0 / josepy==1.13.0. What CertMate uses from cryptography is X.509
parsing and building, Fernet, hashes, key serialization, RSA and Ed25519, and
PBKDF2; the .pfx export calls serialization.pkcs12, a different structure and
a different code path from the PKCS#7 EnvelopedData the Bleichenbacher
advisory describes. Unlike GHSA-537c, whose defect sat in the statically
linked OpenSSL, these three are in cryptography's own code and are reached
through one named API each — which is what makes the argument hold.

And the constraint has tightened: clearing all three needs cryptography 50.0.0,
the exact version SECURITY.md already proves fatal.

The pin does not move. What changes is that the record is complete again, kept
in one place, and guarded:

- SECURITY.md lists all four with severity, defect, the API that reaches them
  and the first fixed version, and says that an advisory not listed there has
  not been assessed.
- The requirements comments no longer enumerate advisories. Naming one is how
  this drifted; they point at the section instead. test_dependabot_holds_the_stack
  anchors on that pointer rather than on a GHSA id for the same reason — a
  pointer does not go stale when an advisory arrives.
- scripts/check_advisories.py asks the repository which advisories it is
  actually carrying (open, or dismissed as tolerable_risk — both are decisions
  to keep running with a known flaw) and fails when one is missing from
  SECURITY.md. A documented advisory that no longer alerts is not a failure:
  that is the normal end of a dismissal. It refuses to run without a token
  rather than report success on an unread list, and follows the Link header,
  because the alerts endpoint answers `?page=2` with 400.
- A weekly CI job runs it. No test can see live alerts, so a merge gate could
  not have caught this.

Verified against the live repository: exit 1 naming the three on the pre-fix
SECURITY.md, exit 0 on the corrected one.

fix: a batch of new domains is no longer a batch of new ACME accounts (#604)

* fix: a batch of new domains is no longer a batch of new ACME accounts

--config-dir is per domain (ca_manager.build_certbot_command), and certbot
keeps its ACME account under the config dir. So every new domain registered a
brand-new account with the CA.

That is not a rounding error in this product. POST /api/web/certificates/batch
accepts 50 domains in one request (cert_routes.py:84), so onboarding a batch
was 50 account registrations from one IP in one run, which no CA allows. It
also left 50 account private keys on disk, each a credential that every backup
then carried.

Before certbot runs, the new domain's config dir is now seeded with the
accounts/ tree of a sibling issued under the same CA provider and CA account.
certbot finds a registered account and skips registration.

This cannot bind a certificate to the wrong account. certbot indexes accounts
by the ACME directory URL, so a tree that does not match the --server in use is
ignored and it registers exactly as before; the ca_provider / ca_account_id
match is the belt-and-braces on top, for two CA accounts with different EAB
credentials on the same server. A domain that already has an account is left
untouched — never clobber a registered key with somebody else's.

Best-effort by design: any failure leaves the directory alone and the run
proceeds unchanged. This is an optimisation on the issuance path, and the
issuance path must not acquire a new way to fail.

Six tests: the reuse, the three cases that must NOT donate (existing account,
different provider, different CA account), a copy failure that never reaches
the caller, and the wiring — because a helper nobody calls fixes nothing, and
after certbot has run it is too late. The wiring test fails when the call is
removed.

Found by the 2026-08-18 audit (#591). The finder's claim about Let's Encrypt's
specific limits was wrong and the verifier said so; what makes this real is the
batch endpoint this repository ships, which was measured rather than assumed.

fix: a revocation no longer disappears into a renewal that was already signing (#603)

* fix: a revocation no longer disappears into a renewal that was already signing

renew_certificate read the certificate's metadata at the top, spent the length
of a key generation and a signature inside create_client_certificate, and then
wrote that snapshot back wholesale to mark the old certificate superseded. A
revocation landing in between was inside the window, and the write erased
`revoked`, `revoked_at` and `reason_revoked`.

That field is what the OCSP responder answers from (ocsp_crl.py:49), so the
responder went back to saying **good** for a certificate the operator had just
revoked — the one answer a client trusts when deciding whether to accept it.

default outcome for a plausible token.

The strength validator matched a denylist of bare nouns — 'api', 'key',
'token', 'secret', 'admin', 'test', 'demo', 'default', 'example' — as

fix: a restore no longer truncates the file it overwrites, nor reports a partial restore as success (#611)

* fix: a restore no longer truncates the file it overwrites, and a partial restore is not reported as success

restore_unified_backup extracted each archive member with
`open(target_path, 'wb')` in the same `with` as the zip member, so the
destination was truncated to zero before the first byte was read. A corrupt
member (a bad CRC pulled back from an off-site copy) or an oversize one then
hit `except: ... continue`, leaving the pre-existing file at zero bytes while
the function returned True and the API answered 200 "restored atomically
successfully". The certificates/ branch — every privkey.pem, every
archive/privkeyN.pem, the ACME account key — had no cleanup at all; the data/
branch removed the half-written file but still reported success.

Measured before the change, over HTTP, against a real Let's Encrypt staging
certificate: restoring an archive whose privkey.pem member was corrupt
returned 200 "restored atomically successfully" and left the live 1708-byte
key at 0 bytes, with GET /api/certificates still reporting exists=true,
needs_renewal=false. The instance looked healthy and could not serve TLS.

Both branches now go through one helper that stages each member into a
sibling temp file and promotes it with os.replace — an atomic rename on the
same filesystem. The live file is untouched until a complete copy exists, so
a failed extract leaves it exactly as it was rather than truncated or
deleted. The permission (0600 for key material, 0644 for public cert
material) is stamped on the temp file before the rename, so there is no
window where a restored key is world-readable.

Using the same helper for both branches removes the divergence that caused
this: one branch cleaning up and the other not was the whole bug. The data/
branch keeps its larger per-entry ceiling and chunked streaming (the audit
log outgrows the 10 MB PEM cap); it just no longer leaves a hole behind.

The second half — reporting success — is closed too. Failed members are
collected, and a non-empty list raises RestoreIncompleteError instead of
returning True. The API turns that into a 500 that names the failed members
and tells the operator the instance is in a mixed state and to roll back with
the pre-restore backup. Good members stay restored; failed ones kept their
pre-existing files.

Measured after the change, same real-cert path: the corrupt-archive restore
returns 500 naming certificates/<domain>/privkey.pem, the live key stays
1708 bytes, and the cert/key pair still verifies. Control: an intact archive
still restores and returns 200. Suite: 2987 passed, 0 failed; 5 new tests
with a behavioural control proving the old code truncates and the new code
raises.

* refactor: the atomic extract helper is 0600 by default, public material relaxed by the caller

CodeQL flagged the helper's `os.chmod(tmp_path, mode)` as "overly permissive
file permissions": passing the mode as a variable, it cannot prove the value
is not world-writable, and 0644 is world-readable. The behaviour was correct
— public certificate material (cert/chain/fullchain) must be readable by nginx
and other containers that bind-mount the cert dir, which is what main already
did with a literal `os.chmod(target, 0o644)` — but a variable mode on the one
chmod is a pattern the analyser rightly distrusts.

The helper now promotes every file at a literal 0600, restrictive by default,
so a private key is never even briefly world-readable. The certificates/
caller widens the public members to 0644 afterwards, with a literal mode, on a
file that is already 0600 — a widening, not a window. The data/ caller wants
0600 for everything and so needs nothing further. Behaviour is identical;
permissions are still asserted by the tests (0600 on privkey.pem, 0644 on
cert.pem).

* fix: close the temp fd when a member fails to open, and document the raised exception

Both from Copilot review, both real.

The atomic extract opened the mkstemp fd and the zip member in one `with`,
with the member on the left: `with zipf.open(file_info) as source,
os.fdopen(fd, 'wb') as target`. If zipf.open raises — a corrupt member header
— os.fdopen is never reached and the mkstemp fd is never adopted by a file
object, so it leaks. One descriptor per failed member, until the process runs
out of them: on a restore of an archive with many bad entries, that is a
denial of the restore itself. Measured: 200 failing opens leaked exactly 200
descriptors. os.fdopen now goes first, so the fd is owned and closed on the
way out even when the member open raises; measured again, zero leaked. New
regression test pins it.

restore_unified_backup can now raise RestoreIncompleteError, but its docstring
still described a True/False contract. Documented the Returns and Raises so a
non-API caller does not assume boolean-only outcomes.

* test: drop the duplicate Path import in the fd-leak test (F811)

bool(data.get('include_secrets', False)), and bool("false") is True — so a

collected deploy_hooks.global_hooks. Per-domain hooks
(deploy_hooks.domain_hooks[<domain>]) run on renewal exactly like global ones
— deployer.py executes both — so a tampered archive could smuggle a rejectable
command under domain_hooks and the restore would install it. The gate now

harden: the private CA refuses a key and certificate that do not match (#614)

* harden: the private CA refuses a key and certificate that do not match

_load_ca loaded ca.key and ca.crt from two separate files and validated only
expiry — never that the private key belongs to the certificate. The two can be
from different generations: a share-safe backup carries ca.crt but excludes
ca.key (it is key material), so restoring one over a node whose ca.key was
regenerated leaves a pair that matches by filename and not by content. CertMate
loaded it, reported the CA healthy (initialize() and is_ca_loaded() both True,
no warning), and kept signing.

The damage is silent and downstream: leaf certificates then fail
verify_directly_issued_by(the published ca.crt), so every new mTLS identity is
rejected by relying parties, and a CRL signed with the mismatched key fails its
own signature check — relying parties discard it as unauthentic and revocation
checking fails open.

_load_ca now compares the certificate's public key against the private key's
and refuses the pair when they differ, with a message that names the likely
cause. Because initialize() returns _load_ca()'s result for an existing CA, a
mismatch now fails initialisation cleanly rather than signing — and it does NOT
regenerate: the on-disk key is left untouched so an operator can still pair it
with the right certificate.

Verified by execution with a control: a key/cert pair from two independently
generated CAs is refused (_load_ca False, is_ca_loaded False, the key on disk
untouched), while a coherent pair and a freshly generated CA still load.
Behavioural control against the pre-change code confirms it accepted the
mismatched pair. Suite: 3038 passed, 0 failed; 227 CA/CRL tests unaffected.

* test: share the two-CA fixture across the module (Copilot)

Generating a 4096-bit RSA CA is expensive; the fixture generated two per test.
The tests only read from them (each copies key/cert into its own per-test dir),
so a module-scoped fixture with tmp_path_factory generates them once. 4.4s -> 2.6s.

create_backup_before_restore exists so a restore is reversible: it takes a

feat: warn at startup when the bearer token hash no longer matches SECRET_KEY (#616)

* feat: warn at startup when the bearer token hash no longer matches SECRET_KEY

api_bearer_token_hash is HMAC-SHA256 keyed on SECRET_KEY. Restoring a backup
onto a host with a different SECRET_KEY leaves the stored hash unverifiable, so
the operator's own token — the correct one — 401s on every request. That is by
design (the hash is bound to SECRET_KEY on purpose, and the instance is not
world-open: the bearer path fails closed), but it is silent: the operator sees
only 401s with no cause, and no restart fixes it without the original
SECRET_KEY.

AuthManager.warn_if_bearer_token_hash_is_stale(), called once at startup after
set_hmac_key, diagnoses exactly this: if the operator supplied a token via
API_BEARER_TOKEN(_FILE) and it does not verify against a stored HMAC hash, it
logs the likely cause (a SECRET_KEY changed under a restore) and the fix
(provide the original SECRET_KEY, or reset the bearer token). It is read-only —
a wrong token at startup must never overwrite the stored hash — and never
raises into startup.

Verified in a container: booting a data dir whose hash was written under one
SECRET_KEY with a different SECRET_KEY logs the warning, and a request with the
operator's token returns 401 — so the warning appears exactly when it is
needed. Unit tests cover the restore case and the silent cases (same key, no
token supplied, no HMAC hash, a legacy sha256 hash, a token read from a file)
plus a guard that the check does not write settings. Suite: 3041 passed.

already tells operators SECRET_KEY is required on a fresh-host restore; this
makes the instance say so itself when they miss it.

fix: removing a domain no longer drops a concurrent registration (lost update) (#618)

* fix: removing a domain no longer drops a concurrent registration (lost update)

The DELETE /api/certificates/<domain> handler and CertificateManager.set_auto_renew
both did load_settings() then atomic_update({'domains': <whole list built from
that snapshot>}). Two problems compound:

- the load is a request-cache HIT. flask.g is primed by the rate-limit
  before_request hook on every request, so the handler reads a snapshot taken
  at request start, not current state;
- 'domains' is replaced wholesale — it is not a deep-merge key — so
  atomic_update's fresh on-disk read cannot rescue it. The stale list wins.

The window is real: delete_certificate runs a storage-backend delete (a
Vault/AWS/Azure round-trip) before the settings write, and set_auto_renew has
the identical shape. A domain registered by another request during that window
is absent from the snapshot and is silently dropped from settings['domains'];
check_renewals iterates only that list, so the dropped domain is never renewed
and expires ~90 days later with no error anywhere.

Both now do the read-modify-write on the FRESH on-disk list via
settings_manager.update(mutator), which reads under the lock with
use_cache=False and touches only the target domain's entry. set_auto_renew
keeps its "return False, no write" behaviour for an unknown domain via a
sentinel exception, so a no-op does not persist the migration.

while B registers concurrently, main ends with domains=[] (B lost); the fix ends
with domains=[b] (A removed, B kept). Suite: 3054 passed, 0 failed; 4 new tests
plus regression guards that both sites use the locked read-modify-write.

  (and triggered an automatic backup) even when the domain was already absent.

  no-op delete leaves settings.json byte-identical.
- The concurrency test now runs the SAME interleaving through both shapes and

* fix: publish the flat PEMs atomically on create/reissue, like the renew path

create_certificate published the served flat PEMs with an in-place loop over
CERTIFICATE_FILES — cert, chain, fullchain, then privkey.pem last — reading and
writing each destination directly, with no staging and no rollback. A failure
on the fourth write (ENOSPC, an EPERM on a hardened privkey.pem, a container

straight off disk by /api/certificates/<domain>/download and pushed to every
deploy hook and storage backend. This is the create AND the replace=True
reissue path, i.e. it overwrites a certificate that is currently being served,
and the renew path's self-healing does not reach it until the certificate's
renewal window ~60 days later.

back the staged set on any error. create_certificate now calls the same helper
instead of its own loop. It returns {filename: bytes}, the same shape the method
already fed to _store_in_backend, so nothing downstream changes.

file, main leaves cert.pem=NEW beside privkey.pem=OLD (a broken pair); the fix
leaves all four at the OLD generation, internally consistent, with no .staging
leftovers. Verified E2E: a real Let's Encrypt staging issuance still returns 201
and the served cert/key pair verifies. Suite: 3054 passed, 0 failed; 4 new

The PATCH /api/certificates/<domain> handler did a metadata.json
read-modify-write with no lock. renew_certificate reads metadata at the start
of its certbot run and writes that pre-renewal snapshot back at the end, holding
the per-domain lock the whole time (up to 1800s). A PATCH landing in that window
was silently reverted — and the divergence was durable, not just a lost edit:
the PATCH's settings write is locked and survives, so settings.json showed the
new dns_provider while metadata.json kept the old one. renew_certificate
resolves the provider from metadata, so every subsequent renewal kept
authenticating through the decommissioned credential and eventually failed
silently until expiry. deployment_host/port/protocol set through the same
handler were reverted the same way.

Adds CertificateManager.domain_lock(domain) — a context manager over the same
per-domain lock create/renew take, raising DomainOperationInProgress on timeout
— and wraps the PATCH metadata read-modify-write in it. PATCH now either waits
for issuance to finish or returns 409, exactly like the create/renew routes; it
never interleaves.

Verified by execution: with a thread holding the domain lock (a stand-in for an
in-flight renewal), a second acquire returns DomainOperationInProgress -> 409;
without a holder it enters; the lock is released after the block; and
renew_certificate takes the same lock object for a domain, so they genuinely
serialise. Suite: 3055 passed, 0 failed; 5 new tests.

* refactor: read PATCH metadata through the manager, clearing the CodeQL path alert

CodeQL flagged cert_dir / 'metadata.json' and the open() on it as "uncontrolled
data used in a path expression". domain is in fact validated by
_validate_domain_path earlier in the handler (which resolves and containment-
checks it), so cert_dir is confined — a false positive — but the barrier is in
another function and CodeQL does not follow it.

Rather than suppress it, read the metadata through
certificate_manager._load_metadata(domain), which builds the path from the
already-validated domain and, as a bonus, quarantines corrupt JSON instead of
the handler's previous open()+json.load that silently returned {} (and would
then be overwritten by the save below, destroying the damaged file). The direct
open() CodeQL objected to is gone; behaviour is unchanged for valid metadata.

* test: mock _load_metadata now that PATCH reads through the manager

The previous commit routed the PATCH metadata read through
certificate_manager._load_metadata; test_patch_probe_config mocks the manager
and wrote metadata.json on disk for the handler's old direct open() to read.
Mirror the real _load_metadata in the fixture (read the on-disk metadata.json,
quarantine-free {} when absent), the symmetric counterpart to the _save_metadata
mock already there. 7 probe-config tests green; full suite 3055 passed.

fix: serialise the CRL rebuild so a concurrent revocation is not dropped (#620)

* fix: serialise the CRL rebuild so a concurrent revocation is not dropped

revoke_certificate rebuilds crl.pem from the ENTIRE revoked set, but held only
the per-identifier metadata lock. Two revocations of different certificates take
different identifier locks, so nothing serialised the global rebuild: thread A
could read the revoked set before thread B committed, and A's crl.pem write land
after B's, dropping B's serial from the signed CRL — while both metadata files
said revoked=true and both calls returned (True, None). Relying parties then
accept B's leaf with `openssl verify -crl_check` until next_update (7 days),
even though the OCSP endpoint says revoked. The same unguarded rebuild is
reachable from the unauthenticated CRL endpoint via CRLManager.update_crl, which
regenerates when the on-disk CRL is missing or past next_update.

PrivateCAGenerator now owns one process-wide crl_lock() (it is the object that
writes crl.pem, shared by both callers via self.private_ca). revoke_certificate
and CRLManager.update_crl hold it around the whole
"list_client_certificates(revoked=True) -> generate_crl" unit, so the rebuild is
atomic. Lock order is consistent (revoke takes the per-identifier lock then the
CRL lock; update_crl takes only the CRL lock), so no deadlock.

Behavioural control with real threads and a real CA, verifying the SIGNED CRL
with cryptography: A reads a partial set and writes last while B writes first
with the full set — without the lock the final CRL contains only [1001] (2002
dropped); with the lock it contains [1001, 2002]. Suite: 3054 passed, 0 failed
(117 CRL/OCSP/revocation tests unaffected); 4 new tests.

* fix: the CRL lock is shared per ca_dir, not per instance (Copilot)

Copilot was right that a per-instance lock is not "process-wide": the factory
makes one PrivateCAGenerator, but nothing stops a second instance for the same
ca_dir in the same process, and two of them would race the same crl.pem with
separate locks. The lock is now keyed on the resolved ca_dir in a class-level
registry, so every instance for a CA shares one lock — the guarantee the
comment claimed. A test pins that two instances for the same ca_dir share the
lock and a different ca_dir gets a different one.

Also from the review: the CRL race test now asserts both threads actually
finished (not just join-with-timeout), so a deadlock or an unset event fails
loudly instead of passing; and the ca fixture is module-scoped
(tmp_path_factory) so the 4096-bit CA keygen runs once for the module, not per
test.

fix: a partial CA is not silently regenerated over the surviving file (#621)

* fix: a partial CA is not silently regenerated over the surviving file

initialize() loaded the CA only when BOTH ca.crt and ca.key were present. With
exactly one present it fell through to _generate_ca(), which overwrites BOTH
paths with a brand-new CA — and _backup_existing_ca() is skipped because it is
gated on force. So the surviving half was destroyed silently, at INFO level, on
every app start (the factory calls initialize() unconditionally).

Both directions are reachable and both are severe:
- ca.crt present, ca.key missing — the exact state a masked restore leaves
  (key material is excluded from share-safe backups). The restored ca.crt, the
  certificate every deployed client trusts, is replaced by a stranger.
- ca.crt missing, ca.key survives — the next start overwrites the CA PRIVATE
  KEY. The old key then exists nowhere: every previously issued client
  certificate fails verification against the new CA, and no CRL can ever be
  signed for the old CA again, so all outstanding certs become permanently
  unrevocable.

initialize() now detects a partial CA (exactly one of the two files present,
and not a deliberate force) and refuses, leaving the surviving file untouched
and logging what to restore. First run (neither file) still generates; a
complete pair still loads; force still regenerates (backing up first) — the
refusal is only for the accidental case.

Behavioural control against the pre-change code: with only ca.key on disk, main
regenerates and the surviving key is gone; the fix returns False and the key is
byte-identical. Suite: 3074 passed, 0 failed (208 CA/client-cert tests
unaffected); 5 new tests covering both partial directions and the three
controls (complete loads, empty generates, force regenerates).

From the HIGH re-triage against current main (finding #9); the twin of #614
(_load_ca key/cert mismatch) on the write side.

* fix: force regeneration backs up a key-only partial CA too (Copilot)

_backup_existing_ca returned early when ca.crt was absent, so a force=True
regeneration from a key-only partial state (ca.key present, ca.crt gone)
overwrote the only copy of ca.key with no backup — the one case where force is
the sanctioned way out of a partial CA. It now returns early only when BOTH
files are absent; the per-file copies already handle whichever exist. A test
pins that force from a key-only partial backs the key up before regenerating.

Also dropped an unused shutil import in the new test.

fix: the deploy-failure alert is always delivered, whatever the event filter (#624)

deploy_hook_failed is the silent-deploy alarm: a renewal succeeds but its deploy
hook (nginx reload, LB push) exits non-zero, so the service keeps serving the
OLD certificate while the dashboard and the renewal API both report success. The
notifier publishes deploy_hook_failed specifically so an operator hears about
that. But notify() drops any event not in the configured events filter, and the
events UI offers only the five certificate_* events — so an operator who ticks
any of them sets a filter that does not include deploy_hook_failed and
permanently silences exactly the alert it exists to raise, with no UI control to
re-enable it. The same happened at the per-webhook filter.

Critical failure events (deploy_hook_failed) now bypass both filters: an
operator must never be able to filter away a failure they need to see. The
master switch still wins — a disabled notifications config sends nothing — and
ordinary events are still filtered normally.

Verified by execution with controls: with a global filter of
[certificate_renewed], main returns {'skipped': 'event not in filter'} for
deploy_hook_failed and sends nothing; the fix delivers it. A per-webhook filter
is bypassed the same way. A non-critical filtered event stays filtered, and
notifications-disabled silences even the critical event. Suite: 3080 passed,
0 failed; 5 new tests.

From the HIGH re-triage against current main (finding #10).

harden: re-check the webhook SSRF guard on every redirect, and drop credentials cross-host (#622)

* harden: re-check the webhook SSRF guard on every redirect, and drop credentials cross-host

The SSRF guard (_webhook_url_is_internal) was evaluated once, on the configured
URL, and the default opener then followed 3xx redirects with no further check.
A receiver that answers a redirect to an internal/metadata address therefore
defeated the guard: the follow-up request was issued to the internal target
from inside the trust boundary, carrying the webhook's Authorization header and
X-CertMate-Signature (urllib forwards every header except Content-Length /
Content-Type across a redirect).

Webhook egress now goes through an opener whose redirect handler re-applies the
guard on every hop — a redirect to an internal target is refused unless internal
webhooks are explicitly allowed — and strips Authorization / X-CertMate-Signature
/ Proxy-Authorization when a redirect changes host, so a credential never leaves
for a host the operator did not configure. The transport stays a single module
function (urlopen) with the same signature, so nothing else changes.

Verified by execution: a request to a receiver that redirects to a loopback
target no longer reaches it and no credential arrives (the internal endpoint is
never hit); a same-host redirect still completes with the header intact; and a
cross-host redirect drops the sensitive headers (asserted directly on the
redirect handler). Suite: 3081 passed, 0 failed; 6 new tests, and the 113
existing webhook/notifier tests are unaffected (the guarded egress keeps the
urlopen signature they patch).

From the HIGH re-triage against current main (finding #12).

* harden: strip webhook credentials on any origin change, not just host (Copilot)

The cross-host credential strip on a redirect only compared hostnames, so a
redirect that kept the host but downgraded https->http, or moved to a different
port, still carried Authorization / X-CertMate-Signature — leaking the token
over an insecure channel or to a service the operator never configured. It now
compares the full origin (scheme + host + port), with default ports normalised
so an explicit :443 is not seen as a different origin from the implicit one.

Also from the review: the test HTTP server now calls server_close() after
shutdown() so the listening socket is released (no fd/port leak across the
suite). New tests cover a scheme downgrade, a port change, and the explicit-
default-port control.

harden: mask the webhook URL as a secret, and never restore a secret by list position (#623)

* harden: mask the webhook URL as a secret, and never restore a secret by list position

Two coupled fixes on the notifications settings path.

A webhook's `url` is a credential: for Slack, Discord, ntfy and Gotify the
incoming-webhook URL embeds the bearer secret in its path, so anyone who reads
it can post to the channel. mask_secrets_in_settings masks by field NAME and
'url' matched no pattern, so GET /api/web/settings returned it in cleartext to
the viewer role (the lowest-privileged), and the share-safe backup ZIP carried
it too. `url` is now masked in the webhooks list context (a new list-name
context so it does not disturb the provider-context masking of e.g.
acme-dns.accounts), and restored on a round-trip like any other secret.

Masking the url made it unusable as part of the restore identity, which forced
out a latent bug: _restore_masked_list_secrets matched prior entries by
(type, url, name) and fell back to LIST POSITION when that missed. A save that
both shifted positions and changed an identity field — deleting one webhook and
fixing another's URL — made position the tiebreaker and copied a different
webhook's credential into the survivor, which CertMate then transmitted to the
wrong endpoint. Identity is now (type, name) and there is NO positional
fallback: an unmatched masked secret is dropped (the operator re-enters it),
never guessed.

Verified by execution with a control: on main, deleting PagerDuty and fixing
ITSM's URL restores ITSM's token as TOKEN-PAGERDUTY (the wrong secret); after
the change ITSM keeps its own token, and a renamed survivor drops the secret
rather than guessing. acme-dns username/subdomain masking is unchanged. A masked
url round-trips back to the real value. Suite: 3075 passed, 0 failed; 5 new
tests plus three existing tests updated to the new contract (url masked; rename
drops instead of index-fallback).

From the HIGH re-triage against current main (findings #16 and #11).

* harden: drop the masked secret for an ambiguous duplicate identity (Copilot)

Matching prior entries by (type, name) and consuming duplicates in list order
still leaked across endpoints when two webhooks shared (type, name) and a save
reordered or deleted one: list position was the only tiebreaker left, and it
restored the wrong entry's secret. An identity shared by more than one prior
entry is now treated as ambiguous — its masked secrets are dropped (the operator
re-enters them) rather than guessed by position — closing the last positional
path #11 could take. A unique identity still restores exactly as before.

Verified: two duplicate-(type,name) webhooks with masked secrets come back with
the secrets dropped (never each other's), while a unique identity still restores
its own token and url. The existing duplicate-identity test is updated to the
new drop contract. Also fixed a docstring line-break that split an identifier.
Suite: 3075 passed, 0 failed.

fix: release prepare refuses a stale local checkout so the gated tree is the released tree (#625)

cmd_prepare checked only that the working tree was clean. It then computed the
real-cert policy from `git diff <last_tag>..origin/main`, ran every gate
(flake8, bandit, the unit/UI suites, the mandatory real-cert E2E, the Docker
build) against whatever was checked out, and only afterwards cut the release
branch with `git checkout -b <branch> origin/main`. So the tree that is gated
and the tree that is released are different trees whenever the local checkout is
behind origin/main — the ordinary state right after merging a PR on GitHub. A
commit on origin/main that is not in the local checkout is never seen by any
gate, and "ALL GATES PASSED" would vouch for a tree no gate examined; the very
next statement checks out origin/main and the release carries the untested
change. The script's own comment flags this hazard and fixed it for `publish`
only.

prepare now refuses, right after the fetch and before any gate, unless HEAD is
exactly origin/main, with a message telling the operator to
`git checkout main && git pull --ff-only` and retry. The gated tree is then the
released tree.

Verified with a throwaway repo: the check dies when HEAD is a commit behind
origin/main and passes once aligned. A static test pins that the check exists
and runs before the first gate. Suite: release-gate tests 39 passed.

From the HIGH re-triage against current main (finding #15).

fix: DNS account lookup recognises every provider's credentials, not a hardcoded six (#626)

* fix: DNS account lookup recognises every provider's credentials, not a hardcoded six

get_dns_provider_account_config fell back to a hardcoded 6-key allowlist
(api_token / access_key_id / api_key / api_url / username / token) when
default_accounts had no entry for the provider — the state a fresh install's
own settings.json is in, since the setup wizard POSTs dns_providers without a
default_accounts key. That list did not cover the real credential fields of
rfc2136 (nameserver/tsig_key/tsig_secret), scaleway (application_token), azure,
google, ovh, edgedns and more, so a fully configured account for one of those
resolved to (None, None) and issuance died immediately with "DNS provider 'X'
account 'default' not configured" — telling the operator to configure
credentials that were already stored. certbot was never invoked.

The lookup (all three fallback sites) and the `configured` flag in
list_dns_provider_accounts now go through one helper that checks the provider's
OWN required fields from _DNS_PROVIDER_CREDENTIALS. A provider not in that
registry accepts any non-empty value rather than being silently rejected, and
an account whose credential fields are blank still counts as unconfigured.

Behavioural control against the pre-change code: a configured rfc2136 account
with no default set resolves to (None, None) on main and to the account on the
fix; cloudflare (already covered) is unchanged, and an empty account still does
not resolve. Suite: 3102 passed, 0 failed (437 DNS/provider tests unaffected);
8 new tests across five providers plus the empty and unknown-provider controls.

From the HIGH re-triage against current main (finding #14).

* refactor: an account is configured only when ALL its required fields are present (Copilot)

_account_has_credentials used any(required) — one credential field present was
enough — which is inconsistent with test_provider(), the existing validation
that requires ALL of a provider's fields and reports each missing one. A partial
account (rfc2136 with nameserver but no tsig_secret) would then resolve and fail
later at certbot with a vaguer error. Changed to all(required) so "configured"
means one thing across the lookup, the configured flag, and test_provider. The
unknown-provider fallback stays any-non-empty (no required list to check
against). New test pins that a partial account does not resolve.

fix: a not-yet-due renewal retries a stranded backend store and propagates a reconcile (#627)

* fix: a not-yet-due renewal retries a stranded backend store and propagates a reconcile

_store_in_backend was reached only from create and the renewed=True branch of
renew_certificate, so a store that failed once (an expired Vault token, a
transient 5xx) was never retried. The local certificate was fresh but the
external copy stayed on the OLD generation — and because get_certificate_info
reads the backend copy when a storage backend is configured, needs_renewal
stayed True forever: every daily run reached the not-yet-due branch, which
never touched the backend, so the store was never tried again and the external
consumer (nginx, k8s, the DR site) served an expiring then expired certificate
with CertMate reporting no failure (#1). Separately, when that branch
republished the flat PEMs after an interrupted publish, the new generation
reached /download and the deploy hooks but not the backend or the PFX (#2).

The not-yet-due branch now pushes to the backend when the external copy is
behind — a prior store failed (storage_warning persisted) or the flats were
just republished — clearing the storage_warning on success, and rebuilds the
PFX when the served pair rotated. A healthy not-yet-due run (no warning, no
stale) still does not touch the backend, so the daily check is not amplified.

Behavioural control against the pre-change code: with a persisted
storage_warning and certbot reporting not-yet-due, main never calls
store_certificate; the fix retries it once and clears the warning. Controls: a
healthy run does not push, and a no-backend instance still returns not-yet-due.
Suite: 3107 passed, 0 failed; 3 new tests driving the real renew_certificate
with a not-yet-due executor.

fix: jitter the renewal sweeps so installs don't all hit the CA at HH:00:00 (#633)

The certificate (02:00) and client-certificate (03:00) renewal cron jobs fired
at exactly the top of the hour on every install, so every CertMate in the world
hit its ACME CA at the same wall-clock second — a synchronised load spike the CA
has to absorb. Let's Encrypt asks integrators to renew at randomised times for
exactly this reason.

Add APScheduler cron jitter (+/- 1 hour) to both renewal jobs: the 02:00 sweep
now lands anywhere in 01:00-03:00 and the 03:00 sweep in 02:00-04:00 — the same
overnight window, de-synchronised across installs. Composes with the existing
6-hour misfire grace and coalesce. Test asserts both jobs carry the jitter.

The metrics collector has always exposed
certmate_background_job_last_run_timestamp, certmate_certificate_renewals_total,
certmate_acme_errors_total and the renewal duration histogram — but nothing in
the application ever called the record_* methods that feed them. Every one of
those series was permanently empty, so the single alert an operator most needs
for a certificate manager ("the renewal sweep has not run in N days" /
"renewals are failing") could not be written: a scheduler that had silently
stopped looked identical to one that was working. Only the scrape-time
inventory gauges populated, which give inventory, not liveness.

Wire the signals at the two points that already know the answer, rather than
inside the issuance hot path and its many return points:

- The scheduled-job wrapper (_run_manager_job) stamps last-run and duration for
  every background job, in a finally, so a sweep that RAISED still records that
  it executed. Liveness and success are different questions: the timestamp says
  the scheduler is alive, the counters say whether it is succeeding.
- check_renewals records per-domain success/failure, the renewal duration and
  an acme_errors entry on failure, where the outcome is already computed.

Telemetry is defensive on both paths: a collector error can never be the reason
a renewal run is lost.

Tests assert the signals move on the real code paths, including that a failing
sweep still stamps, that a certbot "not yet due" result is NOT counted as a
renewal (it would inflate the success rate and hide a sweep renewing nothing),
and that a telemetry failure does not turn a successful renewal into a failure.
Verified two-sided: the behavioural assertions fail against the pre-change code.

* fix: make the persistence check confirm the property it advertises

It wrote a marker file on first boot and logged "Persistent volume verified"
whenever the marker was still there. That only ever proved something had
written to the directory before. A plain `docker restart` keeps the container's
writable layer, so the marker survived and the check reported a verified volume
on an instance with NO volume mounted at all — the reassuring line appeared
precisely while the data was ephemeral, and stayed right until the container

not. Walking up to '/' covers the operator who mounted a parent (/app) rather
than /app/data itself, which would otherwise read as ephemeral and raise a
false alarm; '/' itself is excluded, since treating it as the answer would
report every container as persistent — the same false reassurance in a new
form. A check that cannot answer (OSError) does not answer optimistically.

disagreement between the old rule and the new one so the heuristic cannot
quietly come back.

deps: stop the optional storage sets resolving a cryptography that breaks certbot (#682)

* deps: stop the optional storage sets resolving a cryptography that breaks certbot

The Azure Key Vault storage sets declared a bare floor, cryptography>=41.0.0,
with no ceiling. The floor is deliberate and stays: the Certificate-object path
uses load_pem_x509_certificates and the PKCS12 builder, so a layered install
onto a stripped-down base should fail with a clear constraint error rather than
an opaque ImportError at runtime.

The missing ceiling is the defect. Both files are documented as installable on
their own, and standalone nothing else constrains the package. Measured rather
than argued: resolving requirements-storage-all.txt by itself picks
cryptography 50.0.1 — the exact version SECURITY.md records as installing
cleanly and then killing `certbot --version`. So the documented install path
produces a broken issuance stack. With the ceiling it resolves to 46.0.7, the
held version.

That this had not yet bitten was an accident of Docker's layer order: the main
file installs first and the held version already satisfies >=41. Nothing
enforced it, and `pip install -U` or the standalone path bypassed it.

The ceiling is <47, which is what the stack itself imposes (pyopenssl==26.0.0
requires cryptography>=46.0.0,<47). The authoritative reason for the hold stays
in one place, beside the pin in requirements.txt; these files point at it.

A new guard checks the property directly instead of trusting install order:
every requirements file must accept the held version and must not admit a
version known to break issuance. It catches both files as they were.

fix: stop a cross-process race publishing a cert and key from different issuances (#688)

* fix: stop a cross-process race publishing a cert and key from different issuances

Found by writing the test the safety-net phase was missing, and it is a real
defect, not a theoretical one. Two processes publishing the same domain
produced this roughly one run in six:

    cert.pem BBBB | chain.pem AAAA | fullchain.pem AAAA | privkey.pem AAAA

A certificate from one issuance beside the private key of another. That pair
cannot complete a handshake, and this directory is exactly what
/api/certificates/<domain>/download serves and what every deploy hook receives.

The per-domain lock is a threading.Lock, so it orders threads inside one worker
and nothing else. Promote is four independent renames, and the staging files
are named after their destinations — so two processes shared both the
temporaries and the rename sequence. The renewal flock covers the scheduled
sweep and says in its own docstring that it does not cover this path.

Reachability is bounded but the codebase already anticipates the scenario: an
operator raising --workers, two containers on a shared data dir, or systemd and
docker on the same volume. The flock on the renewal path exists precisely
because that happens; the synchronous issuance path simply had no equivalent.

Stage-and-promote now runs under a per-domain, cross-process flock keyed on the
destination directory, so different domains never contend. Best-effort by
design, matching the renewal lock: where flock is unavailable it yields rather
than refusing to publish, since failing closed would mean declining to install
a certificate the CA has already issued.

Two-sided control, repeated rather than single-shot because the defect is
probabilistic:
  without the lock  5 failures / 12 runs
  with the lock     0 failures / 20 runs

The test also reports how much work each process actually did, so a worker that
died on import cannot let it pass without a race, and a deterministic companion
proves the split-bundle check is capable of detecting mixing at all.

Closes #663

programming error (required, looked up with []) and which are a supported
configuration (optional, .get()), including the CertificateService fallback

harden: constrain usernames where they are created (#701)

A username is a key in settings['users'], a name rendered in the UI, and a
value written into every audit record for that session. Nothing constrained
it, and one of the two ways one can be created is not an operator typing it:
the OIDC path derives it from an IdP claim (preferred_username), so on an IdP
with permissive self-registration the value is chosen by whoever signs up.

The check is deliberately narrow, because the risk here is being too strict
rather than too weak. It rejects control characters — which no person's name
contains — plus empties, and caps the length. There is no character allowlist:
IdPs legitimately issue addresses, dots, apostrophes and non-ASCII names, and
an allowlist would lock real people out of a working SSO deployment to prevent
a problem they do not cause. Most of the new test file is evidence that
legitimate names still pass, since that is the failure mode with users on the
other side of it.

Surrounding whitespace is stripped rather than refused: nobody intends a
trailing space as part of their identity, and normalising means the padded form
collides with the existing account instead of creating a second, visually
identical one.

Applied at the two write points only — create_user and OIDC provisioning.
Existing rows are left alone on purpose: renaming or dropping an account that
is already there would be destructive, and the log paths that consume a
username scrub their own values. The OIDC path declines the login with
'invalid_username', which the callback already turns into an audit failure and

that silently does not work.

fix: stop presenting an unrestorable archive as a restore point (#655) (#703)

Every automatic backup is taken with include_secrets=False, because a leaked
archive must not also be a credential dump. That default is right, and it means
the newest archive on disk almost always CANNOT restore the instance:
installing it writes the mask sentinel in place of every password hash, bearer
token, API key hash, OIDC client secret and DNS credential.

The restore path has known this and refused such archives. The listing did not
say so — `secrets_masked` sat inside `metadata`, naming the mechanism rather
than the consequence — and the UI offered an identical Restore button on every
row. So the entry an operator reaches for first is the one that cannot help.

Each listed backup now carries `can_restore` and, when false, a
`restore_blocked_reason` saying what is wrong in terms of the outcome. The UI
marks those rows and disables their Restore action.

The answer comes from the same predicate the restore path applies:
`_backup_can_restore_credentials` is promoted out of SettingsManager to a
module-level `backup_can_restore`, so there is one definition rather than two
rules that currently agree. A test asserts the two give the same answer on the
same archive, because that agreement — not the presence of a field — is what
keeps the listing honest as the code changes.

Conservative by construction: anything that cannot be inspected reports as NOT
restorable. An unreadable file, an archive with no settings.json, and an
encrypted archive whose passphrase this instance does not hold all answer no.
Presenting an unknown archive as a restore point is the harm itself, so
optimism is never the safe default here. The UI reads a missing field the same
way, so an older server cannot be mistaken for a promise.

This is the first of the three steps agreed for #655 — it removes the active
harm without depending on the design decision the other two need. Automatic
backups that can restore, and an ingest path for a backup taken off the node,
follow.

feat: automatic backups can restore when they can be encrypted (#655) (#704)

Second of the three steps. The listing now tells the truth about which
archives can restore; this makes the automatic ones able to.

include_secrets and encryption are independent knobs in
create_unified_backup, which leaves four combinations. Only two make sense for
a backup taken automatically on every settings save:

  masked   + no passphrase -> a configuration snapshot; cannot restore
  complete + passphrase    -> a DR archive, encrypted at rest
  complete + no passphrase -> a plaintext credential dump written on every
                              save. Never, from this path.
  masked   + passphrase    -> a wasted opportunity, not a hazard.

So the automatic path ties the two together: it takes a complete backup
exactly when a passphrase is configured to encrypt it. Verified by execution
before writing the change — without a passphrase, include_secrets=True really
does leave the bearer token readable in a plain zip on disk.

A manual backup can still opt into plaintext. That is a deliberate,
audit-logged operator choice and it is unchanged.

The passphrase stays the operator's to set: storing it beside the archive it
protects would make the encryption theatre. An instance without one gets a
notice instead — said once per process, not on every settings write, because a
warning repeated on every write is one people learn to scroll past, which is
how the condition it describes goes unnoticed for months.

Two defects in the tests, both found by mutation rather than by review:

The guard named as the most important in the file could not fail. It searched
the archive's raw bytes for the credential, and a zip is compressed — the
credential was present and the search found nothing. It now reads the entries.

The token the tests used was being rejected by api_bearer_token validation
(first for length, then for repeating runs), so the tests were partly
exercising the validator rather than the backup path. Replaced with one that
passes.

feat: a backup kept off this node can be brought back (#655) (#705)

Third and last of the three steps. Restore reads a file that is already in
backups/unified, so after losing the volume there was nothing there: recovery
required out-of-band access to a filesystem that no longer existed. That is the
disaster-recovery story failing exactly when it is needed.

POST /api/backups/upload (admin) stores an archive; a matching control sits in
the settings UI beside the existing backup actions.

Uploading is deliberately not restoring. Storing is harmless, restoring is not,
and keeping them apart means an upload can never be destructive on its own —
the archive lands in the list, is judged by the same restorability check as
every other archive (#703), and the operator restores it explicitly afterwards
through the existing audited path.

Two properties carry the weight:

The uploaded name is discarded. `ingest_backup` is not even given one — a test
pins its signature, so a name added later "for convenience" fails with the
reason. A caller-supplied filename is the classic way to steer a write out of
its directory, and nothing here needs it: the archive's own manifest says what
it is. Driven end to end over multipart with traversal and NUL-bearing names.

The kind of archive is decided from content, never extension. The restore path
branches on the suffix, so an encrypted archive stored as .zip would fail to
open later, at the worst possible moment.

Junk is refused at upload rather than left in the list to be discovered by
someone reaching for it in an emergency: a non-archive, a broken zip, and a zip
that carries no settings.json are all rejected without writing anything.

One of the new tests could not fail. The size-limit case uploaded a blob of
repeated bytes — not an archive at all — so the format check rejected it and

test: give the HTTP layer its own coverage floors, and raise the worst (#662) (#716)

The gated suite had one project-wide --cov-fail-under. A single number cannot
protect a layer: modules/api/resources_ca.py sat at 11% — 99 of its 111
statements never executed — while the project figure stayed comfortably above
its floor, because 3,800 well-covered statements elsewhere absorbed it. That is
the failure this issue describes.

Two halves, and the second is the durable one.

Raised the worst three:

  modules/api/resources_ca.py         11% -> 86%
  modules/web/backup_cache_routes.py  40% -> 100%
  modules/web/settings_routes.py      38% -> 51%

HTTP layer overall 64% -> 68%; project 78.9%.

Writing the CA tests found a real defect rather than only moving a number.
`except requests.exceptions.SSLError` was unreachable: requests' SSLError
subclasses ConnectionError, and the ConnectionError handler came first. An
operator whose private CA presented an unverifiable certificate was told
"cannot reach the ACME host on the required port" and sent to check firewalls,
while the message that names the actual problem — no trust anchor supplied, or
one supplied that does not verify — could never be shown. Handlers reordered,
and the reordering is what the test catches.

The floors themselves are scripts/check_coverage_floors.py, run in the everyday
gate. It fails on three things, not one: a module below its floor, a module
with a floor that has vanished from the report (renaming a file must not retire
its floor), and a module in the layer with no floor at all (which is how
resources_ca reached 11%). An empty report is an error, not a pass.

tests/test_coverage_floors_are_enforced.py guards the checker, since a gate
that passes without gating is the shape of defect this project keeps finding
and this is the file whose whole job is not to have it. It also asserts against
the tree, so a new HTTP module is caught before anyone runs coverage.

fix: a certificate with no usable private key is not healthy (#608) (#717)

get_certificate_info decided a certificate existed from cert.pem alone, so a
directory holding a valid certificate and no key came back as exists=True,
days_left=74, needs_renewal=False — and the renewal sweep left it for another
six weeks, for an instance that cannot complete a handshake for that name.

The state is not hypothetical. Restoring a share-safe backup produces exactly
it, because those deliberately carry no key material: the restore writes back
cert.pem, chain.pem and fullchain.pem and nothing else. An operator verifying a
recovery the obvious way — the API lists my certificates with sane expiries —
is told the node is fine.

private_key_state() answers the real question, and answers the cheaper half of
it too: a key that does not match the certificate cannot handshake either, and
comparing public numbers catches that for RSA and EC alike without knowing the
key type. An unreadable or encrypted key counts as unusable rather than fine.

get_certificate_info now reports private_key_present / private_key_state /
usable, and a missing or mismatched key forces needs_renewal so the scheduler
acts instead of waiting for an expiry that is irrelevant.

The part worth reviewing is what this does NOT do. The storage-backend listing
path calls retrieve_certificate_info, which returns cert.pem alone BY DESIGN —
its entire purpose is to avoid pulling private keys out of a secrets backend
for a dashboard. Reading that absence as a missing key would have marked every
storage-backed certificate as needing renewal. It reports 'unknown', with
private_key_present and usable as null, and does not touch needs_renewal.

That was caught by reading what retrieve_certificate_info actually promises
after a test failed, not by review — the first version of this change had the
false positive in it.

Four tests in two files were asserting threshold arithmetic against fixtures
that wrote cert.pem without a key. Their helpers now write a matching key, so
they test what they mean to.

feat: the backup list says which archives carry private keys (#595) (#718)

Every backup made before v2.26.0 with the default settings contains the private
key of every certificate, while its manifest says secrets_masked: true and the
interface called it share-safe. Archives from v2.22.0 also carry the private CA
key and every client-certificate key.

That is published as an advisory, and an advisory is something an operator has
to go and read. The archives are still on their disk, still described by a
manifest that says the wrong thing, and the published advice — unzip and grep —
assumes they already know to look.

So the listing looks, and the UI marks those rows. The answer is read from the
archive's name list, never from its manifest, because the manifest is precisely
the thing that was wrong. Names only: nothing is decompressed, so this stays
cheap enough to run while a page renders.

The important negative is that an archive which cannot be inspected reports
null, not false. "I could not look" and "there is nothing there" are different
answers, and conflating them would be the same false reassurance the old
manifests gave. An encrypted archive this instance has the passphrase for IS
opened and answered definitely, so null means uninspectable rather than merely
encrypted.

Only a definite true warns in the UI. Crying wolf on the unknowns would train
people to ignore the badge, which costs more than it saves.

new DNS provider configuration, the previous one is forgotten." The certificate

atomic_update merges the top level and deep-merges a named set of subtrees.

fix: make the env bearer token authoritative at startup (#401) (#721)

is_setup_mode() asked whether the OPERATOR supplied a token via
API_BEARER_TOKEN(_FILE); authenticate_api_token() checked the presented token
against the STORED hash. On a fresh install those agree, because the stored
value is seeded from the env one.

They diverge for an operator who ran once without a token — one was generated
and stored — then added or rotated API_BEARER_TOKEN and restarted. The
essential-keys merge never overwrites a token already present, so enforcement
saw the new token while authentication still checked the old one. Reproduced:
has_operator_bearer_token() true for the new token, verification against the
stored hash false. The first-run screen asked the operator to paste the token
they had just configured and answered 401, and the documented way out was a
reset script.

Startup now reconciles: a supplied token that does not already authenticate is
written through the normal save path, which hashes it. The supplied value wins,
which is how enforcement already treated it — and the change is called out in
docs/docker.md, because an operator who rotated via the UI while leaving a
stale variable set will now find the variable winning.

Deliberately narrow. It acts only when a token was supplied, is well-formed,
and does not already authenticate; an instance where the two agree is never
rewritten. It cannot open an instance — the token still has to be presented.
What changes is which token opens it, and that is the operator's own.

Ordering matters and is invisible at the call site: it runs AFTER
set_token_hasher, because the save is what hashes. Called earlier it would
persist the plaintext, so a test asserts the order in the source as well as the
hashed outcome.

One test was rewritten after it failed for a better reason than it assumed. A
malformed API_BEARER_TOKEN does not merely get skipped: load_settings raises
BearerTokenUnusableError and the instance refuses to serve, since ignoring it
would leave no authentication at all. The stronger guarantee is now what the
test records.

fix: OIDC config changes take effect, and an algorithm rejection is not (#720)

permanent (#647)

Reported by a user connecting Authentik: every login failed on the id_token
signing algorithm, and every algorithm they tried failed in turn —
"Algorithm of 'RS256' is not allowed", then the same for ES256 and EdDSA.

The wording is the clue. Authlib restricts accepted signing algorithms to
whatever the discovery document advertised in
id_token_signing_alg_values_supported, and that document is fetched once, when
the Authlib client is first built, then cached.

The client was cached on issuer_url ALONE. Reproduced against the real library:
rotating client_secret or changing scopes returns the same cached client, and
Authlib is never re-registered — so nothing the operator changed, on either
side, reached CertMate again until the process restarted. The instance went on
enforcing an algorithm list from the first login attempt of that container's
life.

Two changes.

The cache is keyed on everything that shapes the client — issuer, client id,
secret and scopes — so saving a rotated secret now does what an operator
expects. The secret is hashed into that key rather than kept in the clear: it
lives on the manager and ends up in comparisons and, one day, in somebody's
debug print.

A failure on the algorithm drops the cached client and returns a distinct
'token_exchange_algorithm', so the next attempt refetches discovery. Without
it, a reconfigured IdP means an SSO that can never work again until someone
restarts the container — which is what the report describes. An ordinary
failure still keeps the cache; refetching discovery on every bad login would
be a request to the IdP per failed attempt.

The log now names the algorithm AND what discovery advertises, and the login
page says which IdP setting to look at. "Algorithm of 'RS256' is not allowed"
is a dead end for an operator; the mismatch between those two lists is the
whole answer.

Also installed Authlib into the local venv, which requirements.txt has declared
since it was added — without it these tests skip, and I would have shipped them
unverified.

fix: adoption is a real issuance, so announce it like one (#640) (#726)

Adopting a discovered certificate calls CertificateService.create(), which
drives certbot and writes new material to disk — but the handler published
nothing on the event bus. Three subscribers hang off that bus and each drops
what it does not recognise:

  factory._on_event                   notifications
  DeployManager.on_certificate_event  deploy hooks
  CacheManager.on_certificate_event   deployment-status cache invalidation

So an adopted certificate ran no deploy hook, and the dashboard kept serving a
cached "deployed & matching" verdict while the load balancer was still on the
OLD certificate, with nothing to tell the operator.

The reporter offered two designs and asked for a steer. A dedicated
certificate_adopted event would have to be taught to all three subscribers
plus two UI filters, and missing any one of them fixes the notification while
leaving the deploy hooks broken — which is the failure this report is about.
So adoption publishes certificate_created, which every subscriber already
honours, and carries an 'adopted' marker in the payload. The notifier bridge
reads that marker and renders "Certificate Adopted", so the alert still tells
the truth and operators keep the single toggle they already have.

build_notification_message is lifted out of the listener closure to make the
rendering assertable without constructing the manager graph.

Tests assert the three consequences rather than the publish, plus a guard that
reads the event name the handler actually publishes and requires every
subscriber to know it — written the other way round it would pass unchanged
while adoption published something nobody handles. All six were confirmed to
fail before the fix, and four mutations (no publish, no marker, no rendering,
dedicated event name) were each confirmed to trip them.

fix: let an operator forget an inventory record (#634) (#727)

Reported by a user: add a domain to the discovery configuration, scan, then
remove the domain again — "xxx.yy is still in list down below and cant be
removed".

That is not a filtering bug. CertInventory had no delete of any kind and the
API exposed no DELETE route, so the inventory was append-only. Taking a domain
out of the discovery configuration stops future scans from finding it, but
every row already recorded stayed forever, and the only way out was deleting
inventory.db.

  CertInventory.delete(fingerprint)     forgets the cert + its endpoints
  DELETE /api/inventory/<fingerprint>   operator, scope-checked
  Forget button                         on every inventory row

Deleting a certificate takes its endpoint rows with it through ON DELETE
CASCADE, which SQLite honours only because _connect enables PRAGMA
foreign_keys. A test asserts no endpoint row outlives its certificate, so that
cannot regress into invisible orphan rows.

This forgets an observation rather than suppressing one: a domain still in the
discovery configuration will be recorded again on the next sweep. Both the API
response and the confirmation dialog say so, because otherwise an operator
deletes the same row after every scan and concludes the button is broken.

Offered for managed records too — the certificate on disk is untouched, so the
only consequence is that CertMate stops listing that observation.

The route sits at '/<string:fingerprint>', the same depth as '/config',
'/scan' and '/crypto-report'. Werkzeug weights static segments above
converters so those still win; that was verified by matching them, not
reasoned about, and is pinned by a test.

Ten tests, all confirmed failing first. Five mutations were each confirmed to
trip them: DELETE without its WHERE clause, PRAGMA foreign_keys off, delete()
always reporting success, the route unregistered, and the click handler left
off the exported object — that last one being a dead button no server-side
test can see.

docs: state the single-instance model where it is read (#673) (#729)

CertMate is single-instance by design — APScheduler runs in the web process and
gunicorn runs one worker, so a second replica is a second scheduler issuing
against the same store. The Helm chart already enforces it: `fail` at template
time when replicaCount != 1.

The README said otherwise. It led with "easy scaling" and "high availability
deployments" while the constraint sat in a docker-compose YAML comment ~73% of
the way down a 2,700-line file. Now it is a note in "Why CertMate?", stated as
the deliberate design choice it is — one writer is what makes certificate state
safe without a distributed lock service — and the Docker and Kubernetes sections
no longer contradict it.

The bigger find was not in the issue. docs/architecture.md carried a **High
Availability** section with operational steps for multi-instance deployments:
shared storage, a load balancer with sticky sessions, rate-limit counters across
instances. Following it produces duplicate ACME orders and the CA's
duplicate-certificate rate limit, not availability. It was replicated verbatim
into all four translations, so the wrong instructions existed five times. All
five now describe active/standby, which is what actually works.

The guard normalises whitespace before matching, and that was not cosmetic:
these files are hard-wrapped at ~80 columns, the English file contained
"sticky\nsessions", and a plain substring check passed on it while the French
file — wrapped differently — failed. A check that depends on where the wrapping
fell is not a check.

It also verifies every in-document anchor resolves, because the storage-backend
heading is translated in each file and the link to it has to be too.

The interesting part is not the move, it is the cleanup contract.

Those temp files are secrets: the DNS credentials ini, whatever a provider
writes beside it (Google's is the service-account JSON — a live cloud private

which cover the failure path.
