fix: constrain the extras install layer, and record the hash-pinning decision (#686) (#747)

* fix: constrain the extras install layer, and record the hash-pinning decision (#686)

The issue asked for `--require-hashes` or an explicit decision not to. The
answer is: not now, recorded as a decision — and the reachable half of the gap
it was standing in for is closed here.

## The reachable half

Each `EXTRA_REQUIREMENTS` file is a separate pip resolution that knows nothing
about what the base layer pinned, so it is free to move those pins. Measured,
not reasoned about: with the base stack installed, a second
`pip install "cryptography<46"` silently takes 46.0.7 down to 45.0.7 — below the
floor `pyopenssl==26.0.0` requires — producing an image where `certbot
--version` no longer answers. With `-c requirements.txt` pip refuses and names
the conflict at build time.

This is not hypothetical. It has already happened here once, and CI's own
comment records it: `requirements-aws.txt` pinned a plugin above the certbot
pin and pip upgraded certbot 2.10.0 -> 3.3.0 in a build that reported success.
That was fixed by correcting the pin. The mechanism that allowed it stayed open,
and the storage extras walk straight back into it — they carry unbounded `>=`
requirements on azure-identity, boto3 and azure-keyvault-*, any of which can ask
for a newer cryptography in a future release.

All documented combinations resolve under the constraint, checked before
changing anything.

## Two combinations were advertised and never resolved

The CI step's comment claims it resolves "every file and every combination the
Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml advertise". Both advertise
`requirements-storage-all.txt`, alone and alongside `requirements-azure.txt`,
and neither was in the list. Both are added, and a test now ties the two places
together so the claim cannot go stale again — the failure mode this milestone
keeps finding.

The test accepts an entry only when it is the advertised combination plus one
base file, not merely a superset of it. Resolving azure+storage-all together
proves storage-all is installable, since a subset is easier to satisfy; it does
not prove that the narrower resolution someone actually gets is the one checked.

## The decision

SECURITY.md now carries the posture in full: what is guaranteed (exact pins,
digest-pinned base, SBOM and provenance, and now a constrained extras layer),
what is not (no hash verification, so a re-published artifact at the same
version is undetected), why hash pinning is not attempted incrementally, and
what would change the answer. The honest summary is auditability, not
integrity.

feat: deploy hooks can be held for a maintenance window (#632) (#748)

* feat: deploy hooks can be held for a maintenance window (#632)

Reported by a user deploying to RDS: "the deployment-script runs at a random
time... this will disrupt end user connectivity."

They are right about the cause. A certificate renews when it is due, which is a
time nobody chose — the sweep fires at 02:00 with an hour of jitter, and only
for whatever is inside the threshold that night — and the deploy hook then ran
immediately. For a hook that restarts a database or reloads a load balancer,
that is an outage at an unpredictable hour.

A `window` separates the two. The certificate still renews whenever it is due;
the DEPLOY is held until the window next opens. Absent means immediately, which
is what every existing hook does and keeps doing.

    "window": {"start": "02:00", "end": "04:00",
               "days": ["sat", "sun"], "timezone": "Europe/Rome"}

The same field works on typed deploy targets, which is usually where it is
wanted: a Kubernetes secret rollout is exactly that kind of deploy.

## The calendar lives on its own

`modules/core/deploy_window.py` is pure functions over an explicit `now`,
because every interesting case is a calendar case: a window that wraps past
midnight (and belongs to the day it STARTS on, so a Friday-night window does
not silently need Saturday ticked), an exclusive end so adjacent windows do not
overlap, and the two DST transitions where local time skips an hour or repeats
one. `start == end` is refused rather than guessed — it reads equally well as
always and never.

## The queue

On disk at `data/pending_deploys.json`, because the window is hours away and a
restart in between is ordinary. Written under a lock: events dispatch on daemon
threads, so two certificates renewing at once write it concurrently.

A second renewal before the window opens does not queue a second deploy — the
hook reads the certificate from disk when it runs. A hook deleted or disabled
while its deploy waited is dropped, because the current configuration says not
to run it. Removing the window releases the deploy at the next drain rather
than making the operator wait one more time. A failure inside the window is not
re-queued. A deploy still waiting after a week is logged as stuck.

Drained every minute, deliberately: a window is at least a minute long, so
minute polling means no window can be missed. It is a true no-op when the queue
file does not exist.

Held deploys are invisible everywhere else — the certificate renewed, the
history shows nothing, nothing failed — so `GET /api/deploy/pending` lists them
with the window they are waiting for and when it next opens.

## Two defects found on the way

Saving deploy hooks deleted every typed deploy target. The Settings -> Deploy
screen has no editor for `targets`: `loadConfig` never reads them, so
`saveConfig` posts a body without them, and `save_config` assigned the whole
`deploy_hooks` block. Opening that screen and pressing Save — without touching
anything — silently removed every configured Kubernetes secret target. Now
absent leaves alone and an explicit value, including an empty list, replaces:
the same rule `CertificateService.update_config` already applies.

The window fields were behind `x-show`, which keeps the inner bindings live, so
`hook.window.start` was evaluated for every hook without a window — an Alpine
error per binding per hook in the console. They are behind `x-if` now.

## Checks

53 tests on the calendar, 29 on the queue, 9 on target preservation, 4 in the
browser. Each load-bearing decision was mutated to confirm a test fails:
inclusive end, the wrapped window's day, the equal-ends refusal, a silently-UTC
timezone, ignoring the timezone, and the whole-block save.

feat: issue and renew from a CSR, so the private key can stay on the device (#599) (#749)

* feat: issue and renew from a CSR, so the private key can stay on the device (#599)

Requested by a user with appliances that generate their key on the device and
cannot export it — HSM-backed boxes, load balancers, network security
appliances. They can hand out a CSR and nothing else.

Pass the PEM as `csr` on the ordinary create endpoint, or paste it in the
create form. CertMate obtains the certificate and manages the chain, and never
sees or stores a private key.

## Two facts about certbot's --csr mode, measured not read

Verified end to end against Let's Encrypt staging with a real CSR:

* it writes cert.pem, chain.pem and fullchain.pem and no private key;
* it creates NO lineage — no renewal/ config, no live/ tree. certbot says so
  itself on success: these "will not be renewed automatically by Certbot. You
  will need to renew the certificate before it expires, by running the same
  Certbot command again."

The second shapes everything. `certbot renew` will never touch these, so
renewal re-runs issuance with the stored CSR, and "did it renew" cannot be
answered by looking at live/ — it is answered by fingerprinting the certificate
before and after, which also means a CA returning the same certificate inside
its reuse window is reported as "did not change" rather than advancing
renewed_at past an expiry that stood still.

## The collision with #608

#608 made a certificate with no private key report needs_renewal, because that
is what restoring a share-safe backup produces and it used to look healthy. A
CSR-only certificate is deliberately keyless. Without a fourth state it would
be reissued on every renewal sweep, burning CA rate limit for a file that must
not exist.

`private_key_state` gains 'external': no key here, and there should not be.
It does not force needs_renewal, and `usable` is null rather than false — the
certificate IS usable, on the device that holds the key. `_private_key_present`
and `_usable` are now written out per state rather than derived, because five
states answer those two questions three different ways.

## What is refused rather than silently reinterpreted

The names come from the CSR: it is signed over its own subject and SANs, so the
CA issues for those whatever the request said. A request carrying both a CSR
and a SAN list, or a CSR and key options, is a 400 — and the create form does
not send them, so that refusal is not something an operator has to discover
after an ACME round trip.

A CSR that does not cover the requested `domain` is refused: the directory is
named for it and renewal, the health check and every deploy hook find it by
that name. A CSR whose signature does not verify is refused before anything is
written. Converting a key-managed certificate is refused — it would leave the
old privkey.pem beside a certificate it cannot serve.

## Deploying one

Shell hooks run normally, and CERTMATE_KEY_PATH is not set rather than pointed
at a file that does not exist. Typed deploy targets all publish the key with
the certificate, so they say exactly that instead of the generic "certificate
files unreadable" they used to report on every renewal.

## Checks

44 unit tests and 7 in a browser. Thirteen mutations, all killed: dropping the
signature check, keeping each of the flags that must go, keeping the ones that
must stay, losing the dedup, letting an external key read as missing, making
`usable` false, accepting a CSR for other names, allowing the conversion,
routing the renewal through certbot renew, and reporting an unchanged
certificate as renewed.

* fix: the CSR renewal actually works, proven against a real CA (#599)

Two defects, both found by the real-CA E2E and neither visible to any unit test.

## certbot refuses to overwrite its own output in --csr mode

A second run dies with `FileExistsError: ... csr-out/cert.pem` before it
contacts the CA. Every renewal is a second run, so the FIRST renewal of every
CSR certificate failed — issuance perfect, then silence until expiry. The
output directory is now cleared before each run. Clearing BEFORE rather than
after is deliberate: it is a staging directory, and the served copies are the
flat ones beside it, so emptying it costs nothing if certbot then fails.

No test with a stubbed executor could see this, because the refusal is
certbot's. The unit test added asserts the precondition instead — that the
files certbot is told to write do not exist when it starts.

## The renewal returned a shape nothing else uses

The renew route reads `result.get('renewed')`. This returned `(bool, str)`,
so every CSR renewal was a 500 with "'tuple' object has no attribute 'get'".

The cause is worth naming: the shape was invented rather than copied from the
ordinary renewal, and every unit test then asserted that invention. They agreed
with each other and with nothing else. The test added for it reads the contract
off the route's own source rather than restating it, so a route that stops
reading `renewed` fails here instead of silently passing.

The CSR renewal now returns the same dict the ordinary one does, and lets
create_certificate's exception propagate — the route turns a RuntimeError into
a classified 422, and swallowing it into a return value would have made every
CA refusal a 200.

fix: an unreadable credential file leaves the instance locked, not open (#753)

`setup_mode_for` decides whether this instance requires a credential at all,
and its first question is whether the operator provided an API bearer token.
When that token is supplied as a file — the documented Docker and Kubernetes
pattern — the answer came from reading it, and any read failure was reported as
"the operator provided no token".

Those are opposite situations and they must reach opposite decisions. A fresh
install with no credential of any kind has to stay open long enough to be
bootstrapped; an instance whose operator named a file as the source of its
credential has to stay closed when that file cannot be read this instant.

of collapsing the two into the same False. `has_operator_bearer_token` treats
it as configured, logs at ERROR, and does not cache it — the previous
memoisation was justified on the premise that the env and the file are fixed
for the process lifetime, which is true of the variable and not of the file it
names. A secret mounted a moment late, a remount with different ownership, an
SELinux relabel: each produces one failed read followed by readable ones, and
caching the first fixed that answer in place until the next restart. Now the
next check retries and the instance recovers on its own.

The case that must NOT change is a genuinely unconfigured install, and it is
the first thing the new tests assert: with no API_BEARER_TOKEN and no

failures, so touching the file by mistake cannot brick onboarding.

rather than deleted, with a note on why that assertion was the defect.

lowered back to debug, caching the failure, and removing the memoisation
entirely. The last two survived a first pass because the tests asserted the

fix: an interrupted deploy leaves a record, instead of leaving nothing (#760)

The deploy history entry, the audit record and the failure event were all
written AFTER the command returned. A hook interrupted by process termination
- SIGKILL, an OOM kill, the container stopped mid-deploy - therefore left none
of them, and an operator reading the history could not tell 'this hook never
ran' from 'this hook was half-way through publishing a certificate when we
died'. The second is the dangerous one: the target may hold a partially
written certificate or a reloaded service, and nothing says to go and look.

A 'running' record is now appended before the command starts and superseded by
the outcome afterwards. The file is append-only JSONL, so superseding means a
second record with the same run_id; get_history folds the pair and keeps the
last, so callers still see one entry per run.

The part that carries the value is telling the two meanings of 'running'
apart. A leftover record means either the run is going on right now, or the
process running it died - and only the process that started it knows which.
The deployer keeps the run ids it has in flight, and that set does not survive
a restart, so after a restart every leftover reads as 'interrupted'. A hook
executing right now still reads as 'running'.

Typed deploy targets had the same gap: run_targets publishes to every target
and only then returns. One 'running' record covers the batch - per-target
records would need the results matched back to the targets that produced them,
and run_targets filters as it goes, so the lists are not the same length. The
batch is the honest unit: what an interrupted record says is 'publishing was
in progress', which is exactly what is known.

The history pane renders three outcomes rather than two. An interrupted entry
used to have no exit code, so it displayed as 'Exit err' - saying the hook ran
and failed, the opposite of the truth.

Records written before run ids existed are passed through untouched: the
history file survives upgrades, and a deploy that happened is not less true
for predating this.

fix: three ways the instance started without knowing its own state (#756)

* fix: three ways the instance started without knowing its own state

Three audit findings that turn out to be the same question - what does this
process know about itself at the moment it says it is ready?

**metadata.json was atomic but not durable.** `_atomic_json_write` wrote a
temp file and renamed it, and said in its own docstring that the mechanism
existed 'to avoid partial writes on crash'. The rename gives atomicity - a
reader sees the old file or the new one - and nothing about crash safety:
neither the contents nor the rename had left the page cache, so a power loss
could replay as a rename onto an empty file. That file records key custody:
private_key_state (the 'external' value that stops a CSR-only certificate
being reissued nightly), the CSR fingerprint, and the CA a private-CA
certificate cannot renew without. Now: flush, fsync the file, rename, fsync
the directory - the same recipe file_operations.py already uses for
settings.json, and three syncs for three different losses.

**A torn publish outlived the restart that caused it.** Promoting a renewed
certificate is four renames, and privkey.pem is last, so a process killed
between the second and the third leaves a NEW certificate beside the PREVIOUS
private key - a pair that cannot complete a handshake, served by
/api/certificates/<domain>/download and pushed to every deploy hook. The
renewal sweep already reconciled this, but only when it next visited the
domain: up to a day. A torn promote is caused by a process dying, and a
process that dies is about to be restarted, so create_app now reconciles every
domain's served files against certbot's live/ copy and republishes the ones
that disagree. One unrepairable domain is logged at ERROR and does not stop
the others, and does not stop the app starting.

**certbot was never checked at startup.** The one dependency without which
nothing works was the one dependency nothing checked: a broken certbot
produced an instance that started, answered /health 200 and /health/ready 200,
scheduled its renewals and found out at the first one. The failure this
project has actually hit twice is not 'not installed' - pip resolves cleanly,
the binary is present, and certbot dies importing its own ACME stack because
cryptography or pyOpenSSL moved under the pinned certbot. Only running it
detects that, so the probe runs `certbot --version` once per process, records
the result, and /health/ready now returns 503 when it failed - for the same
reason a dead scheduler does. A probe that did not run ('skipped', a
non-executing shell double) is not a probe that failed.

The probe's first bound was five seconds and the full suite proved it wrong:
under load, certbot --version inside the container took longer and a working
certbot was reported as broken. Measured cold in the published image at
2-3 seconds; the bound is now thirty. A startup check that produces false
failures is worse than none.

* security: screen the domain where the metadata path is built

CodeQL flagged the write at the end of `_save_metadata` as a path injection.
The category is on this repository's settled false-positive list — validators
run upstream and CodeQL cannot follow them across functions — but reading this
one properly says something the category does not: `_metadata_path` is the
single place the metadata path is built, for every read and for all seven
`_save_metadata` call sites, and it built the path from an unchecked `domain`.
The sink is `open(tmp, 'w')`, so a domain carrying path characters would put
attacker-influenced JSON at an arbitrary location.

Every caller does screen today. That is exactly the problem: the guarantee is
only as good as the least careful of them, and this repository has already
shipped that shape once - `_reject_path_escaping_domain` exists because
extracting code out of `create_certificate` left a unit that no longer enforced
its own precondition (#666), which its docstring records as "exactly the shape
CodeQL flags - and it was right".

and the whole suite is unaffected, which is the evidence that no legitimate
domain was ever unsafe; the tests pin that a wildcard is still allowed, because
a screen that rejected `*.example.com` would break every wildcard certificate.

The other flagged sink, `os.open(directory, O_RDONLY)` in `_fsync_directory`,
is left as it is: it opens read-only and calls fsync, so even a fully
attacker-chosen path reads nothing, writes nothing and discloses nothing.

security: enumerate the routes nothing protects, with the reason for each (#761)

Route protection is expressed three ways here, and all three are legitimate:
the require_role/require_auth/require_web_auth decorators, an inline check
inside the view (/ reads the session cookie itself so the template context
processor sees the user; /api/events/stream does it because SSE cannot carry a
bearer header), and a redirect to a route that is itself checked (/audit ->
/activity, /certificates -> /).

What was missing is the census. Nothing enumerated the URL map, so a route
added without any check looked exactly like the ones that are public on
purpose: an absence, indistinguishable from every other absence.

The three decorators now mark what they guard, which is what makes the census
possible from outside. flask-restx needed both shapes: a Resource declares
`method_decorators = [auth.require_role('viewer')]`, which stores the DECORATOR
and never applies it at import, so the factory is marked too - and a Resource
with some methods guarded and one bare is reported unprotected, because that
asymmetry (a POST added to a read-only resource without picking up its
neighbours' guard) is the defect shape most likely to happen.

PUBLIC_ROUTES names each public path with the reason, and adding to it is the
reviewable act.

Measured rather than assumed: 134 rules over 125 distinct paths, 99 protected
and 26 public. The finding that prompted this said eighteen were public. Each
of the 26 was read: ACME http-01, CRL and OCSP are public by specification;
login/logout/me and the three OIDC endpoints are how one gets in; / and
/api/events/stream check inline; /audit and /certificates redirect to checked
routes; the health probes answer before you are in; swagger and its assets
describe the surface without exposing it; static assets and the two logos load
before any session.

The census aggregates per RULE, not per path. Several paths are served by more
than one rule on separate endpoints - /api/settings by three - and keeping
whichever rule iterated last would let a guarded GET vouch for an unguarded
POST at the same path.

the path it found.

The runtime stage was COPY . . with a .dockerignore denylist, which worked the
way denylists work. Listed inside the published v2.29.0 image, /app carried a

scripts, pytest's own configuration, the Makefile and a systemd unit. None of

consumed by the builder stage, which is the point of a multi-stage build - or a
separate deliverable published on its own channel.

The size is not the problem. A denylist ships whatever nobody remembered to add
to it, and the thing nobody remembers is always the thing that arrived last:
every one of those directories came from a feature that had no reason to think
about the Dockerfile.

The runtime stage now names what it copies. The list was derived by reading the
code rather than by guessing: app.py, modules/, templates/ and static/ are the
application; scripts/ is there because dns_strategies.py executes
scripts/solidserver_hook.py at issuance time; the requirements files stay
because two error paths tell the operator to install one of them into a running
container to add a DNS or storage backend.

scheduler up, and solidserver_hook.py present at the path the code resolves.

a .dockerignore that quietly re-adds a path look identical in review - plus one
that does read the Dockerfile, because COPY . . coming back is the specific
regression and would otherwise need a rebuild to see. Both directions are
covered: sixteen named things that must not ship, and an allowlist check that

Also records in SECURITY.md that a rebuild is not expected to be bit-identical.

commit can differ; pinning breaks on every base-image bump and a reproducible
OS layer needs a snapshot mirror. Writing it down means nobody reads a digest
mismatch between two builds as evidence of tampering.

security: a key file that cannot be read is not permission to invent a key (#764)

SECRET_KEY_FILE names where the Flask session-signing key comes from, usually a
Docker or Kubernetes secret mount. When that file could not be read, or was
empty, CertMate logged a WARNING and generated a fresh key.

The warning said "generating a fresh secret key". It did not say what that
means, and it means three things: every existing session cookie becomes
invalid, so every logged-in user is signed out; the key is regenerated on each
start, so a restart loop signs them out again every time, with nothing
connecting the symptom to the unmounted secret; and the operator believes
sessions are signed with a key they control - possibly one deliberately shared
across replicas - when they are not.

An unmounted secret is a configuration error. This repository already refuses
to start on an unreadable settings.json (SettingsUnreadableError) and on an
unreadable API_BEARER_TOKEN_FILE. SECRET_KEY_FILE is the same shape and now
gets the same answer: SecretKeyUnreadableError, which app.py turns into one
line and exit 1. The message states the consequence and how to get running
again, rather than only the cause.

Two existing tests pinned the old behaviour by name
(test_file_read_error_generates_immediately). Read rather than deleted: the
property they were protecting is that SECRET_KEY must not be consulted after a
file failure - the two variables are mutually exclusive on purpose - and
generating was how that was achieved, not what was wanted. They now assert the
refusal and keep the same claim, which the refusal strengthens: a broken file
cannot be silently answered by a variable the operator forgot was set.

Nothing changes for an instance that never named a file: it still generates,
persists to data_dir/.secret_key and reuses it across restarts, and SECRET_KEY
and its insecure defaults behave exactly as before. Those are controls in the
new test file, because a fail-closed change that also breaks the ordinary path
would be a worse defect than the one it fixes.

README and docs/docker.md record the new behaviour where the variable is
documented.

16 new tests.

data: metadata.json carries the schema it was written with (#765)

settings.json was versioned for exactly this failure: an older build reads a
file written by a newer one, understands the fields it knows, writes it back
without the rest, and says nothing. metadata.json had no version at all - and
it is the file that records key custody: private_key_state (including the
`external` value that stops a CSR-only certificate being reissued nightly), the
CSR fingerprint, and the CA a private-CA certificate cannot renew without.

Losing it does not lose a certificate. It loses the instance's knowledge of
what that certificate is, which is worse, because nothing looks broken.

Two decisions worth stating, because both could have gone the other way.

The stamp is applied in _save_metadata, not by its seven callers. #669 shipped
the caller-stamps version of this for settings.json and it silently stripped
the field whenever a payload omitted it.

The refusal is on the WRITE, not at startup. settings.json is one file and
refusing to boot is proportionate; metadata is one file per domain, and taking
the whole instance down over one certificate would turn a data-loss risk into
an outage. Reading a newer record destroys nothing and the UI should still show
the certificate, so reading warns and writing refuses - which is exactly the
operation that loses fields. CERTMATE_ALLOW_SCHEMA_DOWNGRADE=1 overrides it,
the same variable and the same meaning as for settings.json.

The version is read from DISK immediately before the write, not taken from the
dict the caller handed over: that dict may have been assembled before a certbot
run that took minutes, and the question is about the bytes about to be
replaced. A test pins this by passing a dict that claims the current version
while the file claims a newer one.

test_metadata_corruption_handling asserted the written record equalled the
caller's dict exactly. Its subject is the quarantine surviving a subsequent
save, which it still asserts; the equality is now on the content the caller
asked for, with the stamp allowed.

perf: bound the event dispatch, and make a backlog visible (#767)

* perf: bound the event dispatch, and make a backlog visible

Every publish() started one new thread per registered listener - no pool, no
queue, no ceiling. The process's thread count was therefore a function of event
volume: a renewal sweep across many domains, each publishing to several
listeners, decided how many threads existed. Nothing chose that number and
nothing reported it.

The replacement is a fixed set of daemon workers reading one queue. Three
properties were chosen deliberately, and each is a test, because each could
reasonably have gone the other way.

The publisher never blocks. It is a request thread on the issuance path and the
scheduler on the renewal path, and DeployManager.on_certificate_event runs
deploy hooks with a timeout of up to 300 seconds - putting that on the
publisher's thread would trade a thread problem for a latency problem on the
product's main job.

Nothing is dropped. The SSE path drops the oldest message and then the
subscriber, which is right for a browser that fell behind and wrong for a
deploy that has to happen. Certificate events are rare and each one matters, so
the backlog is unbounded in length and bounded in cost - one small tuple per
queued call.

The backlog is visible. Past BACKLOG_WARN_AT the bus says so, once per episode,
naming CERTMATE_EVENT_WORKERS so the line says what to do about it.

The workers stay daemon, as the per-event threads were. A ThreadPoolExecutor
would have been fewer lines, but its threads are joined at interpreter exit,
which would let a 300-second deploy hook hold up shutdown until the container
runtime SIGKILLs it anyway. They also start lazily: a bus with no listeners -
which is what most of the test suite builds - costs no threads at all.

A listener that raises no longer takes its worker with it. With one thread per
event that was survivable; with a pool it would bleed capacity one bad event at
a time until nothing is dispatched and nothing says why.

The first version of the thread-count test measured AFTER delivery, and mutating
the code back to threading.Thread(...).start() did not fail it: the threads
finish as fast as they are created, so the count is back to baseline by the time
anything looks. It now holds every listener open and measures the peak, which is
the number the finding is about. That is recorded in the test, because the
measurement was wrong rather than the code right.

ops: make the renewal sweep say what it did, and whether it finished (#769)

The nightly sweep counted what it did and logged the counts. That was the whole
of its self-knowledge: no duration, nothing exported, and no way to tell
"finished, nothing was due" from "died half way through". So an instance whose
sweep takes longer every night - and will eventually stop finishing between
runs - looked exactly like one that was fine, right up until certificates
stopped renewing.

Two artefacts, and neither needs a capacity number to be chosen in advance.

A marker file (data/renewal_sweep.json) records that a sweep is in progress and
roughly how far it has got, updated every tenth certificate rather than every
one: the point is to know where a stopped sweep got to, and a write per
certificate would cost the same order as the work it describes. The NEXT sweep
reads it and reports that the previous one never finished, and where it
stopped, because the process that failed to finish is by definition not around
to report itself.

Four gauges make the same thing a graph:
certmate_renewal_sweep_duration_seconds, _certificates_examined,
_completed_timestamp_seconds and _unfinished. Gauges rather than counters
because the question is always about the LAST sweep. The completion timestamp
is the one a duration cannot replace - it stops moving when the sweep stops
finishing, which is the actual symptom.

The summary and the completion log now carry the duration and the number
examined; the opening line says how much work there is, because a duration is
only readable next to a count.

What this deliberately does not do is RESUME from the stopping point. Renewal
is idempotent and ordered by settings.json, so a rerun re-examines cheap
not-due entries rather than losing work; reordering the sweep would be a
behaviour change for a problem nobody has reported. Recording where it stopped
is what makes that decision possible later, with evidence.

Telemetry never breaks renewal: an unwritable marker (a read-only data volume
is a real deployment), a corrupt marker and a failing collector are each a test
that the sweep still completes.

test_check_renewals_summary asserted the summary dict equalled an exact
literal. Its subject is the counting, which it still pins; the two new
reporting fields are excluded there and covered in the new file.

Verified by mutation: removing the unfinished-sweep report fails 2 tests.

instructions say and what an operator following them would actually get.

the backup was taken, automatic backups are written with secrets masked and
cannot restore the instance - so on an install that never set a passphrase, the
newest archive is almost certainly one the restore path will refuse. The

#655; only the runbook did not point at it.

install, and where backups belong is a fact about the operator's
infrastructure, not about CertMate. What changed is that it is now a decision
with an off switch rather than the only shape available, in three steps of
increasing protection:

  persistence.backups.separateClaim   its own claim (survives the pod and the
                                      data volume's contents; the same storage
                                      class is still one failure domain)
  persistence.backups.existingClaim   a claim on storage you manage
  persistence.backups.offsite         a CronJob copying the archives out

yours - but it does decide two things that are easy to get wrong: the backup
volume is mounted READ-ONLY, so a misconfigured copy cannot damage what it is

can read what the app wrote. values.yaml carries a worked rclone example.

silently relocating an existing install's restore points would be a worse
outcome than the one being fixed. Both claims carry
helm.sh/resource-policy: keep - the backup volume more so than the other, since

obs: give every unit of work an id, including the ones that are not requests (#771)

The structured logger has always had a request_id field and a LogContext to
fill it. Nothing ever set either. The field was read off g.request_id, which no
code assigned, and the slow-request watchdog took the raw X-Request-Id header -
so on the overwhelmingly common case of a caller that sends no such header,
every line carried request_id: null, and two lines from one request were
indistinguishable from two lines from different ones.

Background work had nothing at all. A renewal and the deploy hook it triggered
were two unrelated sets of lines, associable only by the clock - on a nightly
sweep where dozens of certificates renew inside the same minute.

Three seams.

REQUESTS get an id in before_request. A caller-supplied one is honoured,
because the point of the header is letting a caller stitch its logs to ours -
but only if it is an opaque token: the value reaches a log line AND a response
header, so an unbounded or newline-carrying one would let a caller write its
own log entries and split the header. A rejected id is REPLACED by a generated
one rather than sanitised, because an id the caller did not send and cannot
match is worse than an honest new one. The id is echoed back, so a caller who
sent nothing can still quote it in a bug report. The context is entered in
before_request and released in teardown_request rather than around the view, so
error handlers and after_request handlers log under it too - and released in
teardown so a view that raises does not leave it bound to the thread.

THE RENEWAL SWEEP mints one for itself. check_renewals became a two-line
wrapper around the existing body rather than growing a `with` around it: the
body is long and already deeply nested, `with` guarantees the release on every
exit path, and the diff stays readable. A leaked context would tag every later
job on that scheduler thread with a stale sweep id, which is worse than no id
at all.

LISTENER THREADS get it from the queued item. This is the seam that cannot work
by accident: contextvars do NOT cross a thread boundary - a worker starts with
an empty context, not a copy of the publisher's - so a change that only set the
id on the publisher's side would pass every test that looked there while the
deploy hook still logged nothing. A publish outside any context carries no id
rather than inventing one, which would look like a correlated unit of work that
nothing else belongs to.

Verified by mutation: dropping the id from the queued item fails 3 tests,
and not generating one when the header is absent fails 6.

Two tests were written wrong first and are recorded that way: werkzeug refuses
to put a newline in a header at all, on the way in as well as out, so that case
cannot be reached through HTTP (the refusal is asserted directly on the
function instead); and Flask returns 500 rather than propagating, so the
raising-view control asserts the release, not the exception.

perf: a dashboard load is not N sequential round trips any more (#773)

* perf: a dashboard load is not N sequential round trips any more

GET /api/certificates called get_certificate_info once per domain in a plain
loop. On a local-filesystem instance that is four small reads per domain out of
the page cache and nobody notices. On an instance whose storage backend is
Azure Key Vault or AWS Secrets Manager each of those is a network round trip,
so one dashboard load was N of them one after another - and the page got slower
in proportion to how much the instance was actually being used for.

The reads are IO-bound and independent, so they now run on a bounded pool.
Measured with a 30 ms round trip, which is optimistic for Key Vault:

     10 domains   0.38s -> 0.07s   (5.1x)
     50 domains   1.82s -> 0.24s   (7.5x)
    200 domains   7.26s -> 0.92s   (7.9x)

Three properties are the point, and each is a test.

ORDER IS PRESERVED. The dashboard lists certificates in settings order, and a
listing that reshuffled on every load would be a worse defect than the latency
it fixes. There is a test with the slow entries first, which is what would
expose an as-completed implementation.

ONE BAD CERTIFICATE DOES NOT LOSE THE REST. executor.map re-raises the first
exception when its results are consumed, which would turn one unreadable
certificate into a 500 for the whole listing. The sequential loop simply got a
falsy answer, so the concurrency must not introduce that; each call is guarded
and a failure yields None, logged with the domain.

A SMALL INSTANCE DOES NOT PAY FOR THREADS. Below four domains the calls stay on
the request thread. The ceiling is 8, matching the gunicorn thread count the
image ships with: one request must not be able to occupy more capacity than the
whole process has for serving all of them.

The settings dict was already loaded once and passed in, and that matters more
now than it did: load_settings caches on flask.g behind has_request_context(),
and a worker thread has no request context - so without it every worker would
fall back to reading settings.json from disk and this change would have been a
regression. There is a test pinning that the endpoint still hands it over.

One test was written with caplog, passed alone and failed in the full suite:
caplog works through the root logger and is therefore at the mercy of anything
else in the suite that touches global logging. It attaches to the module's own
logger now, which is what actually emits. Recorded in the test, because the
measurement was wrong rather than the code.

fix: state the single-worker assumption where it is relied on, and check it (#775)

Two things in CertMate are correct only under one gunicorn worker, and both
fail silently rather than visibly.

_get_domain_lock returns a threading.Lock. It serialises issuance and renewal
for a domain WITHIN ONE PROCESS. With two workers it is two locks, so two
requests for the same domain would run certbot concurrently against the same
--config-dir and interleave the four-file publish with itself - producing the
mixed generation reconcile_served_copies exists to repair, arrived at
deliberately rather than by a crash.

APScheduler is worse: it runs in-process, so two workers means two schedulers
and every certificate examined and renewed once PER WORKER against the CA's
rate limits.

Both facts lived in a CMD line (--workers 1) and in the Helm chart, which pins
one replica and refuses more at template time. Neither was stated in the code
that depends on them, and nothing checked the one route left to violate them:
overriding the command.

The lock's docstring now says it is per-process, names the assumption, and says
why the cross-process shape _publish_lock already demonstrates is not used
here: the whole issuance path would have to hold it, including the certbot
subprocess, and a stale lock file then blocks renewal for a domain until
someone removes it.

warn_if_multiple_workers reads the parent's command line - a worker cannot ask
how many workers there are, since each is a separate process - and logs at
CRITICAL with the consequence and the fix. It answers nothing under
`python app.py`, under pytest, and anywhere /proc is unavailable: a guess there
becomes a CRITICAL in development, and a CRITICAL that fires in development
teaches people to ignore it.

Found while writing it: get_certmate_logger returns a StructuredLogger, whose
methods are (message, **fields) and NOT the stdlib's (msg, *args). The first
version passed lazy %s arguments and raised TypeError - which would have turned
a warning about a broken configuration into a failure to boot, on the rare path
where it matters. The rest of the codebase is already consistent; a test now
keeps it that way by walking every module for the same shape.

api: a certificate request states its own limit, instead of the backup's (#776)

One MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH of 50 MB applied to every endpoint. It exists for the
backup upload, which needs it. Applied to certificate creation it meant the
ceiling on san_domains was "however many names fit in fifty megabytes" and the
ceiling on csr was "however large a PEM fits in fifty megabytes" - neither of
which is a limit anyone chose, and neither of which any endpoint stated.

Both bounds are derived rather than picked.

100 names is Let's Encrypt's own cap per certificate. A request naming more
cannot be satisfied by the CA regardless of what CertMate does with it, so
refusing it at the boundary says so - instead of building a certbot command
line with thousands of -d flags and letting the CA reject it AFTER the DNS
challenges have been set up, which costs an ACME order and a set of DNS writes
to learn nothing.

64 KB for a CSR is generous by more than an order of magnitude: a PEM request
for a 4096-bit key carrying a hundred names is a few kilobytes. It refuses long
before anything reaches the parser.

Both refusals name the limit and what was sent, because a 400 that says only
"too large" leaves the caller guessing at the number.

The type check on csr_pem is part of the same change: len() on a dict succeeds,
so without it a non-text CSR would pass the size bound and then produce a
parser error that describes the wrong problem.

The global limit is deliberately unchanged, and there is a test saying so:
lowering it to fix these two endpoints would break the backup upload, which is
the one endpoint that genuinely receives megabytes.

Verified by mutation: removing both bounds fails 4 of the 11 tests. The
controls matter as much - a request AT the limit is accepted, a plausible CSR
still reaches the parser, bytes are still a valid CSR shape, and the existing
san_domains type check is not shadowed by the new length check.

obs: a renewal that did not reach production says so, once (#778)

The listener that runs deploy hooks caught everything and logged it. So a
renewal that succeeded at the CA and then failed to reach the systems that
serve it was reported, to every other subscriber, as a completed renewal -
while the machines in front were still presenting the previous certificate.

deploy_hook_failed already fires PER HOOK. That is the right grain for "which
target broke" and the wrong grain for the question an operator actually asks
after a renewal: is this certificate live? Answering it meant counting per-hook
failures across a stream, and a notifier had no single event meaning "renewed,
not deployed".

certificate_deploy_incomplete is that event. It carries the domain, the
lifecycle event, and how many of how many targets failed - or the error, on the
path where the listener itself blew up, which was the shape that motivated the
finding: `except Exception: log` made a deploy that crashed indistinguishable
from one that never ran.

It is on _ALWAYS_NOTIFY_EVENTS for the same reason deploy_hook_failed is:
neither is among the five certificate_* events the UI offers, so any filter
drops them, and this reports a failure an operator must not be able to silence
by accident.

WHAT THIS DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO. The finding asked for `deployed: true/false`
alongside `renewed` in the renewal result. That is not reachable: hooks run on
the event bus, so the renewal has already returned by the time any of it is
known. Carrying the outcome back into that result would mean making issuance
wait for a deploy hook - with a 300-second timeout - which is precisely what
the bounded dispatch exists to prevent. An event is where a fact that arrives
later belongs.

Two controls matter as much as the assertions: a fully successful deploy says
nothing extra, and an instance with NO hooks configured is not "incompletely
deployed" - it is a certificate nobody asked to publish. Without the second,
this would fire on almost every renewal on almost every instance.

api: a contract version that moves when the contract does, and a way to deprecate (#779)

The only version a caller could read was the RELEASE number - in the Swagger
document and in /health. It moves on every patch whether or not anything a
caller depends on moved with it, so it cannot answer "will my client still
work". A client that pinned it would refuse a patch that changed nothing; one
that ignored it had nothing else to read.

API_CONTRACT_VERSION is that other thing. Sent on EVERY response as
X-CertMate-API-Version - a header rather than only a field, so a client learns
it from any response including the error it is trying to understand, without a
second call - and reported by /health as api_contract_version for anything that
already polls there.

The rule for moving it lives beside the constant, because a version with no
stated rule is a number that drifts: minor when the surface grows in a way a
caller can ignore, major when something a caller may depend on goes away or
changes meaning. Deprecating does neither.

Which is the second half. There was no deprecation mechanism at all: no
Deprecation header, no Sunset, no marker, no flag. So an endpoint could be
removed abruptly - with a 404 as the first notice - or kept forever because
removing it was the only alternative. Both are choices nobody wants.

modules/api/deprecation.py is the standard shape: RFC 9745 Deprecation as an
@-prefixed unix timestamp, RFC 8594 Sunset as an HTTP-date, and a Link to what
to do instead. Applied at the app rather than per route: a decorator would have
to be remembered on the endpoint being deprecated, which is the one moment
nobody is thinking about the mechanism.

DEPRECATIONS is empty, and that is the honest state - nothing is deprecated
today. Shipping the mechanism before it is needed is the point: the alternative
is inventing it under time pressure in the release where something has to go,
which is the release where it gets skipped. The tests exercise it against an
example entry so it stays tested while nothing uses it, and one asserts the
emptiness so that adding an entry is a deliberate act visible in a diff.

A malformed entry produces no headers rather than an error: a typo in a date
must not turn a working endpoint into a 500. The endpoint still answers; what
is lost is the announcement.

The per-module coverage gate from #662 caught the new file having no floor. It
has one now, at 100: 33 statements of pure logic with no I/O, meant to be
trustworthy on the day it is first used - a day nobody will be testing it.

data: a domain's DNS provider is written once, under one lock (#780)

metadata.json is what issuance reads. The domain's entry in settings.json is
what get_domain_dns_provider reads. Both are authoritative, and they were
updated by two separate writes with the domain lock RELEASED between them:
CertificateService.update_config wrote the metadata under the lock and
returned, and the route wrote the settings entry afterwards.

Nothing reconciled them. A renewal starting in that window read the OLD
provider from settings while the metadata already said the new one - and
neither file was wrong on its own, which is what makes it hard to see.

Both writes now happen inside the same domain_lock section. The route stops
doing half the job; update_config owns the pair.

LOCK ORDERING was checked before doing this, because taking the settings lock
while holding the domain lock creates one. No settings mutate callback anywhere
in modules/ acquires a domain lock, so the reverse order does not exist and
this cannot deadlock. That check is a test rather than a memory: anything that
adds such a callback fails it, naming the file.

The mirror follows the same rule the metadata write follows - absent means
"leave alone" - so a probe-only edit does not touch the provider, and a
certificate with no settings entry (an adopted one) does not gain a
half-populated one that makes it look managed.

The test that pins the ordering was written wrong first: it checked that the
write happened and that the lock was acquired and released, which is equally
true of the broken version it replaces. It now records whether the domain lock
is HELD at the moment of the settings write, which is the only observation that
distinguishes the two - and the mutation confirms it, after a first mutation
attempt that silently failed to apply and therefore measured nothing.

security: what counts as a secret cannot be decided by accident any more (#781)

What counts as a secret for masking and for preserve-on-save is a regular
expression over the field's NAME - seven words - plus a declared list for the
fields whose names it misses. A credential named something else is neither
masked on GET /api/web/settings nor kept out of the share-safe backup, which is
the archive explicitly meant to be shareable.

MEASURED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING: today nothing is missed. All 29 DNS
providers' credential fields are covered. Sixteen are not matched by the regex
and every one is an identifier or an endpoint - including custom-script's
auth_hook, which reads like a place to hide a token and is in fact a script
PATH screened by _validated_hook_path, and acme-dns's username, which the
project already declares as a secret because there it is half of a generated
credential rather than an account name a person chose.

So the finding's risk is entirely about the NEXT provider. Rather than replace
the regex with a frozenset of paths - a refactor whose failure mode is a
forgotten path silently un-masking a live credential, which is worse than the
over-broad matching it replaces - this makes the dangerous condition impossible
to introduce silently: a credential field matched by neither the regex nor the
declared list fails the build, naming the provider and the field.

The "not a secret" classification lives in the test rather than in production
code, because it changes no behaviour. It is a review artefact - the record of
a decision someone made - in the place where the next person is asked to make
the same one, with the reason next to each entry.

test: cover the branches that decide what a failure looks like (#782)

resources_lifecycle.py is the entry point for every certificate create, renew
and reissue, and it carried the second-thinnest coverage floor in the project:
55, against core modules floored far higher. The uncovered lines were not happy
paths - they were the `except` arms, which is where all the behaviour is.

Each arm turns an exception into a status code and a machine-readable code, and
the difference between them is what a client acts on:

    403  the key is not allowed this domain - do not retry
    409  the domain is busy - retry shortly
    404  there is no certificate here
    422  the CA or the configuration refused - retrying unchanged fails the
         same way, and the message says what to fix
    500  something in CertMate broke - the operator's problem

Getting one wrong is not cosmetic. A 500 where a 422 belongs sends an operator
looking inside CertMate for a problem in their DNS provider; a 500 where a 409
belongs makes a client retry-storm a domain that is simply mid-issuance.

59% -> 77.8%, and the floor moves 55 -> 77.

Two of the sixteen are the controls that make the rest mean something. The 422
arm must NOT swallow a genuine fault, so an AttributeError inside CertMate is
still a 500 with a generic message rather than an invitation to fix DNS. And a
409 must publish no certificate_failed event - it is "try again in a minute",
not a failure - while a real renewal failure still publishes one, or the
notifier goes quiet on the case it exists for.

settings_routes.py stays at 50. It is still the thinnest module and the next
one to raise, but nothing here added tests for it: it measures 50.8, so moving
its floor would lock in a number nobody earned.

The floors are 77 and 50 rather than 78 and 51 because the terminal report
rounds up and the gate does not. Measured by running the gate the way CI runs
it, not by reading the percentage.

build: lock the 76 transitive packages nobody chose (#783)

requirements.txt pins 42 packages. Installing it resolves 118. The other
76 were whatever the index served on the day the image was built, and
nothing in the repository recorded which. Two images built from the same
commit a month apart were not the same image, and there was no diff that
would say so.

requirements.lock and requirements-minimal.lock hold the full resolution
for the two main variants, generated by pip's own resolver inside the
base image at the digest the Dockerfile pins
(scripts/regenerate_lockfiles.sh), and the builder installs from them.
The optional DNS and storage sets have no lock and still resolve at build
time, so nothing that could be built before cannot be built now.

Measured, because one lockfile per variant is only correct if the two
published architectures agree: the resolution of both files is identical
on linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. The regeneration script re-checks that
and refuses to write if it ever stops being true.

The lock also becomes the extras constraint. The .txt constrains 42
packages; the lock constrains 118, which is the only way an extras layer
cannot move a transitive out from under the locked base. Every advertised
EXTRA_REQUIREMENTS combination was measured to resolve under it, and a new
CI step re-measures on every run rather than trusting the comment.

The failure this introduces is the reason for most of the test file:
installing from a lock means a bump to requirements.txt does nothing
until the lock is regenerated. Dependabot raises a security patch, it
merges, every check is green, and the image keeps installing the old
version. Nothing would say so — so a test fails when a direct pin and its
lock disagree, and its negative controls prove it would.

The opposite risk, a transitive frozen at a version that later turns out
vulnerable, is already covered: check_resolved_advisories.py asks OSV
about the set actually installed in the built image, on every build, as a
required check. A test asserts that gate is still wired up, because the
trade only holds while it is.

Verified inside a built image (arm64, EXTRA_REQUIREMENTS=storage-all):
all 118 locked packages present at exactly the locked version, and
`certbot --version` still answers.

SECURITY.md withdraws one reason it previously gave against hash pinning
— "two architectures resolving different binary wheels" — because it is
measurably not true for these two files. The hash decision itself is
unchanged: these locks carry no hashes and do not claim to verify that a
wheel is the one that was reviewed.

security: a credential can name where it lives instead of holding its value (#784)

* security: a credential can name where it lives instead of holding its value

DNS provider API tokens and the OIDC client secret rested in settings.json
as cleartext JSON. 0600 is the right permission and is not the point:
that file is the one that gets backed up, copied between hosts, mounted
into a container and attached to a bug report. A deployment already
keeping its secrets in a Docker or Kubernetes secret had no way to keep
them out of it.

API_BEARER_TOKEN_FILE already solved this shape for one secret. This
generalises it to the settings file: beside any field, `<field>_file`
names a path and `<field>_env` names a variable.

    {"accounts": {"prod": {"api_token_file": "/run/secrets/cloudflare"}}}
    {"oidc": {"client_secret_env": "CERTMATE_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET"}}

Resolution happens where the value is USED — the one seam that decides
whether this works. get_dns_provider_account_config resolves; the listing
functions do not, which keeps the secret out of API responses. On the
OIDC side it resolves in _client_secret rather than in _load_config,
because update_config loads the config, merges a payload onto it and
writes the result back: resolving on the load path would persist the
secret into settings.json the first time anyone toggled a checkbox in the
SSO settings page. Both have a test that fails on exactly that.

Three behaviours, each of which is a failure mode if reversed:

- A reference beats a literal. Someone adds api_token_file and leaves the
  old api_token behind; if the literal won, issuance would keep using the
  credential they believed they had replaced.
- Trailing whitespace is stripped. `docker secret` and `kubectl create
  secret --from-file` both produce files ending in a newline, and a token
  with one comes back from the DNS API as an authentication error that
  names nothing useful.
- A reference that resolves to nothing is refused, not treated as empty,
  and the log names the field and the path. Writing the mount into the
  error is the whole point: otherwise the operator debugs a credential
  that is correct.

"Is this account configured" deliberately does NOT resolve. It is asked to
render a settings page, and reading every secret off disk to draw a green
tick would both put credentials in memory for a page view and make the
page fail on a host where the secret is not mounted.

Three call sites had to learn the same rule or the feature would have been
unusable: validate_dns_provider_account (the save path rejected an account
as missing the field it supplies, so a file-backed account could not be
saved at all), test_provider (the UI button), and _account_has_credentials
(a file-backed account rendered as unconfigured).

The suffix rule is only safe while no real credential field ends in _file
or _env. None of the 31 fields across the 29 providers does, and a test
asserts it, so one added later fails a check rather than being silently
read as a pointer to another field.

Documented in SECURITY.md and in docs/docker.md across all five locales.

test: give the three operations with a budget a number (#787)

Exactly one performance property was under test — that /health stays
responsive while certificates are being issued. Everything else had a
budget people reasoned about in comments ("iterates 100s of domains",
"under a CPU-throttled container makes the listing crawl") and no number,
so "it feels slower" could not be turned into a comparison.

Three operations, measured at 120 certificates on disk:

  listing                30-36 ms, 0.25-0.30 ms/domain, 0 settings loads
  remote-backed listing  155-168 ms cold / 120 round-trips,
                         1-4 ms warm / 0 round-trips
  renewal sweep          24-67 ms, 1 settings load

What is ASSERTED is a count, not a time. A wall-clock ceiling measures the
runner as much as the code: one GC pause fails it with nothing wrong, and
the reliable response to that is to raise the ceiling until it never
fires. The counts do not vary with the hardware and are the numbers that
actually decide whether these operations scale — settings loads per
listing, backend round-trips per domain, settings loads per sweep. The
timings are printed and recorded in the docstrings so a later run has
something to compare against.

Each count was mutation-checked rather than assumed:

  - calling get_certificate_info without threading settings through:
    0 loads becomes 120
  - turning the cert-info cache off: 0 warm round-trips becomes 120

Two controls guard against a count that is low because nothing happened:
every domain must come back parsed with the expected days_left, and the
sweep must not have shelled out to certbot — otherwise the sweep number
would be measuring a MagicMock rather than the loop.

The remote-backend double refuses retrieve_certificate outright. That path
pulls the private key out of a secrets backend for a view that only needs
cert.pem, and a regression to it would be invisible in a timing.

refactor: one function per health check, one per diagnostic collector (#788)

create_health_resources was the most complex unit in the repository:
cyclomatic complexity 64, higher than the certificate renewal path it
reports on. The complexity was not one hard decision. It was twelve
independent try/except sections inlined into two request handlers, none
of which could be entered except through Flask.

The practical cost was that a branch was only reachable by building an
app. Exercising "the configured storage backend failed to initialise and
CertMate silently fell back to local disk" — the check that exists
precisely because that used to be invisible — meant standing up a whole
application to get at four lines. It had no test.

Now:

  a CHECK      takes ctx, returns (name, state, severity).
               HealthCheck.get is a loop over HEALTH_CHECKS taking the
               worst severity.
  a COLLECTOR  takes ctx, returns (fields, errors).
               DiagnosticsSnapshot.get is a loop over
               DIAGNOSTIC_COLLECTORS merging both.

Every unit in the module is now under complexity 10, and a test pins that
at 12 so the split has to stay split.

The severity ordering used to live implicitly in four `if overall ==
'healthy'` guards — correct, and one edit away from not being. It is one
`max` now, with a test that unhealthy beats degraded.

The collector loop catches what a collector lets escape and records that
section as failed. That is the property each of the twelve hand-written
blocks was implementing separately, and it now also covers the thirteenth
that someone adds without one. This is what people attach to a bug
report; losing all of it because one subsystem is broken is the case it
is most needed in.

Behaviour is unchanged, and that was checked rather than asserted: the
old and the new module were run against identical inputs and the JSON
diffed, once with every subsystem working and once with every optional
subsystem raising. Both payloads were byte-identical, including the
errors map and the legacy single-account DNS provider shape.

19 new tests, all of which call a check or a collector directly. Coverage
70% -> 84.4%; the floor moves 70 -> 80.

fix: the renewal sweep names the certificates it cannot renew (#759) (#789)

* fix: the renewal sweep names the certificates it cannot renew (#759)

Reported as a private-CA certificate with a 31-day lifespan and a 30-day
threshold that never auto-renewed. The detail that matters is in the
report and not in the title: the log carried NOTHING for that domain.
Not a failure, not a skip, not a "not yet due".

The threshold arithmetic is not the cause. Reproduced against the real
code at eight points across the certificate's life, a REGISTERED
certificate with exactly those numbers is picked up from day zero
(days_left 30, and `30 <= 30`), and `ca_provider` never enters the
decision at all:

  giorno  days_left  needs_renewal  esito dello sweep
       0         30           True  checked=1 tentato_rinnovo=1
      25          5           True  checked=1 tentato_rinnovo=1

The cause is that `check_renewals` iterates `settings['domains']` and
nothing else, while the rest of the application answers "which
certificates exist" differently:

  digest.py            union of settings['domains'] AND the certificate
                       directories -> reports it as expiring
  get_certificate_info reads the disk -> dashboard shows it, with
                       needs_renewal: true

So a certificate present on disk and absent from settings is visible
everywhere except in the one component whose job is to renew it, and
that component said nothing. That silence is why the report reads as a
threshold bug: there was no other evidence to read.

The sweep now reconciles what it considered against the certificate
directories and, for each one no settings entry named, logs a warning
naming it and what to do, and counts it in a new `unmanaged` field. The
completion line carries the count.

It reports; it does NOT adopt. Renewing a certificate the operator never
registered would issue against a CA for a domain CertMate was not asked
to manage — a half-restored backup would start requesting certificates —
and a background sweep is not where that decision belongs.

Two things this deliberately does not do:

- The pre-existing warning in settings.py stays as it is. It only fires
  when `domains` is entirely empty, which is why an instance with nine
  registered certificates and one orphan was told nothing; broadening it
  would put a scandir on every load_settings call, and the sweep now
  emits a better message once per run instead.
- No new Prometheus gauge. `record_renewal_sweep` is part of the
  /metrics surface and widening it belongs in its own change.

Found while writing the tests, and recorded in them: `load_settings`
strips a domains entry it cannot read a domain out of — both a dict with
no `domain` key and a bare number come back as `domains: []`. That makes
the sweep's own `skipped_invalid` branch unreachable through normal
loading, and it means a typo in a hand-edited settings.json used to
remove a certificate from renewal with nothing said anywhere. The
reconciliation catches that case too.

8 of the 10 new tests fail against the code they replace; the 2 that
pass are the diagnosis, which describes behaviour that was already
there.

* fix: a metadata write that does not happen says why (#757)

Reported as a wildcard problem: configuring a deployment probe failed with
"Failed: Failed to update metadata for domain: *.xx.xx" and nothing else.
The reporter concluded from the message that wildcards were the cause, and
from the domain field — a text input with a datalist, sitting next to a
real dropdown — that the form was not wired to anything.

Neither was it. Reproduced against a running instance with three seeded

returns 200, the datalist populates with all three domains, and a domain
with no certificate returns a clear 404.

What produces that message is `_save_metadata` returning a bare `False`.
Two unrelated situations do:

  - the file cannot be written — a read-only volume, or a certificates
    directory owned by a different uid, which is the shape a Kubernetes
    deployment gets wrong and the reporter runs on Kubernetes;
  - the write is refused BY DESIGN, because metadata.json on disk declares
    a newer schema than this build understands.

Both reasons were computed, logged server-side, and thrown away before
reaching the person who had to act on one of them. Measured, both:

  {"error": "Failed to update metadata for domain: X"}   HTTP 500

  permission   500  could not write /…/metadata.json: Permission denied.
                    Check that the certificates volume is mounted writable
                    and owned by the user CertMate runs as (uid 1000…)
  schema       409  metadata.json declares schema v99 and this build
                    understands v1 … set CERTMATE_ALLOW_SCHEMA_DOWNGRADE=1
                    to overwrite it anyway
                    code: METADATA_SCHEMA_DOWNGRADE

409 rather than 500 for the refusal: a guard doing its job is not a server
error, and reporting one sends an operator looking for a fault in CertMate
instead of at the version they rolled back from.

`write_metadata` raises; `_save_metadata` stays as the boolean wrapper.
That split is the point rather than an accident: six call sites write
metadata during issuance and renewal and ignore the result, and if they
started raising, a cosmetic metadata problem would abort an issuance that
had already obtained a certificate. Only the one call site whose outcome
reaches a person uses the raising form.

The refusal keeps its ERROR level and its domain-as-log-argument, which a
test already pinned.

Four existing test files stubbed `_save_metadata`; they now stub
`write_metadata` and signal failure by raising, because returning False
would be reported as success. One assertion changed from the old message

perf: the private key is not re-validated on every certificate read (#799)

`private_key_state` answers whether a usable private key sits beside a
certificate, and it answered it by loading the key — which OpenSSL validates
as it parses. Measured on one machine: 51.6 ms for RSA-2048, 275.5 ms for
RSA-4096, 0.020 ms for EC P-256, and 58.7 ms against 0.19 ms for a whole
`get_certificate_info` call with and without a loadable key beside the
certificate. CertMate's default key shape is `rsa`/2048, so on the common
installation ~99% of the cost of reading one certificate's information was
re-answering a question whose two input files had not moved.

It is called once per domain by the dashboard listing, by every Prometheus
collection — serially, on the request thread — and by every renewal sweep, so
the cost is multiplied by the size of the estate the README says this scales
to. At 120 domains the listing measured 5631 ms.

The answer is now remembered per `(sha256(privkey.pem), sha256(cert.pem))`.
Hashing both costs tens of microseconds against tens of milliseconds, and
unlike an mtime or a TTL it is exact: any change to either file produces a
different digest and the comparison runs again. That matters for this answer
in particular, because the condition it exists to catch is a torn publish
leaving a NEW certificate beside the PREVIOUS key — so the certificate side
has to be part of the key, and it is.

Measured after, in the project's own benchmark at 120 domains:

    rsa  cold 5631 ms (46.93 ms/domain)  repeat 9 ms (0.08 ms/domain)
    ec   cold   13 ms ( 0.11 ms/domain)  repeat 8 ms (0.06 ms/domain)

That benchmark could not see any of this before: its fixture generated EC
keys, the one shape where loading a key is free, so the per-domain figure it
recorded described an estate almost nobody runs. It is parametrised over both
now, and the RSA row is the default one. The counts it asserts are unchanged
and key-shape independent; only the timings differ.

Also split the comparison into `_compare_key_to_certificate`, so the cheap
decisions and the lookup stay readable and a test can count how often the
expensive half actually happens. The new tests assert that count rather than
a wall-clock ceiling, and they fail against the old code.

fix: the metrics /metrics exports are the ones the instance measures (#800)

Six recorder methods on the collector had no caller anywhere in the
application, so five series were exported at every scrape and were permanently
empty: certmate_certificate_requests_total, the creation duration histogram,
certmate_acme_rate_limit_hits_total, and the cache hit/miss counters. A missing
metric is a gap somebody notices while building a dashboard; a dead one is a
flat line and an alert that never fires, which reads as "nothing is going
wrong". monitoring/prometheus-alerts.yml already said so, and omitted four
alerts for that reason.

Two of them mattered. Certificate CREATION recorded nothing at all while
renewal recorded three things, so "how many did we issue this week, and how
many attempts failed" could not be answered from /metrics — and because the
only record_acme_error call site was the renewal one, a CA outage during a
burst of new issuance registered as zero ACME errors. And rate-limit hits are
the first series an operator of ACME software would alert on.

What changed:

fix: the event bus says what it could not deliver (#801)

* fix: the event bus says what it could not deliver

The dispatch workers are daemon threads on purpose — joining them would let a
300-second deploy hook hold shutdown open until the container runtime killed it
anyway — and that trade is written into the bus. What was not written down is
what the trade cost: the bus had no stop, drain, close or join at all, so a
container stopped during or just after a renewal sweep discarded whatever was
still queued. Typically that is the deploy hook for a certificate that HAD been
renewed, so the service keeps serving the old certificate, the dashboard shows
a success, deploy_hook_failed never fires (the hook did not fail, it never
started), and nothing anywhere records it.

`stop(timeout)` does not change the daemon decision. It bounds the loss and
names it: queued dispatches get a deadline to reach a worker, and whatever is
left is taken off the queue and logged with its event and its domain, so the
line an operator finds after a restart says which certificates to redeploy by
hand. It waits for the QUEUE to empty rather than for the workers to finish —
an item that has reached a worker is running, and waiting for a deploy hook is
the one thing this must not do.

A publish after stop() is refused rather than queued, because accepting work
after the report would put it in a report that has already been made. SSE
subscribers still receive: it is the listener dispatch that is refused, and a
browser holding a stream open during shutdown should still see the last event.

Wiring, in the two places that exist: atexit — which runs when a gunicorn
worker exits on SIGTERM and does not run on SIGKILL, exactly right for a drain
that must never delay a kill — and app.py's KeyboardInterrupt handler, after
the scheduler stops so no new renewal can queue a deploy mid-drain. The atexit
registration lives in the factory rather than in EventBus.__init__ so that
constructing a bus, which most of the test suite does, leaves no handler behind
holding a reference to it.

different bodies:

  GET /api/does-not-exist          {"code": 404, "error": "Not Found", "message": ...}

reporting the identical condition, one of which set CERTIFICATE_NOT_FOUND while
the other set nothing. A client could not branch on the field without checking
its type first, which is the same as not having the field. The SDK this
repository publishes already documented it as "CertMate's machine-readable
error code (e.g. DOMAIN_OUT_OF_SCOPE) when present", so the string was the
intended type all along.

  flask-restx's abort cannot do it: its own first parameter is named `code`, so

fix: two answers that outlived the thing that invalidated them (#806)

* fix: a migration that could not read the source is not a migration of zero

migrate_certificates wrapped its whole body in `except Exception: log` and then
returned the per-domain results it had accumulated. Everything inside that body
which can fail per certificate already records False for that certificate, so
the only thing reaching the outer handler is the enumeration of the source — an
expired Vault token, a role without ListBucket, an unreachable endpoint. It
returned {}.

The route then computed successful=0, total=0, and answered HTTP 200 with
`success: true`, "Migration completed: 0/0 certificates migrated", and an audit
record stamped status='success'. An operator moving off a backend before
decommissioning it was told the move had worked.

"Enumerated nothing" and "could not enumerate" are different answers and cannot
share a return value, so the enumeration failure is raised. The route already
had the other arm — 500, a failure message, a failure audit record — and now
reaches it; tests/test_audit_hardening.py already exercises that arm with a
manager that raises.

The controls matter as much as the change: a source that genuinely holds no
certificates still returns {} and still succeeds, and a per-certificate failure
— a store that refuses, a retrieve that raises — is still recorded as False for
that certificate while the rest of the run continues. Only the enumeration is
fatal, because only the enumeration means the result set itself is unknown.

* fix: the certbot answer does not outlive the evidence for it

The readiness probe ran `certbot --version` once per process and froze the
result for the life of that process. Both directions of that are wrong, and
both are quiet.

A transient failure at startup — a filesystem still settling, a fork refused
under memory pressure — records FAILED, and /health/ready then answers 503
"until this is fixed", which for a running container means until somebody
restarts it. Under an orchestrator that is a restart loop rolling the same dice
on every attempt. And a certbot that breaks AFTER startup — a volume remounted,
a dependency changed inside the container — never turned readiness red, so the
endpoint an orchestrator uses to decide rotation went on saying yes while
nothing could be issued.

The answer now has a TTL (CERTMATE_CERTBOT_PROBE_TTL, default 300, clamped
30-3600). The TTL is what makes re-checking affordable: readiness is scraped
every few seconds and running certbot that often would be its own problem, so
at most one probe per TTL with the recorded answer in between. A lock around
the refresh means a burst of scrapes on an expired answer runs certbot once
between them rather than once each.

Half the defect was in the routes, and a TTL alone would not have touched it:
/health and /health/ready both read managers['issuance_status'], the dict
written once at startup. They now ask for a current answer, and the refreshed
one is written back to that key so nothing else keeps reading the snapshot.

Unchanged: `skipped` and `unknown` are absence of evidence, not evidence, and
still count as ready — reporting them as failure would flip every test app and
every startup window out of rotation.

claimed as the cause of #786: that report is about the certificate list, whose
