feat: the renewal sweep takes on a certificate that can say how it was issued (#792) (#810)

#759 was fixed in two halves. #789 made the sweep report a certificate that is
on disk with no settings entry naming it — until then the log carried nothing
at all for that domain, which is why the report read as a threshold bug. What
to do with those certificates was a product decision about issuing, so it was
recorded as #792 rather than taken inside a bug fix.

The decision, with the reasoning in the issue: renew the ones that can say how
they were issued, report the rest.

The objection that had carried the most weight was that a half-restored backup
or an old volume snapshot would start requesting certificates on its own. It
does not distinguish the options: settings.json lives on the same volume as the
certificates and is in the same backup, so an instance brought up on an old
snapshot already renews everything that snapshot registers. And "a domain
CertMate was not asked to manage" describes a different situation than this
one: a certificate under CertMate's own certificate directory, beside a
metadata.json CertMate wrote, was issued by this instance.

The sweep now asks collect_domain_sources — the one implementation of "which
certificates exist" (#670), which the listing, the digest and discovery already
use — so all four components answer that question the same way. The loop over
registered domains still walks settings directly, deliberately: it is what
counts a malformed entry as skipped_invalid, and the union silently drops
those. A typo must not become an absence.

A disk-only certificate is renewed when its metadata names the DNS provider and
account and that provider is configured on this instance now, or when it is
http-01 and needs no per-domain credential. The guard is not a second copy of
the renewal path's requirements: it calls the same resolver the renewal calls,
so the two cannot disagree about what renewable means. Everything else is
reported exactly as before — no metadata, no provider named, or a provider this
instance no longer has. The old behaviour is the fallback, not the thing
replaced.

On success the domain is written back to settings through the mutator form, on
the fresh on-disk list, so a registration that landed mid-sweep is not lost.
Without that the warning returns every night for the life of the certificate,
and a warning that repeats forever is one an operator learns to scroll past —
which is how #759 stayed invisible long enough to be reported as something
else. After this the warning only ever names certificates the sweep genuinely
could not take on.

The per-domain body is extracted into _renew_if_due and both paths go through
it. Two copies of one operation growing apart is this codebase's own recurring
defect (create/renew, #423), and adding a second renewal site without a shared
unit would have been the next instalment.

A control test caught a regression this change introduced on the way: the
reconciliation reads the certificate directories after the sweep has done its
work, and reading them unguarded would have thrown away a completed sweep on an
unreadable directory. The guard moved with the read.

fix: the shutdown handles that had no caller are called (#813)

* fix: the shutdown handles that had no caller are called

`IssuanceExecutor.shutdown()` had no caller anywhere in the tree, and the
slow-request watchdog's `stop_event` was handed to the container and never set.
Both read in review like a safety net — a reader finds a shutdown method and
stops asking what happens on SIGTERM — and neither ran.

What was wired was half of it: app.py's KeyboardInterrupt path stopped the
scheduler and drained the event bus, and only for `python app.py`. Under
gunicorn, which is how the image runs, an atexit hook drained the bus and
nothing else. A container stopped during an async issuance left the pool's
queued jobs recorded nowhere: the registry is in memory, it dies with the
process, and the certificate the operator asked for never appeared.

`stop_background_work(container)` is now one ordered shutdown, called from
atexit (both deployment shapes) and from app.py's Ctrl-C path. Producers stop
before consumers — the scheduler queues renewals, a renewal publishes, a
publish dispatches a deploy hook — so draining the bus first would drain a
queue still being filled. Nothing is joined: the scheduler is asked not to
wait, the pool cancels what no worker has started, the bus drains against a
deadline, and what could not be finished is named in the log instead.

Two consequences of calling shutdown for the first time, both handled here:
a submission after shutdown would have left a job at 'queued' forever, since
the pool raises and nothing would ever run it; and a scheduler that was never
started must report that rather than warn, or every clean exit carries a
warning and the real one stops being read.

name that temporary file, so nothing ever waited on that lock and nothing was
ever excluded. `safe_file_read`'s shared lock was the other half of a pair
whose first half was never on the same file.

That is worse than no lock: a reader of this function finds locking, is told it
is for safety, and stops asking how concurrent writes are handled — so the
answer in the source was one that had never been true.

The real guarantee is the rename, and it is a good one. The content is built
and fsynced in a private temporary file and then renamed over the target; POSIX
rename is atomic, so a concurrent reader gets the whole old file or the whole
new one, and a reader holding the old handle goes on reading a complete file
one version behind. What it does not give is protection against a lost update
across a separate read and write — which a lock inside this function could not
have given either, and which is why settings mutation goes through
`SettingsManager.update` and its lock spanning both halves.

Both docstrings now say that, including what the removed lock did not do.

Verified by breaking it: with the rename replaced by an in-place write, three
of the eight new tests fail — the partial-read sweep, the held-handle case, and
the fsync-before-rename ordering.

feat: the issuance queue has a bottom, and a 429 when it is reached (#815)

`IssuanceExecutor.submit` accepted everything. The pool has two workers by
default, each running a certbot subprocess that takes tens of seconds to
minutes, and the queue behind them had no limit — so a client in a retry loop,
or a script walking a domain list, could park hundreds of jobs there. Every one
of those callers got 202 Accepted and a job id for a certificate that would not
be attempted for hours.

The registry's own bound does not cover this. `_evict_locked` drops the oldest
terminal jobs past the history cap and deliberately never evicts an unfinished
one, so a backlog of queued work is exactly the case that cap declines to
touch.

CERTMATE_ISSUANCE_QUEUE_LIMIT (default 20, clamped 1-500) bounds how much
unfinished issuance may exist at once, queued and running together. Past it
`submit` raises IssuanceQueueFull and the three async endpoints answer 429
ISSUANCE_QUEUE_FULL with the depth and the limit, instead of a job id that
means nothing. The check and the registration are under one lock, so two
requests arriving together cannot both take the last slot.

The depth is a gauge, with the limit beside it so they can be read against
each other, and the event bus's backlog goes with them — `pending_dispatches()`
had no caller anywhere, a number computed for nobody.

`_submit` sits at module level rather than in the resource closure because
mccabe counts a nested function against its enclosing one, and the complexity
budget added in #812 refused the change until it moved. Removing the now-dead
`_job_accepted` helper took that closure from 61 to 60, which the same gate
then asked to be recorded.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: a webhook that will never work is not retried three times (#816)

`_send_webhook_with_retry` left the loop on success and on nothing else. A
webhook pointing at a URL the receiver does not serve — a Slack app removed, a
path typo, a token revoked into a 401 — was sent three times with 1s + 2s of
sleep between the attempts, on every notification, for as long as it stayed
configured. Under a renewal sweep that is once per certificate, on the sweep's
own thread.

`_send_email_with_retry`, ten lines above it in the same file, already had the
shape: it leaves the loop when the failure is a static configuration problem,
because retrying cannot change one. The webhook path had the same idea started
and never finished — `config_error: True` was set by two return paths in
`_send_webhook` and read by nobody.

Two kinds of failure are now permanent. The receiver answered and said no with
a 4xx that describes the request rather than the moment (408, 425 and 429
excluded: those describe this attempt, and 5xx is what backoff is for), or
CertMate refused to send at all — no URL, a non-http scheme, an SSRF-guarded
target, a channel missing its token, a broken payload template, an unusable
method or timeout. Every one of those returns is now marked. DNS, connection
refused, TLS and timeouts still get the full backoff.

HTTPError is also caught separately from URLError, so a rejection carries its
status instead of arriving as prose in a free-text error field. The delivery
log records 404 rather than None, and one attempt rather than three — which is
the difference between reading it as a flaky receiver and reading it as a
webhook to fix.

perf: the audit tail stops at the entries it found, not at a block count (#817)

`get_recent_entries` walks the audit log backwards in 8 KiB blocks, which is
the right shape — the file rotates at megabytes and the caller wants the end of
it. The stop condition counted the wrong quantity:

    while remaining > 0 and len(blocks) <= limit:

One block per entry ASKED FOR, not per entry FOUND. An audit line is a
timestamp, a level and a JSON object, around 170 bytes, so a hundred entries
live in two blocks and the loop read a hundred and one. Measured on a 3.2 MiB
log of 20,000 entries:

    limit=10      90,112 bytes  ->   8,192
    limit=100    827,392 bytes  ->  24,576
    limit=500  3,377,780 bytes  ->  90,112   (the entire file, before)

The counter is the entry marker itself — the same string the parse splits on,
defined once so the two cannot drift — rather than newlines, so a traceback or
a non-INFO line in the tail cannot make the read stop short. `len(blocks) <=
limit` survives as a second condition, so a tail containing no entries at all
reads exactly what it read before instead of walking to the start of the file.

Writing the test for that found a second defect in the same function: the
result was sliced as `raw_lines[-limit:]`, which is `limit` LINES. Anything in
the tail that is not an entry came out of the caller's allowance — a log with
two noise lines per entry returned 33 rows for a request of 100, with nothing
to say why. It now parses first and takes the last `limit` entries.

fix: the certificate status nothing ever assigns is no longer exported (#820)

* fix: the certificate status nothing ever assigns is no longer exported

`certmate_certificates_by_status` was exported with five labels and the
collector assigned four. Every scrape, for every deployment, carried

    certmate_certificates_by_status{status="renewal_failed"} 0

An operator who finds that series writes an alert on it and gets one that can
never fire — which reads, for as long as nobody checks, as "no renewal has ever
failed here". A constant zero is worse than an absent series: an absent one
makes the rule visibly broken, or is caught by absent().

an oversight. It is not a state a certificate is IN: one whose renewal failed
is still valid, expiring_soon or expired. The other four partition the set and
this one overlaps all of them. The failure is an EVENT, and it is already
counted as one by certmate_certificate_renewals_total{status="failure"}, which
_record_renewal_metrics increments from the renewal sweep and which the shipped
CertMateRenewalsFailing rule alerts on with increase(...) over 6h.

series nothing could emit, and from the monitoring README's list of things that
are "not populated yet" — it is not going to be.

fix: a domain entry has one shape, and normalising it invents nothing (#824)

settings['domains'] accepted a bare string or an object, both spellings were
live, and nine modules decoded that union independently. Three defects came out
of it and only the first is a tidiness problem.

The union never ended. The load-time migration converted only when EVERY entry
was a string, so the moment one object entry existed the list was frozen mixed
-- which is the state of any instance that added a domain after the object
format arrived. And save_settings wrote a validated string entry straight back
as a string, so even a fully converted list could be un-converted by the next
save. Normalisation was not a fixed point.

The normaliser that did run was not lossless. migrate_domains_format filled in
dns_provider and account_id from the global defaults, and two of its callers
invoke it inside a settings mutator -- set_auto_renew and the sweep's
re-registration -- so those invented values were persisted. An entry naming no
provider means "follow the global setting"; an entry naming one is pinned to
it. So an unrelated write silently converted the first into the second, and
from then on changing the global DNS provider had no effect on any existing
domain. Measured on a mixed list before the fix, after one unrelated write and
setting the global provider to route53, both domains still resolved to
cloudflare. Nothing ever read the injected fields: the provider comes from
get_domain_dns_provider, the account from the certificate's own metadata.

The flag one spelling cannot carry. A string entry has nowhere to put
auto_renew, so it reads as True -- which stays correct after normalisation only
because {'domain': x} is read as True as well. That equivalence is what makes
the conversion safe, and it is now pinned by test rather than assumed.

modules/core/domain_entries.py is the one home for what an entry is: one
decoder (entry_domain, entry_auto_renew, iter_domains) and one lossless
normaliser that turns a string into {'domain': ...} and invents nothing else.
It is applied at both boundaries -- load_settings normalises per entry rather
than only all-string lists, and save_settings emits the same shape it reads --
so normalisation is a fixed point and the object form can eventually be the
only one. The nine decode sites now ask it, and a test fails if a tenth is
written.

Verified by reverting the production change with the tests in place: 9 of the
30 fail against the old code, including the provider-pinning regression.

fix: the advisories gate asked for the wrong permission, and asking narrowed the token (#831)

The weekly advisories job has failed on 2026-08-31, 2026-09-07 and 2026-09-14,
every time with the same 403 from the Dependabot alerts API, so the gate added
in #601 to catch exactly this kind of drift has never once read an advisory.

The cause is in the block that was meant to document the permission:

    permissions:
      # Listing Dependabot alerts needs this explicitly; the workflow-level
      # read-all already grants it, but a job that reads security data should
      # say so where someone reviewing the job can see it.
      security-events: read
      contents: read

A job-level permissions block replaces the workflow-level read-all, it does
not add to it. Measured in the run logs rather than reasoned about: the
ca-endpoints job, which declares nothing and so inherits read-all, gets

    Actions: read ... SecurityEvents: read, Statuses: read,
    VulnerabilityAlerts: read

and the advisories job, which declares its own block, gets

    Contents: read, Metadata: read, SecurityEvents: read

VulnerabilityAlerts is the permission the endpoint checks, and writing down
the wrong guess is what removed it. `vulnerability-alerts` is the documented
key for "Read Dependabot alerts"; `security-events` is a different permission
and does not open that endpoint. The script's own 403 message named the wrong
one too, and now says which is which.

What the gate could not tell us while it was blind, run locally against the
same API: three hono advisories published 2026-09-08, none of them documented.
All three are fixed in 4.13.5 and the lock carried 4.13.1:

  GHSA-crvj-82cr-hjcx  query parser reads parameters after the URL fragment
  GHSA-g6gw-c38x-mqfc  unbounded dot-notation nesting in parseBody()
  GHSA-gqvv-2mrq-wpjv  toSSG() still writes outside the output directory

hono is a transitive dependency of @modelcontextprotocol/sdk under mcp/, which
the Dockerfile does not copy, so none of this is in the shipped image. It is
still cheaper to fix than to write down: the lock now resolves hono 4.13.8 and
npm audit reports 0 vulnerabilities. SECURITY.md needs no new entry, because
nothing is being carried.

tests/test_advisory_checker_is_wired.py asserted `security-events: read`. It
was written to protect this gate and instead pinned the defect in place,
staying green over three blind weeks. It now asserts the permission the
endpoint needs, tolerates a job with no block at all (read-all does grant it),
and says in its docstring that the only real proof is a workflow_dispatch run.
Checked by putting the old permission back: the test fails.

fix: a certificate's key state and expiry were both answered by the wrong thing (#829, #830) (#834)

Two defects from #786, reported three times over six months by an operator
running a private CA. Both were invisible to the suite because both were wrong
only on the path a running instance takes.

#830: private_key_state was 'unknown' on every default installation

create_container always builds a StorageManager, StorageManager defaults to
local_filesystem, and get_certificate_info takes the storage branch whenever
one exists. So the filesystem branch below it, the only branch that inspects
the private key, is unreachable outside unit tests. On the storage branch the
key state was read off the shape of a dict, and the base
retrieve_certificate_info fetched the whole bundle and then dropped everything
but cert.pem. The key was read off the disk and thrown away.

Every certificate therefore reported private_key_state 'unknown',
private_key_present null and usable null, and since needs_renewal only forces
attention on 'missing' or 'mismatched', a certificate with no private key at
all reported needs_renewal false. That is the sentence #608 was closed for, on
the path #608's fix never ran.

The base implementation now carries privkey.pem through when the retrieve
produced one: it had already paid for it. Dropping it never saved a fetch
there; the backends where it does save one override the method. The caller
compares the key to the certificate rather than believing a dict key, so
cert.pem from one issuance beside privkey.pem from another is caught, and asks
the backend whether its answer covers key material at all, so a backend with a
genuinely cheap info-only path keeps saying 'unknown' instead of being read as
'missing'. That question is answered `is True`, not truthily, so a backend
that does not implement it and a test double that answers every attribute both
land on the safe side.

#829: a certificate with hours left reported that it had expired

days_left is (expiry - now).days and timedelta.days truncates, so anything
under 24 hours comes out 0. Six places in dashboard.js, one in cmd-palette.js
and one in base.html read `<= 0` as expired, so a valid certificate got a red
Expired badge, the Expired tile, the expired filter and the label "0 days ago".
24 hours is step-ca's default lifetime, so that was every certificate on a
default private CA.

days_left keeps its meaning, whole days, because clients read it. The two
questions it cannot answer at once get their own fields: `expired` and
`seconds_left`, both None on the branch where the certificate could not be
parsed, because unknown is not the same as fine. Every renderer now asks the
API instead of deriving it, sorting uses seconds so a 23-hour certificate and
one that lapsed an hour ago are not both 0, and "0 days left" is now "less
than a day left".

API contract 2.1 -> 2.2. MINOR: nothing changed type or disappeared. The rule
for choosing that number moved to sit immediately above the constant, because
each version added had been pushing it further away until the test that checks
the rule is written down stopped finding it.

Verified against a real certificate, not a fixture. tests/test_cert_lifecycle
issues from Let's Encrypt staging over Cloudflare DNS-01 into a container, and
now also reads the certificate back through the API. On this branch it passes;
with the same test against the code before it:

  AssertionError: the instance just issued this certificate and holds its key,
  yet reports 'unknown'

Unit coverage goes through a real StorageManager with the real local backend,
the way the application does, because a CertificateManager built with
storage_manager=None cannot fail on #830 and that is exactly how it survived
five releases. Nine tests for #829 use certificates whose remaining life is not
a whole number of days, which no existing test did.

Suite: 4909 passed, 0 failed. Real-certificate E2E: 10 passed.

ci: an exception budget, instead of a number that only grows (#839)

#671 counted 397 broad `except Exception` handlers, 7 silent `pass` bodies and
1 bare `except:`. Measured again today with the AST rather than grep:

  broad handlers   397 -> 425
  silent pass        7 -> 0   (among broad handlers)
  bare except        1 -> 0

Two of the three were fixed and the third grew by 28 while the issue stayed
open, because nothing measured it between one reading and the next. A number
written into an issue is read once; a number in CI is read on every push.

So the two that reached zero become rules, and the one that grows becomes a
ratchet, in the shape scripts/check_complexity_budget.py already established
here and for the same reason: one number for the whole tree is set by its worst
file, and everything under the worst is ungated.

`except Exception` is not a defect on its own. A supervisor loop, a health
probe, a best-effort cache write all genuinely want to survive anything. What
is a defect is the count climbing without anyone choosing it, and a handler
that discards the exception without recording it, which is why that one is
absolute rather than budgeted.

Five failure modes, each checked by producing it:

  bare except appears                     names the file and line
  a broad handler whose body is only pass names the file and line
  the total grows past the pin            "426 ... over the pinned 425"
  a budgeted file exceeds its entry       "private_ca.py: 12 ... budgeted 11"
  the total falls and the pin does not    "424 ... below the pinned 425.
                                           Lower TOTAL_LIMIT to 424"

The last one is the arm that matters most over time: it is how the complexity
pin at 559 outlived the closure it was set for by nine months, reading like an
enforced limit while enforcing nothing.

A sixth thing came out of testing it: a file that does not parse used to kill
the script with a bare traceback, which reads as "the budget script is broken"
rather than "that file does not parse". It now says which, and points at
flake8's E9.

The twelve budgeted files are not targets. They are what the tree measures
today, and the entries move down.

docs: a translation records the English it was made from, and says when that moved on (#840)

#674 calls the four extra locales "a standing correctness liability on
documentation that includes security guidance", because "stale translated
security docs are worse than none". That is not a worry about the future here.
24 of the 64 translated pages are behind, and two of those are not merely
incomplete:

  docs/mcp.md was fixed on 2026-08-10 by a commit titled "the documented
  job-polling loop could not run". All four translations were last touched on
  2026-06-24, so all four still describe the loop that does not run.

  the docs/api.md translations predate the change that unified the error
  envelope and made `code` a string everywhere: a breaking change, contract
  2.0 to 2.1. Four translations describe a contract that stopped being true.

A reader has no way to tell, which is what makes those worse than a missing
page.

Translating the backlog is not the answer and would be the wrong hands: a
breaking API contract change machine-translated into three languages nobody
here can review is how you ship a confident error. Dropping the locales is the
decision #674 is about, and it is not mine. So each of the 24 now opens, under
its own title and in its own language, with a line saying it is behind, which
document governs, and a link to it.

Every one of the 64 records which English it was translated from:

    <!-- CERTMATE-TRANSLATED-FROM 13de52d0ee4b09b1 -->

and scripts/check_translation_freshness.py compares that against the English
page today. It does NOT require current translations, which no gate can
produce. It requires that improving the English either brings the translation
with it or leaves it marked, and that choice is always available, so this can
never be the reason not to improve the English.

The first version compared commit dates and defeated itself in the commit that
introduced it: marking a page as stale is an edit, an edit makes it the more
recently committed of the pair, and all 24 pages it had just marked came out
looking fresher than their sources, failing the opposite arm. Caught by running
it, not by reading it. The recorded hash is of the ENGLISH text, so nothing
done to a translation can move it, and it needs no git history, so the job
needs no full clone. That property is now a test of its own.

Four failure modes, each checked by producing it: behind without the notice,
the notice while in step, the English changing under a page, and a page with
no recorded source at all.

Two things the work turned up. The checker found docs/*/probes.md with no
docs/probes.md, because the English page is probes.en.md, the only one in the
tree with that suffix; tests/test_docs_navigation.py already decided how to
pair it, so the mapping is mirrored from there rather than invented again, and
a test fails if the two disagree. And the required-checks registry caught the
new job as unclassified, which is what it is for: registered advisory, because
blocking a code fix on a German markdown file would make the gate the reason
not to improve the English.

feat: the client CA subject is yours, and it can be rebuilt (#578) (#841)

From #562 (@mbw2001). The private CA that signs client certificates was
generated once with five hardcoded attributes, so every CertMate install on
earth signed its staff's certificates with

    C=CH, ST=Switzerland, O=CertMate, OU=Certificate Authority, CN=CertMate CA

and there was no way to rebuild it from the UI or the API.
PrivateCAGenerator.initialize(force=True) could already back up and regenerate;
nothing ever called it with force.

The subject is now configurable, from `client_ca_subject` in settings. A field
left empty is omitted rather than written as an empty attribute, because not
every organisation has a state; common_name falls back to the old value. An
install that configures nothing gets exactly the subject it has always had,
attribute for attribute, and a test asserts that rather than assuming it.

`country` is validated as an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code before anything touches
the disk. cryptography refuses a longer one at signing time, with a message
about attribute lengths that an operator cannot act on, and by then there is
half a CA on disk.

The property the whole feature rests on: the subject is read WHEN THE CA IS
CREATED AND NEVER AGAIN. initialize() already returns early when both files
exist, so an edit in Settings cannot silently replace the CA and stop every
certificate it ever signed from verifying. There is a test for that, because
it is the one thing that must not regress.

Changing it afterwards is POST /api/client-certs/ca/reset (admin), which does
the two halves together: regenerates the CA, backing up the old one, and
removes the client certificates it signed, because nothing can verify them any
more. Doing either half alone leaves a lie behind. It republishes the CRL,
which was signed by the old key and is unverifiable the moment that key
changes, and writes an audit record. It does not touch server certificates,
settings or DNS accounts, which is what the tests spend most of their time on.

`confirm` is a typed phrase, not a boolean: `{"confirm": true}` is what a
mis-sent form or a retried request produces, and neither of those means
"discard every certificate we have issued". A bad subject is refused before
anything is backed up, moved or deleted, and a test checks the certificates
are still there afterwards.

Three things the repository's own gates caught while this was being written,
all of them fixed rather than waved through:

* _save_ca_metadata wrote `"issuer": {"country": "CH", "organization":
  "CertMate"}` as literals. True only while the subject was, and it would have
  started lying on the first configured CA. Read off the certificate now.
* The complexity budget refused the new resource: defining one more class
  inside create_client_certificate_resources took that closure from 89 to 98,
  and its entry is a ceiling that only comes down. The resource is built by a
  module-level factory taking its dependencies as arguments, so the closure is
  back at 89 and this is the shape the rest of them should take.
* The exception budget refused three new broad handlers. One wrapped
  CRLManager.update_crl(), which already catches internally and returns None,
  so it could never fire: removed. The other two log and mirror a pattern
  already in the same files, so the pin moves from 425 to 427 with the reason
  written into scripts/check_exception_budget.py, which is what raising it is
  supposed to cost.

Also: the first version of the audit call used `log_event`, an interface this
collaborator does not have. The test I had written asserted it, so the test
agreed with the invention. Both now use `log_operation`, which is what
_audit_scheduled_renew has always called.

Not included: the UI. This is the API and the core, and the issue asks for both
a UI and an API path; a destructive button deserves its own change.

fix: a refusal answers like a refusal, not like an empty result (#842)

`GET /api/certificates` without a credential answered 401 with this body:

    {"domain": null, "exists": null, "expiry_date": null, "days_left": null, ...}

Every field of a certificate, all null, and no `error` or `code`. docs/api.md
states the contract plainly: "Every failure carries a human-readable `error`
and a machine-readable `code`." Four endpoints did not. A client reading the
body rather than the status could not tell "you are not allowed to look" from
"there is nothing there" — the same confusion between unknown and fine that
#829 and #830 were about, in the response envelope this time.

The cause is decorator order, not a missing branch. flask-restx's
`marshal_with` reshapes whatever the view returns, and `require_role` rejects
by returning `({'error': ..., 'code': ...}, 401)`. With the marshaller outside,
that rejection is marshalled into the success model: undeclared keys are
dropped, so `error` and `code` disappear, and every declared key becomes null.
With `require_role` outside, the rejection never reaches the marshaller.

Seven resources combine the two decorators. Four had the wrong order:
CertificateList, BackupList, CacheStats, CacheClear. Measured both ways, by
reading the decorator blocks and by making the requests: 5 refusals lacked the
envelope before, 1 after, and the one left is `/api/auth/me`, which answers
`{"user": null}` with 401 as its own documented contract for a UI deciding
whether to render a login form.

The codebase had already met this without naming it: models.py declares `error`
and `code` on the deployment-status model with a comment saying `marshal_with`
would otherwise strip `code` from a 403. That patched one model. The new test
asks every parameterless credentialed GET for its refusal and requires both
fields, so the next resource to gain a marshaller cannot reintroduce it. It
fails on the code before this commit, naming the three offenders it can reach.

No contract bump. These four were violating the published error format, not
defining one; bringing them into conformance is a fix, and the status codes are
unchanged.

Two things found by the same measurement:

- `modules/web/backup_cache_routes.py` bound `/api/cache/stats` and
  `/api/cache/clear` in addition to the flask-restx resources on the same
  paths. The restx ones win (verified by asking the url map which endpoint each
  path resolves to), so the web bindings were dead — the same shadowing
  cert_routes.py documents for `/api/certificates/create`. Not harmless while
  it lasted: the restx CacheClear writes an audit entry and this one does not,
  so a change in registration order would have silently stopped auditing cache
  clears. The dashboard calls `/api/web/...` only. Removed, and
  tests/test_backup_cache_web_routes.py no longer asserts the behaviour of
  code no request reached.

- docs/api.md said the contract version "is **2.1**" in the error-handling
  section while another section already described 2.2. Corrected to name both
  steps. I wrote a test to pin this and removed it: the document was
  inconsistent with itself rather than simply behind, so catching it needs the
  wording pinned, and a gate that makes the reference harder to reword costs
  more than the drift it prevents.

fix: a handler that records nothing turns a failure into an answer (#671) (#843)

#671 is 425 broad handlers. Most are the right call: a supervisor loop, a
best-effort cache write, a probe that must survive anything. The tractable part
is narrower and measurable — a handler that discards the exception AND says
nothing about it, so no reader and no caller can tell a path that worked from
one that failed and decided not to mention it.

Measured with the AST: 46 broad handlers record nothing at all, and 38 of those
carry no comment saying why silence is right. Two of them had turned a failure
into a confident answer, and both are fixed here.

**The storage health check answered "ok" when it could not look.**
`check_storage` exists to answer one question: are the certificates really in
Azure/Vault/S3, or did the backend fail to initialise and CertMate quietly fall
back to local disk. When `get_fallback_backend()` raised, the handler set the
result to None and fell through to the healthy return, logging nothing. So an
instance that could not look reported the same thing as one that had looked and
found everything in order.

The severity is NOT changed, and that part I had wrong first. An existing
control says an exception here must not become a degraded status, because
inventing one out of a question that could not be asked would page someone for
nothing. That reasoning is right and stands. What was wrong is the word: `Check`
keeps `state` and `severity` apart precisely so a check can be honest in the
detail without moving the aggregate, so the state is now 'unknown', the failure
is logged, and nothing new pages.

**The bearer-token file reader decided in silence.** `_operator_supplied_token`
returned '' when API_BEARER_TOKEN_FILE could not be read. Declining to
reconcile is correct — an unreadable file supplied nothing, and the function
never clears a stored token, so it cannot open an instance. Doing it silently
is not: an operator who rotated the token in that file then gets 401 on every
request with nothing anywhere saying the file could not be opened, which is the
symptom #401 exists to have fixed, reintroduced through a different door. The
security question is asked elsewhere and already fails closed (`setup_mode_for`
raises; see tests/test_bearer_token_file_failures_fail_closed.py).

**A third ratchet on the budget.** scripts/check_exception_budget.py already
holds two rules at zero (no bare except, no `pass`-only body) and pins the

docs: one file per release, and an index nothing has to keep up to date (#674) (#847)

RELEASE_NOTES.md was 4,780 lines across 94 releases. The size was the symptom.
The problem is that one file held two different kinds of document: an
append-only archive of statements that were true once, and a page the gates
read as a description of the product now. A note saying v2.4.12 pinned
cryptography 42 is correct forever and describes nothing about today.

So every gate that walks the documentation had to carve out an exception for
that one filename. Five did, as a copied
`_SKIP_FILES = ("RELEASE_NOTES.md", "CHANGELOG.md")` tuple — and CHANGELOG.md
has never existed in this repository. Five copies of a rule, one of them
fiction, is how a rule stops being read.

Each release now owns docs/releases/vX.Y.Z.md. The split was mechanical and
checked: re-joining the 94 sections reproduces the original file byte for byte
before anything else was touched.

RELEASE_NOTES.md is now 381 lines and is GENERATED from that directory by
scripts/build_release_index.py. Generated rather than maintained because the
failure mode of a hand-kept index is silent: a release missing from the list
looks exactly like a release that was never cut. It is checked the way a
lockfile is checked, with `--check`, in the suite and in release.sh.

Two things the index keeps on purpose. Every `## vX.Y.Z (title)` heading
survives, so any link to a section anchor still resolves; this is a public
repository and those anchors are not ours to break. And the title is read from
the release file rather than retyped, so the index cannot describe a release
differently from the release.

The procedural half:

* scripts/release.sh reads docs/releases/v$version.md directly. It used to awk
  a section out of the big file, stopping at the next `---` rule, so a stray
  horizontal rule inside a section would have silently truncated the GitHub
  release body. A file has ends of its own. `prepare` also fails if the
  generated index is stale, so a release cannot ship omitted from its own list.
* The emoji workflow scans the directory as well as the index, and points the
  annotation at the file someone actually edits. It fails if the directory is
  empty rather than passing on nothing to read.
* tests/test_version_consistency.py checks that the current version has a file,
  instead of a heading in a 4,780-line one.
* tests/test_release_notes_are_modular.py holds the structure: index in sync,
  every file named after the release its heading declares, the current version
  present, the release script actually reading the directory. Both arms
  falsified by producing them.

And the exception shrinks instead of growing. tests/historical_documents.py is
one definition of "this records the past rather than describing the present",
covering the directory as well as the index, and the five gates use it. A
per-file exclusion list would otherwise have had to grow with every release.

Three walks in tests/test_frontend_state_regressions.py had no exclusion at all
and only passed because the archive was one file they happened to skip by name.
They fail honestly against the split, and are filtered now: a release note
naming `/api/settings/dns-providers/` is naming it to say it was wrong.

probe: a served certificate is checked for revocation, and only a verified answer counts (#857)

* probe: a served certificate is checked for revocation, and only a verified answer counts

The deep TLS probe describes a certificate: who issued it, when it expires,
what key it carries. None of that says whether the issuer has since revoked
it, and a revoked certificate that is still being served looks healthy on
every other axis. CertMate's own ocsp_crl.py is the responder for its private
CA; nothing in the product asked an issuer about a certificate it observed.

A discovery sweep now asks, OCSP first and the CRL as fallback, and the answer
is stored with the inventory record. The CRL is not a corner case: Let's
Encrypt turned OCSP off in 2025, and Google's WR2 certificates are CRL-only
too, so for most of what a sweep sees the CRL is the only source.

An answer counts only if it is verified, because a revocation answer nobody
checked is worse than none:

- OCSP: status successful, the CertID names this serial under this issuer's
  key, signed by the issuer or by a delegate the issuer signed that carries
  id-kp-OCSPSigning, thisUpdate not in the future, nextUpdate not passed.
- CRL: issued by this issuer, signature verifies against its key, not past
  nextUpdate.

Anything short of that is `unavailable` with the reason, never `good`.
`revoked` is final in the inventory: a CA cannot un-revoke, so a later sweep
where the responder is down does not overwrite it.

The issuer comes from the served chain where the interpreter exposes it
(Python 3.13+) and otherwise from the certificate's AIA caIssuers URL; the
image is 3.12, so in practice that is the AIA path, and the issuer must have
actually signed the leaf either way.

Every URL fetched comes from a certificate someone else wrote, so each goes
through the probe's SSRF guard with the connection pinned to the validated
address; only http is fetched (the payloads are signed), redirects are not
followed, bodies are capped. Issuer certificates and CRLs are cached, so a
hundred hosts behind one CA cost one CRL download.

Measured, not assumed:

- Against the internet, through the real API, sweep, probe and inventory:
  revoked.badssl.com comes back revoked (CRL, key_compromise, a real Let's
  Encrypt certificate); letsencrypt.org good via CRL; www.digicert.com,
  github.com (Sectigo) and www.actalis.it good via signed OCSP;
  self-signed.badssl.com not_applicable. Five hosts in two seconds.
- The tests use a real CA and a real HTTP server, no mocks of the
  cryptography. Each verification step was removed in turn and a test failed
  each time. The first pass of that exercise found a hole in the tests
  themselves: with OCSP signature verification deleted, all 25 tests still
  passed, because the only forged response was rejected earlier at the
  responder lookup. There is now a test with a correctly addressed response
  whose signature is broken, and one that replays a genuine `good` issued for
  a sibling certificate.
- The inventory page was looked at in a browser: the Revoked card, the row
  badge with date and reason on hover, and a grey "Revocation not checked"
  that gives its reason rather than looking fine.

caa: a record that refuses the chosen CA is said before the order and explained after it fails (#858)

* caa: a record that refuses the chosen CA is said before the order and explained after it fails

A CAA record (RFC 8659) names the CAs allowed to issue for a domain, and a CA
must refuse when it is not named. When the record names a different CA than
the one CertMate is about to use, the operator learned it from an ACME error,
and for a renewal that is weeks after anyone last looked.

It now surfaces in two places, and gates neither:

- warn: the create form asks POST /api/certificates/check-caa as the domain,
  SANs, CA and challenge type change, and shows an amber box only when a
  record would make the chosen CA refuse, with the record to add in a copyable
  block. An allowed answer, or a lookup that merely failed, shows nothing.
- explain: when certbot fails a create or a renewal and a CAA record refuses
  the CA, the error says which record, what it allows, and what to add. It is
  looked up only after the failure, so a working issuance never pays for it.

It never blocks because CertMate's resolver is not the CA's: split-horizon
DNS, a record changed a minute ago. Refusing an issuance the CA would have
accepted is a worse failure than a warning that turns out wrong. The create
endpoint does not consult it.

The logic follows RFC 8659: climb from each name towards the TLD and use the
first record set found; wildcards use issuewild when the set has any; an
unknown tag with the critical flag refuses; an empty issuer refuses every CA.
RFC 8657 validationmethods is honoured, since a record can allow a CA for
dns-01 only. accounturi is reported, not enforced. The issuer names per CA
come from the CCADB CAA identifiers report; ZeroSSL issues under Sectigo and
answers to Sectigo's names; a private CA is not_applicable.

Measured:

- Against real DNS: letsencrypt for google.com and maps.google.com is refused
  (google.com allows only pki.goog, reached by climbing); google is allowed;
  github.com allows letsencrypt and sectigo (so ZeroSSL) but not actalis;
  *.letsencrypt.org is judged by issuewild; certmate.org has no policy.
- In a browser, on a real instance with a logged-in admin: typing
  maps.google.com into the form brings up the warning with the record to add;
  switching the CA to Google Trust Services clears it.
- Every rule was removed in turn and a test failed each time: stopping at the
  first record set, issuewild, validationmethods, the critical flag, the issuer
  match, no-policy, the scope gate, the name cap, and the wiring into create
  and into renew.

The endpoint gates each name through the caller's scope, as the DNS-alias
check does since audit M5, so a scoped key learns nothing about names outside
it; out-of-scope SANs are refused before a single lookup. Errors carry codes.
conftest.py keeps the whole suite off the real DNS for CAA: dozens of tests
fail certbot on purpose with a MagicMock executor, and each would otherwise
have resolved example.com and its parents.

Three things decided, not assumed:

- dnspython still arrives transitively, through the DNS plugins. Pinning it
  directly is right and was tried: regenerating the locks for that line also
  re-resolved a dozen unrelated packages, filelock 3 -> 4 among them, which

inventory: when each domain's registration expires, from RDAP, WHOIS where there is no RDAP, and never a guess (#861)

A certificate that renews on time is worth nothing on a domain whose
registration lapsed: the name stops resolving, and every certificate under it
goes with it. The inventory now tracks the second date too. For an agency it is
the same kind of risk as the first.

Each registrable domain CertMate knows about is asked once, however many hosts
sit under it. The sources are:
- managed domains and their SANs, read from each certificate's metadata;
- optionally what discovery found;
- any extra domains the operator lists.

Names are reduced with the Public Suffix List bundled in tldextract, read
offline, with no list downloaded and nothing written to disk.

Where the answer comes from:

1. RDAP, at the server the IANA bootstrap lists for the TLD. The expiry is the
   `expiration` event; the registrar is the entity with the registrar role.
2. WHOIS, only for a TLD with no RDAP, at the server IANA names for it. That is
   not a corner case. The bootstrap lists no RDAP for .it, .eu, .de, .es, .ch,
   .at, .io and .co, so RDAP alone would have covered none of an Italian
   agency's own domains.

Nothing is guessed. DENIC (.de) and EURid (.eu) do not publish an expiry date
over either protocol; they only say the domain is registered. That is reported
as `not_published`, and the dashboard says "Not published by the registry"
instead of showing a number. A WHOIS expiry in a form not understood, or an
answer that names no domain (a rate-limit notice), is `unavailable`, not a
date. A lookup that fails keeps the expiry already known, because a registry
that timed out today has not changed the date it published yesterday.

Registries rate-limit, and some answer a burst with a temporary ban, so the
sweep is gentle:
- daily at 06:00, after discovery and the CT poll, and on Scan now;
- at most 100 lookups, one second apart;
- a domain is asked again daily within 60 days of expiry, weekly otherwise,
  and after 6 hours when the last lookup failed.

It is opt-in, like the rest of discovery.

Measured against the real registries:
- google.com, web.dev, bbc.co.uk and afnic.fr are answered over RDAP;
- nic.it over WHOIS;
- google.de and google.eu are not_published;
- a name that does not exist is not_registered, over both protocols.

Through the real API: six domains in nine seconds, five of them the deliberate
pause. The panel was checked in a browser. The parsers are tested against
those registries' real answers, with people's names and street addresses
replaced. Fourteen rules were removed in turn and a test failed each time,
the scope filter included. The first version of the scope test passed for the
wrong reason: an instance still in setup mode serves every request as admin
and ignores the scoped key. The test now sets an operator token first and
asserts setup mode is off.

Also in here:

- GET /api/inventory/domains (viewer, scope-filtered), and a

`certificate_expiring` has been offered in Settings -> Notifications, named in

channel can filter on. Nothing ever published it, and nothing could have
rendered it if it had: `_EVENT_TITLES` had no entry, so
`build_notification_message` returned None and the notifier was never reached.
An operator who ticked that box got silence. The weekly digest was the only
warning, so a certificate that failed to renew on a Monday was first mentioned
the following Sunday.

Now there is a daily job at 07:00 — after the renewal sweep at 02:00 and the
registration check at 06:00, so what it announces is what is still true this
morning — that publishes two events on the same bus every other alert uses:

* `certificate_expiring` at 14, 7, 3 and 1 days, and on the day it lapses. The
  first mark is deliberately well inside the renewal window: with auto-renew on,
  a certificate still unrenewed at 14 days has failed roughly a dozen nightly
  attempts, so this cannot fire in ordinary operation. With auto-renew off the
  first warning is at the renewal threshold, because nothing else is going to
  act.

  registration is renewed by a registrar on its own schedule, so the notice
  starts far earlier. A registry that publishes no expiry (.de, .eu) is not a
  warning: an answer is not a date.

database (schema v3 -> v4). A renewed certificate has a new expiry and starts
again from the first mark; a repeated run says nothing; an operator who never
fixes it is told at each mark rather than every morning. The mark announced is

auth: setup mode only bootstraps, and credentials left over from it are reviewed (#862)

* auth: setup mode only bootstraps, and credentials left over from it are reviewed

Until the first operator credential exists — a local admin with local login on,
API_BEARER_TOKEN, or OIDC — CertMate serves every request as admin to anyone who
can reach it. That is deliberate, it is how the instance is bootstrapped, and
the README warns about exposing an instance in that state.

What did not follow from it: credentials created in that window outlive it. An
API key minted while the instance was in setup mode stays valid after the
operator completes setup, and so does a second admin user. The operator, who
sees anonymous requests answered with 401 from then on, has no reason to look.

So setup mode now only bootstraps:

* POST /api/keys is refused with 409 SETUP_BOOTSTRAP_ONLY while setup is
  incomplete. Keys are created afterwards, by someone who signed in.
* POST /api/users creates the first admin and refuses any further user with the
  same 409. The setup page already reads 409 on that step as "an admin exists,
  go on and enable login", so a half-finished setup still completes — there is a
  test for exactly that.
* Both refusals are audited: an attempt to create credentials in the setup
  window is worth a record.

Keys that earlier versions allowed in that window are recognisable, because they
carry created_by = setup_user. They are not revoked automatically: an operator
who created one themselves would lose it with no warning. Instead:

* GET /api/keys reports created_during_setup and needs_review;
* the key listing shows a red "created during setup: review" badge, with Confirm
  beside Revoke;
* PATCH /api/keys/<id> {"confirmed": true} records who vouched for it and when,
  and clears the flag. It is refused in setup mode, because the same anonymous
  admin who could mint the key could otherwise vouch for it;
* startup logs, once, how many keys are waiting for review.

Not on /health. That endpoint is unauthenticated, and telling the internet how
many unreviewed keys an instance has is telling whoever planted one that it is
still there.

api: a host can be asked what it is serving, and the answer carries the revocation (#869)

* api: a host can be asked what it is serving, and the answer carries the revocation

CertMate could probe what its discovery configuration named, and could compare
a managed domain against what is actually deployed. It could not answer "read
the certificate at this host" about a host nobody had configured. So every tool
that wanted that answer implemented TLS again, and at least one of them —
nis2-public, in this ecosystem — reported an OCSP status it had assumed from
the presence of a responder URL rather than checked.

POST /api/probe is that answer: the same deep probe the inventory sweep uses,
pointed at a host named in the request, with the verified revocation from
#857. The response is the probe's own shape, so nothing new has to be learned
by a caller that already reads the inventory.

What it refuses, and why each one is there:

* a scoped key may only probe hosts its allowed_domains cover, the boundary
  the inventory and the DNS-alias check already enforce. `server_name` is
  checked too: it is the name the probe asks the host for, so leaving it out
  of the boundary would leave a scoped key a way to name someone else's host.
* a private, loopback or otherwise non-global address is refused by the
  probe's SSRF guard, which answers `blocked` rather than raising.
* `port` must be an integer in range, `host` must be a non-empty string,
  `check_revocation` must be a JSON boolean (#863's rule, through the same
  helper).

It is rate-limited as its own category at 30/minute: each call opens a TLS
connection to a third party and, with revocation on, fetches that CA's OCSP or
CRL. Cheap for CertMate, not free for them.

Verified: 19 tests, including three against real hosts — letsencrypt.org comes
back described and with a revocation answer, revoked.badssl.com comes back
revoked, and `check_revocation: false` returns None rather than a guess. Five
mutations, each caught: the scope check, the SNI half of it, the port
validation, the empty-host check, and the boolean coercion.

The checks that are about the name, not the certificate (#870)

* feat: the checks that are about the name, not the certificate

A certificate that renews on time and a registration that does not lapse
still leave an agency answering for a site that stopped receiving mail, or
one whose address landed on a blocklist. Those checks lived in a separate
tool; they belong next to the certificate and the registration, because they
are about the same thing — the name, and whether it still works.

Five checks, daily, over every name the inventory already tracks: SPF, DMARC
and MX on the registrable domain (DMARC falls back to the organisational
domain, so asking _dmarc.www.example.com alone would report "no DMARC" for a
domain that publishes one), the DNS blocklists, and the HSTS header each host
serves.

The blocklist is the one worth the care. The tool this came from recognised
Spamhaus's 127.255.255.x refusal codes, logged a warning, and then returned
"not listed" — reporting a domain clean on the strength of a query that was
never answered. Here a refusal is `unknown`, and `unknown` is never rendered
as a pass.

That alone is not enough, which only showed up by running it. On this machine
the system resolver answers NXDOMAIN for 2.0.0.127.zen.spamhaus.org — an
address Spamhaus keeps permanently listed — while 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, 9.9.9.9
and OpenDNS all answer 127.255.255.254 for the same name. So a refusal
reaches a client in two shapes, and one of them is indistinguishable from
"not listed". Each list is therefore asked about its own test point first, by
the convention that keeps 127.0.0.2 always listed and 127.0.0.1 never listed;
a list that cannot answer that is not asked about anything else and is named
in `unanswered`. Against certmate.org this turns a false "ok — not listed"
into "warning", naming Spamhaus as the list that said nothing.

framing, MIME sniffing and unsanctioned script, and does the response
volunteer which software, at which version, is answering.

Three checks now share one HEAD. A site should not be asked three times to
produce the same reply.

`security_headers`. A missing header is a warning; a *broken* one is a
finding, because it is worse. `X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM …` is ignored by
every modern browser, and a Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only with no
enforcing policy reports violations and blocks nothing — both answer "are we
covered?" with a yes. CSP `frame-ancestors` counts instead of
X-Frame-Options, not as well as it: demanding both would report a correctly
configured site as unprotected.

`disclosure`. Reported only when `Server` carries a version — `nginx/1.24.0`
tells an attacker which CVEs to try, `cloudflare` does not. The tool this came
from flagged any Server header at all, so it reported `Server: cloudflare` as
"Server Version Disclosed". `X-Powered-By` and friends exist only to disclose,
so any value is the finding. Never more than a warning.

Redirects are followed, which is the part that makes the rest true. Most
estates answer their apex with a 301 to www, and the protective headers live
on the page: reading them off the 301 would report "no CSP" for a site that
serves one. At most three hops, https only, only within the same registrable
domain — following one off the estate would be reading someone else's headers
and filing them under this domain — and the SSRF guard re-runs on each. HSTS
is still read from the first response, because that is what a browser records
from a 301.

Verified against certmate.org, where all three decisions show at once: the
apex 301s to www carrying HSTS, www serves CSP with frame-ancestors, and
`Server: cloudflare` is correctly not a disclosure.

feat: ask a host whether it still accepts TLS 1.0 or 1.1 (#872)

The last thing DomainMate did that CertMate could not. RFC 8996 deprecated
both in 2021 — MUST NOT be used — and a server that still accepts them is
rarely doing it on purpose: a load balancer nobody re-read, a vhost that never
picked up the profile the others got.

Nothing here could see it. Both existing probes set
`minimum_version = TLSv1_2`, so they report the version that was negotiated
and never the version the server would also have agreed to. This one offers
the old version and sees whether the host says yes.

The whole module is built around one trap. A probe for old TLS is easy to
write so that it can never find anything: modern OpenSSL builds refuse to
*offer* those versions — openssl.cnf raises MinProtocol, or the security level
excludes every cipher they can use — and then every handshake fails on this
machine, before a byte leaves it, and a probe reading "handshake failed" as
"the server said no" reports a clean estate having asked nothing. The same
defect as a blocklist that reads a refusal as "not listed".

So the runtime is asked first, in memory and against no server, whether it can
produce a ClientHello for that version at all. If it cannot, the answer is
`unknown`. "Refuses old TLS" is only reached when this process could
demonstrably make the offer and the host declined it, and an acceptance is
only recorded when the handshake completed *at the version offered* — a
mutation showed that without the second half, a context that failed to pin its
maximum would negotiate TLS 1.3 with a healthy host and report it as accepting
TLS 1.0.

Verified against servers that exist for it: badssl's TLS-1.0 and TLS-1.1
endpoints are both detected, github.com and certmate.org both refuse. Two of
the tests are marked `network` and do that for real, because a probe nobody
has seen succeed is not evidence of anything.

- API contract 2.10 -> 2.11; `weak_tls`, and `check_weak_tls` in the config
- off by default: the only check that opens connections a host did not invite,
  two handshakes per name, carrying no data

- 38 tests, module at 100%, 17 mutations run and 17 killed

docs: the webhook page shows what a receiver can do with the payload (#396) (#853)

#396 asked for agent-based deployment, so that CertMate would not hold
credentials for every host it deploys to. The answer given at the time was that
webhooks already invert it: CertMate fires an event, and something else, which
already holds the credentials, does the deploying.

@tuxpowered then built that answer and shared it — an n8n workflow that takes
the deploy-hook payload, fetches what it needs from OpenBao, and pushes the
certificate onward, plus a second listener so a host can ask for its own
certificate against a per-domain key. It is the clearest worked example anyone
has produced of the pattern, and docs/webhooks.md did not mention it, or n8n,
or the pattern at all: 120 lines about how to configure a webhook and nothing
about what makes one worth configuring.

The shape is documented rather than the tool, so it reads for whatever runner
someone already has, with his workflow linked as the concrete instance. And the
property that motivates it is stated outright, because it is the reason to
accept the extra hop: CertMate never holds a credential for a host it deploys
to. A certificate manager that can reach every server is worth attacking.

docs: something does reference pkcs7 now, so say which part and why it is fine (#874)

SECURITY.md's reachability argument for the held cryptography advisories said
the shipped stack "references ... `pkcs7` or `EnvelopedData`" nowhere. As of
the revocation check added in this release that is false: revocation.py calls
pkcs7.load_der_pkcs7_certificates and load_pem_pkcs7_certificates to read an
AIA caIssuers payload, which CAs publish as a certificates-only PKCS#7 bundle.

The conclusion does not change. GHSA-jwv3-5hgf-82ww is about decrypting
EnvelopedData — pkcs7_decrypt_der/_pem/_smime, PKCS7EnvelopeBuilder — and none
of those is called in modules/, app.py, or the pinned certbot/acme/josepy.

The fix is to name the functions instead of the module. "Nothing touches
pkcs7" is the kind of blanket claim a later change falsifies silently, and
this is the change that did it: the analysis stayed correct while its stated
reason stopped being true, which is worse than being wrong outright, because
anyone re-checking it finds the reference and loses confidence in the whole
section.

Four ways a check could still have answered "clean" (#878)

* fix: four ways a check could still have answered "clean"

The module was written so that a check which cannot answer says so. Four
paths through it still could not, each the same shape as the defect it exists
to prevent, one level further down. All four were found by the
certmate-website session reading the code in order to describe it.

1. SPF matched `all` as a bare word, and a dot is a word boundary, so
   `v=spf1 include:all.example.net` — a record with no all-mechanism at all —
   reported `ok` instead of `warning`. It is a mechanism now, matched as a
   whole token with its optional qualifier, so `a:mail.allied.net` no longer
   counts as one and a bare `all` is still read as `+all` per RFC 7208.

2. The blocklist self-test uses 127.0.0.2 and 127.0.0.1, which prove a list
   answers about IPv4 and say nothing about IPv6. AAAA addresses were being
   queried anyway, and most DNSBLs either do not list IPv6 or use a separate
   zone for it — so an empty answer was indistinguishable from "this list
   does not serve IPv6", and an IPv6-only domain came back "not listed on 4
   blocklists" having been asked nothing. This is precisely the false-clean
   the self-test was added to stop, one layer below the refusal codes. IPv6
   addresses are now named in `unanswered` and never queried; a domain with
   only IPv6 is `unknown`.

3. A negative-control lookup that failed still passed the list. The control
   exists to catch a list, or a resolver, that answers everything, and a query
   that never came back cannot rule that out.

4. `addresses()` returned None on an A-lookup failure without trying AAAA, so
   a name that would have answered on IPv6 reported "could not look". Only
   both families failing is that now.

Also folds in the closed #877: "Five checks, run daily" and "Three of the five
checks" had kept counting the old set after #871 and #872 added three more,
and the module docstring listed five of the seven it runs.

And the doc/code disagreements found with them: `weak_tls` unknown has three
causes and the text named one; a partial blocklist sweep downgrades to warning
rather than standing as-is; "asked again only once a day" is 20 hours; "at
most 100 registries" is 100 lookups; an example detail string had drifted from
the one the code produces; and five places still described the five-check set.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: an IPv6 address is a boundary, not a hole, so it does not raise a warning

The previous commit put IPv6 addresses in `unanswered`, which downgrades the
result to a warning. Most real domains are dual-stack, so nearly every healthy
domain would have sat at a permanent amber — and a warning that is always on
is one nobody reads, which is the same failure as a "clean" nobody can trust,
in a different colour. Raised by the certmate-website session while writing
the page that would have had to explain it.

The two cases are different and now report differently:

  unanswered   a list refused, or a lookup failed — a hole in coverage of
               something we should have been able to check.    -> warning
  not_covered  an IPv6 address, which these lists do not answer about at
               all.                                            -> no change

So a dual-stack domain whose IPv4 addresses are clean is `ok` and still says
what it skipped; a domain resolving only to IPv6 is `unknown`, with a detail
that says why rather than blaming the resolver; a list that really did refuse
still downgrades, IPv6 present or not.

One test asserted on the detail string's exact wording, which a control
mutation caught by dying when it should have survived. It asserts on the
substance now.

feat: name the resolver CertMate asks, because the advice said to and could not (#882)

Closes #881.

When no blocklist gives a usable answer the check says "point it at a resolver
of your own". There was no way to. The resolver was a bare
dns.resolver.Resolver() reading /etc/resolv.conf, in domain_health and in caa
alike, so the only lever was the host's or container's DNS — changing it for
every process on the machine, and not mentioned anywhere near the advice.

`dns_resolver.nameservers` in the discovery configuration, or
CERTMATE_DNS_RESOLVERS in the environment, which is where this problem lives:
a container whose resolver is the engine's stub, set by whoever wrote the
compose file. The stored setting wins over the environment — the other way
round, saving a resolver in the interface would appear to work and change
nothing.

One setting, both resolvers. "Which nameservers does this instance ask" is one
question, and a per-feature answer would age badly.

Addresses only: resolving a nameserver's hostname would need the resolver
being replaced, so it would either depend on the thing the operator is trying
to stop using or fail in a way that looks like the new one being broken.

A port may follow, which arrived from the test rather than from the design.
The obvious test — point at an unroutable address, assert the lookup fails —
does not fail here: the network this was written on transparently intercepts
every query to port 53, and `dig @192.0.2.53 example.com TXT` answers in 30ms.
The premise was false, not the code, but a test that cannot fail proves
nothing. So the proof is positive: a responder on a free port, answering with
a string nothing else would return, and the assertion that the answer came
from it — plus the negative half, that without the setting it is never
contacted. That needs a port, and a resolver on a non-standard port is a real
deployment anyway.

Contract 2.11 -> 2.12 for the new config field. The remedy text now names the
setting, in the detail string and both docs, with the system resolver as the
documented fallback.

fix: a hook written for "revoked" now runs, because it never did (#883)

docs/deploy-hooks.md offers "revoked" in on_events, documents
CERTMATE_EVENT=revoked for the hook to read, and says hooks run "after a
certificate is issued, renewed, or revoked". The configuration accepts it and
stores it. DeployManager.on_certificate_event mapped certificate_created and
certificate_renewed and returned early on everything else, so the hook was
saved, shown back to the operator, and never run.

That is the worse kind of gap. Not a missing feature someone can see is
missing — one the product offers, accepts and displays, where the only way to
find out is to revoke something and watch nothing happen.

certificate_revoked maps to "revoked" now, and the rest of the listener treats
it like the other two: a successful hook publishes certificate_deployed, a
failed or raising one publishes certificate_deploy_incomplete. Those were
wired for the two events they were written for.

Two things stay as they are, deliberately:

The default for a hook that names no events stays ['created', 'renewed'],
now DEFAULT_ON_EVENTS so it is one statement rather than a literal. The doc
said "all three" and the code has always said two; two is the conservative
reading, because no hook has ever run on a revocation — nothing fired one — so
putting it in the default would start running commands on an upgrade that

split-horizon name still has its public addresses checked.

`is_private` answers False for 100.64.0.0/10, so a check written with it would
have kept sending carrier-grade NAT addresses out. There is a test per family
for exactly that reason.

The hook guard blocks what the page says it blocks (#891)

`docs/deploy-hooks.md` has a Blocked shell patterns table. Nothing tied
it to `DeployManager._is_command_safe`, and one row did not hold.

The rule for the `.` source shorthand was `\b\.\s+/`. `\b` before a dot
needs a word character immediately before it, and a command either
starts with `. ` or has ` . ` after a space or a pipe — in all of those

exists and the rule never fired. What it did match was `x. /opt/s.sh`,

argument, so its shorthand is too; the asymmetry was the defect, not the
absolute path. The page's table says so in all five languages. Hooks
people actually write are unaffected, and six of them are pinned as
still passing — a blanket rule on the dot would have refused every path
with an extension in it.

`main()` had a check that could never fail:

    signer = audit_signing.AuditSigner(Path(args.key_dir))
    if not signer.available:
        print("FAIL: no audit signing key")
        return 2

`AuditSigner.__init__` mints and persists a key when it finds none —
right for the application's first run, wrong for a tool pointed at an
instance that already exists. Measured on an empty directory: available
True, and a `.audit_signing_key` now sitting in it.

So `--key-dir` pointing anywhere writable was accepted. Prune deleted
the archived prefix and signed the replacement anchor with a key the
instance had never used. `verify_chain` refuses that anchor, which is
the right answer arriving after the records are gone, and a stray
private key is left behind.

`AuditSigner(..., create=False)` for tools. A missing key is then a

answer "which instance is this", and this is the one operation where
getting it wrong destroys the evidence that would have shown it. The
fingerprint comes from `verify_bundle`, derived from the public key it
checked the signature against.

the first version read `manifest['fingerprint']`, and the field is

every bundle — refusing everything, while looking like it worked. A dead
guard replacing a dead guard. There is now a mutation for it.

bus dispatches handlers and some of them append audit entries; sealing
before that would sign a head about to move and leave the entries
written while shutting down outside the checkpoint this exists to
create. A test drives a bus whose stop() writes an entry and requires

moment looks exactly like one written at the right one.

not run on one — and an operator holding the key can still re-sign over

and a test keeps it saying so.

than worked around. The handler could have been narrowed — write_checkpoint
catches Exception itself, so only a manager without the method really
escapes — but the contract of that function is that nothing escapes it,
every other step in it is broad for the same reason, and an audit

The login redirect guard parses instead of guessing (#915)

safeNextUrl() decided whether `next` was same-origin by looking at its first

* A restore keeps the secrets it was told to keep

A share-safe backup masks secrets on the way out — that is what makes it
shareable — and the restore merges against what is on disk so the masked
values are left alone. That worked for a secret nested in dicts and not for
one nested in a list.

_strip_masked_values recurses into dicts and returns lists unchanged, so a
Kubernetes deploy target's token, which lives at

    {'a': {'t': [{'config': {'token': '********'}}]}} -> unchanged

protect, and returned True. The restore is the path an operator reaches when
something has already gone wrong, which is the worst place for a silent
write.

has solved exactly this since webhooks grew list-nested secrets. It runs over
the whole merged tree rather than per key, because deploy_hooks is not in
_DEEP_MERGE_SETTINGS_KEYS and so never reaches the per-key branch.

Verified through the shipped functions, not a restatement of them:
create_unified_backup writes '********' into the archive,
restore_unified_backup returns True, and the real token is still on disk
afterwards. Two controls: an archive carrying a REAL value still replaces
(or a full backup would be unrestorable), and the dict-nested secrets that
were never broken still survive.

* A renewal threshold that leaves the replacement room

renewal_threshold_days is written as 30 at creation and never reconsidered
against the certificate's own validity, while _inherited_days_valid makes
the replacement reuse that validity. A certificate at or below 30 days is
therefore born inside its own renewal window, and so is everything it
produces. Measured: a 10-day client certificate renewed on EVERY sweep —
seven runs, seven renewals, eight CA-signed private keys on disk, and nothing
prunes them.

The threshold is clamped to a third of the validity, so a replacement has two
thirds of its life before it is due again. The configured value still wins
when it already leaves room: a 365-day certificate keeps its 30 days
unchanged. Under three days the sweep refuses and logs which certificate and
why, because a third rounds to zero and no threshold could make a nightly
sweep manage a two-day certificate.

Not "stop renewing short certificates", which would have passed the
regression test and silently broken the feature — and broken it in the
direction #395 is heading, with six-day certificates. Measured after: a
10-day certificate is not renewed at four days left and is at three, and its
replacement is not due on the next sweep.

Why the existing guards missed it: every test in that file creates with the
default 365-day validity and moves expires_at by hand, so the replacement is
always a year out. The one that checks two runs says so in its own comment.

A boolean threshold was read as one day, because bool is an int subclass —
the sibling _inherited_days_valid has guarded that for the same reason since
it was written. Found by a control in the new tests, not by review.

Still open, and separate: nothing prunes superseded generations. With a sane
cadence the growth is one certificate per renewal period rather than one a
night, so it is housekeeping now and not an outage.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* The deployment probe knows where it is going

deployment_host is validated for shape when it is set — a bare hostname, no
scheme, no path, no whitespace — and for nothing else. The probe then opened
a socket to it, wherever that pointed.

The obvious fix would have been wrong. cert_probe.ip_is_blocked already
exists and refuses loopback, private, link-local, reserved, multicast and
anything non-global; applying it here would not harden this feature, it would
delete it. The deployment probe exists to check the operator's OWN servers,
and those are routinely 10.0.0.5, an internal IIS, or loopback behind a
reverse proxy. That policy answers "is this a safe public endpoint to probe",
which is the discovery question and not this one.

deployment_target_refusal answers this one: it refuses what is never a server
an operator deploys a certificate to — link-local, where the cloud metadata
endpoints live, multicast, and the unspecified address — and permits loopback
and private, because they are the point. Both policies are tested against
each other so nobody unifies them later.

The other half is the resolution: the name is resolved once, checked, and the
connection made to that address, so it cannot answer one way to the check and
another to the connect. A refusal raises ConnectionError, which is what a
closed port already raises, so the route's existing handler reports it as
unreachable with the reason and no caller learns a new shape.

Both legs go through one opener now. They had drifted: direct TLS tunnelled
through HTTPS_PROXY and SMTP-STARTTLS opened a raw socket, so on a host
behind an outbound proxy an HTTPS probe worked and an SMTP one could not
connect at all — the fix for #326 reached one of the two. With a proxy the
guard cannot apply, because the proxy resolves and there is no address to
pin; the opener tunnels and says so rather than pretending.

The probe timeout tests needed the resolution stubbed too. Patching only the
connect left a real DNS lookup inside a unit test, which is a hidden network
dependency — and for a name that does not resolve, a failure about something
else entirely.
