* An IdP demotion ends the sessions it demotes

create_session snapshots the role at mint time, so writing the new role into
the user table changed what the table says and nothing about what the user's
open session could still do. A demoted admin stayed an admin until the
session expired — up to the full session lifetime, on every device they were
already signed in on.

update_user has killed sessions on a role change since it was written ("the
user re-authenticates under the new role, or is blocked"). This is the same
rule on the other path, and it runs outside the settings lock and before the
callback mints the new session, so the login in progress is untouched and
only the user's other sessions end.

Three controls, because the ways to get this wrong are all quiet ones: an
ordinary login that changes nothing must keep its sessions, or authenticating
would sign you out of your other devices; a demotion refused by the
last-active-admin guard must keep them too, since the role did not change and
killing them would log out the only admin over something that did not happen;
and both paths call the same thing.

That last one is why AuthManager gained a public name for it. update_user
reached for the private one because it lives in the same class; crossing
modules for a leading underscore is how a private method becomes an interface
without anyone deciding that it is one.

Three quiet ones: a timing oracle, a cookie flag, a queue reported as a fault (#918)

**A login told you whether a username exists.** Both early returns in
authenticate_user — unknown user, disabled user — answered in microseconds
while a real username paid for bcrypt. Measured on this project's own bench:
180.47 ms against 0.29 ms, a ratio of 628 with no overlap. One request was
enough to learn whether a username exists, a second whether it is disabled;
the rate limiter bounds how fast that can be asked, not whether the answer is
there. Both paths now verify against a decoy hash built once per process, at
the cost factor _hash_password uses, so the two stay in step if that is
tuned. Measured after: 1.01x.

**The session cookie shipped without Secure whenever the request looked
plain.** `secure=request.is_secure` is a per-request fact, and behind a
TLS-terminating proxy it is False unless BEHIND_PROXY wires ProxyFix — so an
operator who declared HTTPS still got a session cookie without Secure while
their users were on HTTPS. factory.py already computes exactly that decision
for Flask's own cookie, with the reasoning beside it; both hand-rolled cookie
sites read it now, falling back to request.is_secure when nothing was
declared.

Not simply `secure=True`: a browser REFUSES a Secure cookie over plain HTTP,
so on an install with no HTTPS signal that would not harden anything, it
would stop anyone logging in. The False cases are tested for that reason.

**A busy domain was reported as a renewal failure.**
DomainOperationInProgress landed in the sweep's generic handler, so a domain
whose lock was held by a manual renewal or a reissue drove a failure metric,
an audit failure entry and a certificate_failed notification — an operator
paged for a queue. Every request-facing caller already distinguishes it and
answers 409. It is `skipped_busy` now, in every shape of the summary and in
the completion log, with no metric, no audit and no notification.

Two tests of mine were weak and were rewritten rather than left: one
recomputed the cookie decision in its own body instead of reading it from a
real app, and carried an `or True` that could not fail; the other stubbed a
CertificateManager that died on an attribute the sweep never reaches, which
says nothing about the branch under test.

comment says it outright — "SSE holds 1 thread per browser tab; 4 was too
few". subscribe() appended to an unbounded list (20,000 registered in 0.08s
without complaint) and stream() was `while True`, so nine tabs left nothing
to answer an ordinary request with and the instance stopped responding with
nothing wrong.

Four concurrent streams now, and each ends after fifteen minutes: EventSource
reconnects on its own, so the close is invisible and the thread comes back.
Both are needed — a cap alone would have let the first four tabs of the
morning own the pool until someone closed them. Past the cap the route
answers 503 with Retry-After, which is "come back", not "something broke".

counter only when _ingest_new SUCCEEDED, while the crt.sh fetch inside it
happened either way. Measured before: a cap of 5 against a client whose every
fetch failed issued 1000 requests and reported truncated: False — the 2s
min_request_interval throttles the rate and bounds nothing. Measured after: 5

so it reported zero requests for a run that had not happened yet, and would

* A refusal that names itself, and two answers that were being discarded

**A cleared Timeout box was a 500.** `_validate_hook` did
int(hook.get('timeout', DEFAULT_TIMEOUT)) with nothing around it, and the
shipped UI binds x-model.number — Alpine emits null for an empty numeric
input. int(None) raises, the route's blanket handler turned it into 500
"Failed to save deploy config", and clearing a field was a server error with
no clue.

Absence and error are now different answers, which is the distinction
save_config already draws for `enabled`: a cleared field takes the default,
as on_events and enabled do beside it, and a value that is PRESENT and not a
number is refused by name — "hook 'reload' timeout must be a number".

**A missing certificate was a 422.** renew_certificate raised
FileNotFoundError inside its try and the catch-all re-wrapped every exception
as RuntimeError, so the `except FileNotFoundError` arm in
resources_lifecycle.py — which returns 404 — was dead code, and an operator
asking to renew something that is not there was told the CA had refused.
Measured on a real manager: RuntimeError("Exception: No certificate found
for domain: ..."). FileNotFoundError and DomainOperationInProgress pass
through now; everything else is still wrapped, which is what the catch-all is
for.

**A hook that backgrounded anything was a timeout.** capture_output=True
makes subprocess wait for EOF on the pipes, and a backgrounded grandchild
inherits them — so `curl ... &` was reported as "timeout after Ns" although
the direct child had exited at once. Measured with a 2s timeout: `sleep 6 &`
timed out with pipes and returned in 0.01s with files, while `sleep 6` —
genuinely slow, not detached — still times out both ways. That control is the
point: this stops the timeout firing on a process that has already exited, it
does not remove the timeout.

MockShellExecutor now writes its canned output to the files it is handed. A
double that answers only through the returned object does not stand in for a
process writing to a file, and three tests went red holding output the code
no longer reads — a double that does not honour the contract hides whatever
depends on it.

Three of my own probes were wrong and are recorded as such: the DeployManager
constructor takes the executor as its second positional, not a keyword; and
two hook probes used `;` and `>`, which the command guard refuses — so they
measured the guard, not the timeout. What the guard actually permits is
pinned now, and the two rows that matter sit next to each other: `&` is
allowed, `> /dev/null` is not, which is exactly why "it timed out" was the
only answer an operator could get.

What a scoped key may read in the activity feed (#922)

/api/activity takes the viewer role and returns audit entries, and it had no
scope filter. Every neighbouring route that returns domain-bearing data has
one: CertificateList.get filters, and Settings.get was given the filter by
audit finding M4, whose words were "a scoped API key could therefore
enumerate every domain the host had ever issued a cert for, regardless of
scope". The activity feed is the same disclosure by another door, and it was
the route left without it.

Measured before: a viewer key scoped to tenant-a.example.com read
tenant-b's domain out of the feed.

The fix is the filter, not the role. Raising the route to admin would remove
a feature — that page is built for the read-only role and is the only window
a viewer has on what is happening — while leaving the real problem in place,
because the problem is not "a viewer reads the audit" but "a key restricted
to one tenant reads another". A single-tenant install never had the first;
a multi-tenant one has the second even between two administrators.

Instance-level entries are withheld from a scoped key too: a login, a
settings change, a backup. A key restricted to one tenant has no claim on
which administrator signed in or from where. It still sees the administrator
and the address on its OWN tenant's entries, deliberately — that entry is
about its domain, and withholding it would leave the feed unable to say who
did what to the thing the key is scoped to.

An entry's domain is `details.domain`, or `resource_id` for `certificate`
entries only — the one resource type whose id IS a domain. On a login
`resource_id` is a username and on a backup a filename, and reading either as
a domain would let a scope pattern match by accident.

Both paths of the route are filtered. A filter on the recent-entries path
alone is a filter that can be walked around by adding a query parameter.

Scoping applies to API keys; a session and a local user carry no
allowed_domains, so no dashboard user loses anything.

A probe that can reach out, and a sweep that runs once (#923)

**Nothing but the deployment probe honoured HTTPS_PROXY.** #326 taught that one
to tunnel with HTTP CONNECT. Four other things that dial a host kept opening raw
sockets, and a raw socket does not read those variables at all: the deep TLS
probe (the inventory sweep, and POST /api/probe), the OCSP/CRL fetch behind
every revocation answer, the HSTS/header check, and the TLS 1.0/1.1 check. On a
host whose only route out is a proxy, a scan reported every endpoint
unreachable, every revocation unavailable and every header check unknown.

One opener decides the transport now, and the order matters: a target that
resolves to a non-global address is dialled directly whatever the environment
says, because no outbound proxy serves 10.0.0.5 and routing it through one
would break a probe that works today; otherwise the proxy where one applies;
otherwise the pinned address, as before. The SSRF guard runs first either way,
so what the caller resolved still decides whether the connection happens at
all. Through a tunnel there is no address to pin — the proxy resolves the name
itself — and that is now written where the opposite was claimed. The docs also
gained the second exception nobody had written down: WHOIS on port 43 cannot go
through an HTTP proxy, while RDAP can.

**A scan could start on top of a running one.** The scheduler kept its four
jobs apart with one file lock each; POST /api/inventory/scan calls the managers
directly and went past all of it. Two clicks, or a click landing on a scheduled
run, probed every endpoint twice and asked crt.sh, the registries and the
blocklists at twice the rate each paces itself for.

The guard is in the sweeps, not in the endpoint, because the endpoint is not
the only caller: a guard on the route would have stopped two clicks and let a
click overlap a scheduled run, while looking like it had stopped both. It
answers in the vocabulary the summaries already use — skipped + reason — with
already_running beside disabled, and the endpoint answers 409 with every leg's
summary still in the body. The Scan button swallowed any non-200; it now says
why nothing happened.

Renewal timing the CA can move, not only a number we picked (#926)

CertMate renews at `days_left <= renewal_threshold_days`, default 30 — the
same opinion for every certificate and every CA. RFC 9773 lets the CA publish
its own, per certificate: a `renewalInfo` endpoint answering a window during
which it wants that certificate replaced.

The TLS renewal sweep now asks. For every certificate the threshold has NOT
already called due, it fetches the CA's window and renews now if the window
says so. That is how an instance learns about a batch replacement — a
mis-issuance, a compromised intermediate, a CA/Browser Forum ruling — days
before the revocation lands rather than when the certificate stops working.

**It can only bring a renewal forward.** ARI is consulted only after the
threshold has declined, so nothing here can delay a renewal, and a CA that is
down, slow or wrong cannot push a certificate towards expiry. Every absence
falls back to the threshold. A test reads that ordering off the call site,
because it is the whole safety argument and an edit could reverse it without
failing anything else.

Within the window one point is chosen from the certificate's own identifier:
the same on every sweep, and different per certificate, which is the spread
RFC 9773 asks for.

**Why this did not wait for #103.** `acme` 3.3.0 has no ARI method and
certbot is 2.10.0, which is why #393 was filed as a child of the certbot 5.x
migration. But ARI is an unauthenticated GET that only informs *when*:
issuance stays where it is. The dependency was read the wrong way round.

The encoding was verified against Let's Encrypt production rather than
against a reading of the RFC — a wrong identifier and a pruned certificate
both answer 404, so only a live certificate proves it. That check is in the
suite, marked `network`.

`ari_enabled: false` turns it off. The sweep summary counts `ari_advanced`.

Deliberately not done: letting ARI defer a renewal past the threshold. That
half matters for short-lived certificates and arrives with #395.

The composition root moves above the layers it composes (#928)

`modules/core/factory.py` imported `modules.api` and `modules.web` to register
them on the Flask app — the one upward edge in the system, which
docs/architecture.md drew and argued for: a composition root has to know what
it composes, and the alternatives are a layer that constructs its own
dependencies or a registry hiding the same edge behind indirection.

The argument was sound and the conclusion was not. A composition root does not
have to live *inside* one of the layers it composes. It is
`modules/factory.py` now, and `modules/core/` imports neither layer above it.

**The cycle was one function wide.** `api/client_certificates.py` imported
`error_code_for_status` back from the root, closing core -> api -> core
through the composition root itself. Deriving NOT_FOUND from 404 has nothing
to do with composing an application; it is `modules/core/http_errors.py`.

**The landmine was the path anchoring.** `resolve_state_directories` derives
the certificate, data, backup and log directories from
`Path(__file__).parent.parent.parent` — three levels up from the old
location. One level higher, three levels up is the directory ABOVE the
checkout: every default path would have moved silently, and an upgraded
instance would have come up unable to find a single certificate. Three anchors
in the source and seven in tests, one of which failed on its CONTENT rather
than on an import — "booting the application left a certificate beside the
previous key", because it had booted against an empty tree.

`tests/test_the_layers_point_one_way.py` keeps the direction, for all three
packages and both import spellings — including `from . import x`, which is how
a deferred upward import gets added without even showing up as a circular
import. Not hypothetical: that form is the one the first pass missed, and it
took create_app out entirely.

`test_the_composition_root_is_the_only_upward_import` asserted the exception.
It is now `test_the_diagram_is_right_that_every_arrow_points_down`, borrowing
the enumeration from the new file rather than carrying a second copy.

`ZombieScanner.check_domain` turned `*.example.com` into `example.com` and
probed that. A wildcard does not cover its own apex (RFC 6125), so the apex is
frequently a name that resolves to nothing or serves nothing while every host
the certificate protects is up — and the scanner reported `zombie`, which is
its word for "delete this".

`scan_certificate` read `deployment_port` and ignored `deployment_host`, the

fixed in #207/#381; this is the same refusal with the same word.

asserted `check_domain('*.wildcard.com') == 'alive'` and
`mock_dns.assert_called_with('wildcard.com', None)` — the apex resolved, and
the certificate called alive on that basis. The assertion was about the
mechanism rather than the meaning, and the mechanism was the defect.

Two things beside it, the same shape: a scan that CRASHED was reported as
`zombie`, so the scanner's own failure became a statement about the estate;
and the README described this feature in five languages as a "filesystem
scanner to identify and clean up orphan certificates", which is not what it
does.

anywhere". True of templates/static/mcp, and the conclusion was wrong — it is

One way to write a date (#940) (#947)

The activity feed printed `08/09/2026` on one line and `8 set, 16:23` on
the next, for the same event. `set` is `settembre`: the second followed
the BROWSER's locale, in an interface that is entirely in English — it is
the documentation this project translates, not the application — and the
first was numeric, which is 8 September or 9 August depending on a
convention the page never states.

Twenty-one call sites formatted a date. Five pinned `en-US` and sixteen
took whatever the browser had, and client-certs.js did both four lines
apart. There was no decision, only two habits, and neither is visible
from an en-US machine — which is why it survived.

Two decisions, and only one of them is about locale.

Named months, never numeric: `08/09/2026` is ambiguous in every locale,
and "Sep 8, 2026" cannot be read two ways.

Pinned to `en-US`, because a date in the reader's language inside an
English interface is an inconsistency rather than a courtesy, and because
a screenshot in a bug report should show what everyone else sees. The
TIME ZONE stays local — an operator wants their own clock — so only the
language is fixed. And the clock is 24-hour, stated rather than
inherited: `en-US` would render "04:27 PM" next to log lines, while the
Italian these sites fell into was already giving 16:27. Keep what was
being read, lose only the ambiguity.

Four shapes, because four things are being said: a day, a moment, an
audited moment (seconds order two entries in the same minute), and a
clock reading. An unparseable value formats as empty rather than as
"Invalid Date", which in a table reads as data.

The rule is derived: nothing outside certmate.js may call
toLocale...String. The exemption list is what is hand-written, and its
"still earned" test rejected my own first entry — the vendored ReDoc
bundle contains `toLocaleString` only as a STRING in a polyfill's list of
property names, never as a call, so exempting it was a reason written for
nothing.

Mutation: a page formatting its own kills the derived rule; the locale
falling back to the browser kills the stated-once check; and the clock
going back to 12-hour is caught ONLY by the test that executes it, since
the source still reads `hour12: false` either way.

An identity you cannot edit away (#950) (#956)

A webhook now keeps its secrets when you rename it.

Masked secrets are put back on save by matching the submission to the entry
already on disk, and the match was `(type, name)` — the two fields an operator
edits. So renaming a webhook, or changing its type, meant the save could not
find the entry the secrets belonged to and dropped them. The webhook stayed
`enabled`, lost its URL, its bearer token and every custom header, the save
answered 200, and nothing on screen said so, because the URL is never
displayed. Reproduced on a live instance: `200 {"message":"Notification

delivered.

save: assigning at save would leave exactly one unprotected save, the first
after upgrading, and that is the save someone makes to fix a name.

a client that returns a shape it did not receive both keep the behaviour they
had. Nothing gets worse for anyone.

positive claim about which entry this is; falling back would hand a submission
whatever secret happens to share its name, which is the cross-endpoint leak the
identity scheme exists to prevent.

Akamai Edge DNS waits long enough, and the wait is editable (#974) (#997)

CertMate passed --edgedns-propagation-seconds 90, from its settings default
and its strategy default alike; the Akamai plugin's own default is 180 and its
docs suggest 240. Edge DNS takes minutes to reach all of its authoritative
nameservers, which is where Let's Encrypt looks, and a reporter on Akamai saw
nearly every order fail with 'Some challenges have failed'.

- The default is 180. Every install that ever saved its settings has the old
  default stored, so a stored edgedns 90 in a file last written by 2.40.0 or
  older is moved to 180 once and written back; after the first save by a

Setup mode only bootstraps: the first admin closes it, and nothing that outlives it runs (#1001)

Setup mode serves every caller as admin until a credential exists, so a fresh
instance can be bootstrapped. It now:

- closes with the first admin: creating it also enables local auth, and the
  response says so. Setup used to take two requests, and an instance whose
  second one never came stayed open while its operator believed it had an
  admin. The setup page skips the second step when the server took it; an
  admin left over from an earlier half-finished run still completes the old
  way.
- refuses its anonymous admin, with 409 SETUP_BOOTSTRAP_ONLY, deploy-hook
  changes, tests and runs, certificate and key downloads, and backup
  creation and download. One list, at the point where the setup identity is
  granted, so a new route cannot forget it. Restore and upload stay allowed:
  that is how an instance is recovered onto a fresh host.

Contract 2.31 -> 2.32 (new answers to existing requests, counted as a
security fix on the 2.7 precedent); docs/api.md.

Test harness: the shared e2e container now runs with an operator bearer token,
like any instance past its first minutes, because the release gate's
real-certificate tests downloaded certificates anonymously from a setup-mode
container. A browser-only session keeps a tokenless container, since the UI
suite bootstraps like a person does. The tests about setup mode itself build
their own in-process instances. #862's tests follow the one-request setup.

docs/deploy-hooks.md said references to CertMate's sensitive files are
'rejected outright'. The check matches the names as written: a glob
(settings*), a ? wildcard or a name split by quotes (settings"."json) get

says so and why (only an admin can save or run a hook, and an admin can

private*key and .pem as blocked, which has not been true since certificate
